cnn.com.title: Alberta rejects secession referendum, chooses to remain part of Canada, CBC projects
cnn.com.text: The oil-rich province of Alberta has rejected the pathway to secession and will remain part of Canada, public broadcaster and CNN newsgathering partner CBC News projected Monday. Alberta, a province roughly the size of Texas, has long harbored a fringe independence movement. Separatists there argue that Canada’s federal system underrepresents its population of 5 million in parliament, that Canadian efforts to fight climate change threaten Alberta’s lucrative fossil fuel industry and that Alberta’s conservative politics are often outweighed by the more liberal eastern provinces. Though separation frequently polled low in Alberta, the movement grew louder after Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal Party won the 2025 federal elections amid a trade war with the United States. In May, Alberta’s Premier Danielle Smith announced that the province would hold a referendum on whether to remain in Canada, or to have a “binding provincial referendum” on independence later. Smith, though not a separatist herself, has previously cautioned against “demonizing” independence supporters. “We have had, from time to time, these kinds of initiatives flare up,” Smith told CNN in 2025. “And they’re almost always in response to a federal government that’s out of control. But they have all subsided when the federal government got back in its own lane.” Carney, who grew up in Alberta, nodded to that frustration in a speech in Calgary last week urging voters to reject secession. “The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Carney said. But, the prime minister said, separation would only “burden” Albertans “with years of deep division and great uncertainty.” Canada’s deteriorating relationship with the US also hung heavy over the referendum. Some separatists believe that the US would be a better partner to Alberta than Canada, a notion that was championed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent  and the movement possesses a Trumpian flavor. At one secessionist rally CNN attended in 2025, some participants wore red MAGA-style “Make Alberta Great Again” hats. A minority even said that Alberta ought to skip independence and become the 51st US state. Earlier this year, secessionist leaders met with US officials in Washington to try and negotiate support from US President Donald Trump’s administration. Jeffrey Rath, a prominent separatist and lawyer who was part of the group in DC, told CNN last year that Trump’s election in 2024 gave independence activists hope. “If anybody is going to have the guts to recognize an independent Alberta, (it) would be the Trump administration,” Rath said. News of the meetings at the time incensed Canadian politicians, who accused separatist leaders of “treason.” “It is completely inappropriate to seek to weaken Canada,” said British Columbia Premier David Eby, “to seek to go and ask for assistance to break up this country from a foreign power.” Last week, Carney made an oblique swipe at the US in his speech. “This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” Carney said in Calgary. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.” Monday’s vote was the first plebiscite of its kind in Canada since the 1995 Quebec referendum, where the predominantly French-speaking province narrowly voted against secession. This is a developing story and will be updated.

cnn.com.title: Trump uses antisemitic term ‘Shylock’ while defending Sen. Marshall’s lawsuits against his patients over medical bills
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump used an antisemitic term as he​ defended Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall against criticism over medical billing practices Monday​, a slur he has used publicly at least once before. Trump invoked the term “Shylock” while defending Marshall’s​ suing more than 700 patients for outstanding medical bills during his time as an obstetrician-gynecologist, as first reported by The New York Times. “You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people, and they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” Trump said at a rally in Kansas. “If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law. He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability.” Trump has previously faced criticism for using the term.​ In July 2025, he  said it during a rally in Iowa. He later claimed he didn’t know the word was viewed by some as antisemitic. “I’ve never heard it that way. To me, Shylock is somebody that’s a money lender at high rates,” Trump told reporters at the time. “I’ve never heard it that way, you view it differently than me. I’ve never heard that.” The Anti-Defamation League last year condemned the use of the word by Trump, calling it “very troubling and irresponsible.” “It underscores how lies and conspiracies about Jews remain deeply entrenched in our country. Words from our leaders matter and we expect more from the President of the United States,” the ADL wrote in a post at the time. In 2014, former President Joe Biden apologized for using the word.

cnn.com.title: She made an anti-war drawing as a child in Russia. Four years on, she’s still living with the fallout
cnn.com.text: Masha Moskalyova has spent a quarter of her life in jeopardy or on the run because of a picture she drew when she was just 12 years old. Four years on, she and her father are living in hiding in a small village in eastern France and still worry about their safety. One of the few things they still have of their former lives in Russia is the drawing itself. “Even though it’s a child’s drawing and seems so simple, who could have expected it to have such consequences?” Masha says, as we consider the drawing together. Drawn in colored pencil, it shows a mother protecting her child from the bombs being launched from Russia. A Ukrainian flag reads “Glory to Ukraine,” while a Russian flag beside says, “No Putin, no war.” She drew it just a few weeks after Russia had invaded Ukraine in 2022. In her hometown of Yefremov, about 300 kilometers (185 miles) south of Moscow and about halfway to the border with Ukraine, Masha’s teacher had asked the class to draw pictures supporting Russian troops. Most of the children drew tanks, or the letter Z, used by Russia as a pro-war symbol. Masha, who is now 16, decided to do something else. “I drew the situation as I actually saw it, what I believed to be the truth,” she says. “After the lesson, one of my classmates, who had seen the drawing, came up to me. Perhaps she was the one who reported it, leading to everything that followed. In any case, the drawing ended up in the hands of the police. And that was when all our problems began.” Shortly after that her father, Alexey Moskalyov, was charged with “discrediting the Russian military” and sentenced to two years in a penal colony. Masha, whom he’d been raising alone, was sent to an orphanage. After his release, the pair fled, traveling through Armenia and onto France, where they arrived earlier this year and where they have been given a temporary visa. A dog that Masha had been given in the orphanage has now arrived from Armenia, which she is pleased about. Still, what’s striking is how alone they seem, with nothing of their former lives and only each other for company. Alexey’s health is fragile because of his time in jail and Masha is now schooled in a language she doesn’t speak. Both fear for their safety. But Alexey says he is just proud of his daughter. “Everything I’ve lost, everything I had in Russia, is compensated for by the fact that we can now speak freely and tell the truth,” he says. “By the fact that we are now in a country where people are not persecuted for their words or their opinions.” And words are exactly what Masha intends to keep using. Outside of school, Masha spends her time trying to reach audiences inside Russia and beyond, through YouTube and social media. And her criticism now extends to US President Donald Trump’s handshake with his Russian counterpart. “I want to say that what Trump is doing is terrible,” she tells CNN. “The fact that the president of a free country shakes hands with a murderer,” she says, holding Russian President Vladimir Putin responsible for the deaths caused by the war in Ukraine. “The fact that you could say he is being controlled by him is another matter altogether.” Going home remains a distant prospect. “I would return to Russia with enormous joy,” Masha says. “But when will this regime change? I don’t know. How many decades will it take? How many decades before Russia becomes a democratic and free country?” It is hard to fathom that a single child’s drawing could have angered the Russian authorities as much as this one did, but Masha seems to get it. After all, the point of authoritarianism is that it cannot allow any dissent, however childish. “Here was a child who spoke the truth, who wasn’t afraid,” she says. “And if that child isn’t alone, if there are many children like her, if it’s not just one teenager but a thousand teenagers, not just one adult but a million, then that is what will change Russia for the better.” The last four years have clearly taken their toll on Masha, who seems mature beyond her years and graver than any 16-year-old should be. Perhaps the most surprising thing is that after everything she has endured – being sent to the orphanage, her father’s incarceration and their time on the road – she still has the drawing in her possession. It was as they were preparing to flee their home that she found it on a shelf by chance, among her childhood notebooks. “It hadn’t been confiscated,” she says. “They hadn’t found it or paid any attention to it. Perhaps because the police hadn’t thought to search through a child’s belongings.” So, today, one of Masha’s only belongings from her former life is the very drawing that ended it.

cnn.com.title: As midterms loom, Democrats learn to speak a new language: American
cnn.com.text: “I’m a border security Democrat.” With five words at a CNN and Jubilee Town Hall last week, Texas Senate candidate James Talarico sought to dodge the stigma of the Biden administration’s failure to secure the southern border. Talarico is one of a crop of Democratic midterm election candidates choosing language that pivots away from past election failures. For future political viability, the Democratic Party must reclaim voters alienated by its perceived contempt for politically and culturally more conservative Americans — including those who were once the foundation of its blue-collar base but defected to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement. One way to do this is to craft messaging on issues like affordability that connect with working Americans and highlight the link between Trump’s decisions — like the Iran war — and the cost of groceries, gasoline and housing. Democrats also face a linguistic minefield as they try to again talk like the voters they want to attract without angering the party’s new base of more liberal urban and highly educated voters. In recent years, Democratic messaging has often seemed academic, esoteric, politically correct or choked with jargon. Terms like “unhoused people” and “birthing people” were adopted to include and respect people who are marginalized or vulnerable. Such language shows regard for the humanity and individual rights of others. But it has sometimes obscured meaning and baffled people who are not deeply political, or turned away voters with more conservative values. In some cases, Republicans have used Democratic language to drive a wedge between the party and persuadable voters and to suggest it has tacked to the left. The most hard-hitting ad of the 2024 election season attacked Democratic nominee Kamala Harris over transgender issues, telling voters that “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.” The term “defund the police” became a national slogan after the murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. Republicans soon co-opted it to argue that Democrats were weak on law and order — a narrative that circulated for several elections, even though senior party members like former President Joe Biden publicly repudiated it and its policy implications. And in one of the most notorious examples of loose language haunting Democrats, 2016 nominee Hillary Clinton suggested some Trump fans belonged in a “basket of deplorables” — handing MAGA a rallying cry to underscore Trump’s claim that establishment elites viewed his voters with disgust. ‘I understand why you voted for Trump’ One reason — apart from Trump’s unpopularity — why Democrats are competitive in more states than expected during this year’s midterms is that they’ve selected candidates who sound like their states. In North Carolina, Senate nominee Roy Cooper has developed a colloquial way to argue he’d “Make Stuff Cost Less.” He appears to be rebuilding the broadened coalition that made him governor twice in a reliably Republican state. Talarico speaks the language of faith in pious Texas to distinguish himself from progressive Democrats. His “border security Democrat” phrase balances his support for both a hard border and a softer immigration purge that would target only undocumented criminals rather than “small business owners, grandmothers and infants.” In Iowa, which Trump won by double digits only two years ago, Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek brands himself a “prairie populist” and tells voters, “I understand why you voted for Trump” before he lambasts the president for raising costs and starting the kind of war he vowed never to fight. In Maine, Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson refused to apologize for telling Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during a debate. The incumbent Republican suggested he was guilty of sexism. But Jackson, a former logger, turned the conceit of supposed establishment contempt for working people against his opponent. He said on CNN’s “State of the Union” Sunday that, “What I’m not going to be is talked down to by Senator Collins.” Jackson added: “I’m fighting for Mainers. And, I mean, I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me.” Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has meanwhile developed his own searing linguistic critique of Trump that links alleged White House corruption to the economic struggles of millions of Americans. “Under the failed president Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home,” Ossoff said at a rally earlier this month. “They promised to drain the swamp. Instead, it’s the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it.” Of course, Democrats have one big advantage that facilitates their linguistic balancing act: It’s far easier to find language to attack an incumbent Republican president over high prices and economic insecurity than it was for the party to defend the Biden administration for its struggles on the same issues in 2024. And a party that failed to take advantage of a president who boasts about an economic “golden age” when Americans are paying $4.30 for gasoline and dread their grocery bills would be guilty of gross political incompetence. ‘Talk like a normal human’ In August 2025, the moderate think tank Third Way published a memo warning that the while Democrats spent “billions of dollars trying to find the perfect language to connect to voters” they used “an awful lot of words and phrases no ordinary person would ever dream of saying.” The memo concluded that “the effect of this language is to sound like the extreme, divisive, elitist, and obfuscatory, enforcers of wokeness. To please the few, we have alienated the many—especially on culture issues, where our language sounds superior, haughty and arrogant.” In the wreckage of another defeat to Trump, some top Democrats agreed. Former Obama administration White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, told CNN’s Michael Smerconish a year ago that in 2024, the party allowed itself to be framed as “culturally, not only distant, but culturally isolated from where the general public is.” Emanuel added: “You have to build a winning coalition, which means it has to be big. It has to be broad, and other voters have to be respected, something elements of our party don’t do. They like to lecture people to be exactly like them.” Another possible Democratic presidential candidate, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, has been striking similar notes this year. He said at a dinner in Michigan that he was a “pro-diversity” governor but that to win, Democrats needed to “talk like a normal human.” He criticized terms like “food insecure” for hungry and “justice-involved population” instead of prison inmates. “Sometimes these terms make it feel like we’re talking down to people, like we’re talking at them, instead of to them,” Beshear said. Matt Bennett, executive vice president of public affairs at Third Way, said Democrats this year were doing a better job of finding ways to connect with voters. “For the most part, we’re delighted with the people that have won their primaries and the races that they’re running, and they seem very well suited,” he said, pointing especially to the example of Cooper, who has prospered in a state that last voted Democrat for president in 2008. “He has done what it takes to win the trust of these voters.” The general election campaign has been kinder to Democrats so far than primary season, which threw up several viral moments quickly seized upon by Republicans to portray Democrats as extremists. In an interview with Fox News, Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Megan Romer advocated abolishing the Senate, replacing the presidency and the Supreme Court, and defunding the Pentagon. She said prisons could be abolished under long-term plans, along with national borders. The encounter ran on a loop on conservative media for days as the GOP tried to define all Democrats by association. But Republicans are now creating their own viral moments with language that seems deliberately aimed at excluding citizens and groups. Trump has been inciting Islamophobia in the crudest and most inflammatory terms by mocking the name of Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayedand falsely calling him a jihadist. On Monday, Vice President JD Vance suggested that a protester — a person of color who shouted that he was an American citizen — must have crossed the border illegally. Democrats may not be the only party with a language problem.

cnn.com.title: Vance declines to endorse Netanyahu’s reelection bid, breaking with Trump
cnn.com.text: Vice President JD Vance on Monday declined to say whether he endorses Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection, after President Donald Trump recently threw his support behind the Israeli prime minister. “I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterm,” Vance said in an interview with journalist Mark Halperin aboard Air Force Two. “I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections.” Yet, Vance traveled to Budapest, Hungary, earlier this year to support Trump-endorsed Victor Orbán ahead of his election, which the longtime prime minister lost. Vance said he wasn’t for or against endorsing Netanyahu. “I’m not anti-endorsing him. I’m not pro-endorsing him. I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said. Trump had also previously held off endorsing Netanyahu. “I’m not involved in [Israeli] politics anymore,” Trump told Time earlier this month. But Trump gave his full-throated endorsement Saturday for Netanyahu, calling him a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” in a post on social media. Vance’s apparent break from Trump in declining to endorse the prime minister comes just days before Israel’s election and as US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth traveled to Israel in an unannounced trip, according to two sources familiar and a US official. Hegseth met Monday evening with Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, according to an Israeli source familiar with the details and another source familiar.

cnn.com.title: The Trump team’s disdain for judicial orders is blowing up in court. Accountability has been slow in coming
cnn.com.text: A federal judge raked President Donald Trump’s administration over the coals on Monday in a case involving his plans to renovate a public golf course in Washington, DC. After the administration cut down more than 430 trees without properly notifying US District Judge Ana Reyes, she said last week she was “furious” and issued a court order to stop it. Then, after Trump on Sunday said construction would begin “immediately” despite the judge’s order, she forced officials to testify on Monday and sought to highlight the apparent unwillingness of Justice Department lawyers to vouch for the administration’s claims in court. All of this comes as the administration accuses the judge of “egregious” behavior and seeks to remove her from the case. It’s been quite the scene. But it’s also been a long time coming. Reyes’ exasperated displays come after a series of similar examples of the administration flouting and even violating court orders. District judges like Reyes ruled that the administration had violated court orders in at least 31 lawsuits over 15 months, according to an Associated Press investigation in May. That’s in addition to more than 250 other examples of noncompliance that judges have found related to immigration cases. And the judges finding these violations are often Republican-nominated ones. Any one of these examples could be understood as a mistake or a mishap. But the growing volume of them — along with Trump and those around him often speaking openly about violating court orders, as Trump did Sunday — suggest there’s something more going on. (A whistleblower last year also claimed that a top DOJ official explicitly spoke about the possible need to ignore court orders.) At the same time, there’s been no accountability that is seeming to make the administration change its approach. Because this just keeps happening. Let’s recap some of the high-profile examples of the administration flouting or violating court orders, and what became of them. The government funding freeze Mere weeks into Trump’s second term, a federal judge in Rhode Island found the administration had violated a court order by failing to un-freeze many of the federal grants it blocked after he ordered it to do so. The conclusion: The judge opted not to hold the administration in contempt of court, but he did issue a warning. He quoted from a 1975 Supreme Court ruling that said: “Persons who make private determinations of the law and refuse to obey an order generally risk criminal contempt even if the order is ultimately ruled incorrect.” The Alien Enemies Act flights US District Judge James Boasberg ordered the administration to turn around planes that were deporting migrants to a notorious prison in El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act. But the flights continued. The conclusion: Boasberg initiated contempt hearings, saying that “probable cause exists to find the Government in criminal contempt.” But after a lengthy process that included plenty of stops and starts, two Trump-nominated judges on a divided appeals court ended the inquiry and called it a “clear abuse of discretion.” Kilmar Abrego Garcia US District Judge Paula Xinis found the administration had engaged in “willful and intentional noncompliance” with her orders related to the deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whom the administration wrongfully deported to El Salvador, later charged criminally and tried to deport again. The conclusion: Xinis also repeatedly floated possible contempt. But eventually, in June 2025, Abrego Garcia was returned, despite the administration having previously claimed it didn’t have the power to make that happen. Third-country deportations Around the same time, US District Judge Brian Murphy of Massachusetts said that the administration’s rapid third-country deportations of migrants despite his injunction were “unquestionably violative of this court’s order.” He also accused the administration of manufacturing chaos and trying to evade court orders. The conclusion: Murphy said he would leave the contempt question “for another day,” but he didn’t proceed with such an inquiry. The many immigration orders Other judges have found hundreds of instances of immigration authorities failing to comply with immigration-related court orders. Patrick Schiltz, the GOP-nominated chief US district judge in Minnesota, said he found more than 200 such instances. The conclusion: Schiltz at one point took the extraordinary step of summoning Todd Lyons, then the acting director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and threatening him with contempt. But Schiltz canceled the contempt hearing after ICE complied with an order to release a wrongly detained man from Ecuador. The media ban Despite a court order blocking Trump from barring media outlets whose coverage he didn’t like, including CNN, from the White House grounds, those journalists were initially unable to access the grounds. And Trump has since then barred CNN from traveling with him on Air Force One. The conclusion: The access to the grounds was soon restored as the case proceeds. The access on Air Force One wasn’t explicitly mentioned in the court order, and the White House has continued to block CNN from boarding on its assigned pool days. The political ads Despite another federal judge ruling that the administration had to cancel all future airings of Trump’s controversial taxpayer-funded political ads, the administration was again slow to comply. The ads aired hundreds more times, CNN reported last week. The conclusion: A Justice Department lawyer apologized “to the court and the plaintiffs,” and no further legal action has been taken. The young deportees Trump-appointed US District Judge Stephanie Gallagher of Maryland has found that ICE wrongfully deported more than 50 unaccompanied minors who had blanket court orders barring their removal. And in a separate case, she found it twice wrongfully deported an asylum-seeker to El Salvador, in violation of three court orders. The conclusion: These two examples appear to be the only ones in which a judge has found the administration in contempt. Gallagher held the administration in contempt for the first one in August, according to Law360, and for the second one a few weeks ago. Despite those two rulings, the administration has flouted or delayed complying with court orders in three other cases — the media ban, the political ads and now the golf course — since then.

cnn.com.title: GOP attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith come to a head in heated town hall exchange
cnn.com.text: The Muslim Brotherhood has become a flashpoint in Michigan’s Senate race, with Republicans trying to cast Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terror and El-Sayed arguing that he is being unfairly accused of the same “dual loyalties” that former Presidents John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama once were. El-Sayed this weekend denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement founded in Egypt in 1928 — first in a heated exchange with a voter, and later when speaking with reporters — after Republicans have sought to highlight his family’s ties to the group and his past comments about it. “I do want to talk about why they want to make this their closing argument,” El-Sayed told reporters after a rally Sunday in Flint. “They want to speak to a certain implicit dual loyalty. This has a long history in our politics, that notion that people might pray a little bit differently, have a dual loyalty. It was the same thing they did to JFK when he ran for president, the notion that because he was Catholic that he somehow had dual loyalties. They did the same thing to President Obama simply because his father was of Muslim origin, even though his father is an avowed Christian.” He added: “This is nothing new. This is what they do when they have no message about the real issues in people’s lives.” GOP attacks on El-Sayed Republicans have increasingly drawn attention to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith in the closing weeks of one of the most important Senate races on the 2026 midterm election map. President Donald Trump, at a campaign rally Friday night, referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and falsely declared that the Democratic former public health official is a “jihadist.” Those comments have become staples of recent Trump rallies and social media comments. El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, said Sunday on CNN that he has “never called him a terrorist” and said he does not “speak for the president.” But Rogers accused El-Sayed of aligning with the Muslim Brotherhood. The Muslim Brotherhood is an Islamist movement with global offshoots that once wielded significant political power in Egypt, where it was founded. The movement officially rejects the use of violent means to secure its goals. However, offshoots of the group have been linked to attacks in the past. Trump signed an executive order in November that initiated a process by which certain chapters or other subdivisions of the Muslim Brotherhood could be considered for designation as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. “You know, he wants to play the victim. This is not about that. This is about the way you think, not the way you pray,” Rogers told CNN’s Dana Bash. “This is about your ideology and how dangerous it is.” El-Sayed’s town hall exchange The GOP efforts to tie El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, and Islamic extremism, burst into the open this weekend at a town hall in Caro. An attendee repeatedly pressed El-Sayed about the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he had yet to hear the candidate reject the organization. “Abdul, will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?” the man shouted from the crowd. El-Sayed, after disavowing the movement, blasted the man for implicitly assuming his “dual loyalty.” “You assume … that because I am Muslim, that somehow I would have some allegiance to something that is not our Constitution,” El-Sayed said. He later added, “For me, that Constitution is the guiding light.” The audience member walked out after the exchange as the crowd cheered for El-Sayed. Family history scrutinized The GOP attacks come after old tweets from El-Sayed’s half-sister resurfaced online, including a post from 2012 in which she described having “an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.” El-Sayed has said he does not know what his mother was doing in Egypt during the 1970s, explaining he was 3 when his parents divorced and didn’t see his mother for years. He was primarily raised in Michigan by his father and stepmother. El-Sayed in 2012 also signed an open letter supporting then-Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who had been elected earlier that year with the support of the Muslim Brotherhood after the overthrow of the country’s authoritarian government. A year earlier, he penned a Huffington Post op-ed calling on the United States to support young Arab protesters in Egypt, and downplaying concerns that supporting democracy there would lead to Muslim Brotherhood control of the nation. During a recent debate, Rogers pointed out that El-Sayed’s mother worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, a non-profit that the Treasury Department in 2004 designated as an organization supporting terrorism. “Are you going after my mom?” said El-Sayed. “I was going after that organization that was indicted for funneling money to Al Qaeda,” Rogers said. “Look, that’s your mom. My mom worked at a small chamber of commerce. I’ll put my mom up any day for that.” El-Sayed responded he is a “dad and a doctor” who wants to “get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for All.” He said Rogers “wants this to be about anything but his own record.” El-Sayed in recent days also addressed his sister-in-law, Mariam Jukaku, being placed on the federal Terrorism Screening Database — a situation she challenged as part of a 2016 class action lawsuit. It’s not clear why Jukaku, who was once president of UCLA’s Muslim Student Association and is now a home-school teacher and writer in California, was added to the list. “She did nothing wrong and was captured on that and then sued and got off,” El-Sayed told Fox News when asked about his wife’s sister being placed on the terrorist watchlist, which was created in the wake of the September 11, 2001, attacks. “You’ve got this system where folks are guilty until proven innocent because they’ve got different kinds of names, because of the infrastructure that people like Mike Rogers set up.”

cnn.com.title: Trump calls on New Mexico to change its name to ‘New America’
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump on Monday called on New Mexico to change its name to “New America” — the latest example of him seeking geographical name changes that fit his political agenda. “New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!” Trump wrote on Truth Social, shortly before departing the White House for a midterm rally in Kansas. His comments about New Mexico — a blue state he lost by 6 points in 2024 — come as Republicans are anxious about holding their congressional majorities in November, with voters saying in polling that the president isn’t paying enough attention to the country’s most pressing problems. Trump claimed, without citing any evidence, that “home values and incomes would rise” because of a name change. And he repeated his baseless claims about rigged elections by adding, “Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!” Trump has previously suggested renaming New Mexico, although not so forcefully. In September, he posted to social media a map of the state with the word “Mexico” crossed out and “America” written underneath — an image that was reposted by the White House X account. It’s just the latest renaming push from Trump. He signed an executive order in August to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” as part of his ongoing trade war with Canada. He took similar action last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico to “Gulf of America.” The president has also repeatedly floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz the “Trump Strait.” But while Trump has the power to rename what geographic landmarks, such as bodies of water, are called in the Geographic Names Information System, he doesn’t have the constitutional ability to legally rename states. That process would need to happen within the state. New Mexico’s name predates the founding of the United States back to the 16th century, according to a fact sheet on the origin of state names from the Bureau of Indian Affairs. New Mexico Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Monday evening dismissed Trump’s comments. “Let me repeat: New Mexico was New Mexico long before the United States existed and we’ll be New Mexico forevermore,” she wrote in a post on X. Sen. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico wrote in a social post that the state’s name “carries generations of history, culture, and rich traditions that continue to shape who we are.” “We are New Mexicans. We’re proud of our name, proud of our home, and we’re keeping both. Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we’ll still be New Mexico,” he continued.

cnn.com.title: Gangs in Haiti target foreign troops in the biggest attack since a new force began operations
cnn.com.text: Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armored vehicle over the weekend, leaving four soldiers from El Salvador unaccounted for in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operations in the violence-wracked Caribbean country. The attack occurred Sunday in Croix-des-Bouquets, a once-peaceful community in Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, that is now controlled by violent gangs. The armed forces of El Salvador said in a statement Monday that the four aviation technicians were returning to camp when their armored vehicle was attacked with explosives and set on fire. The military noted that the four men managed to flee the burning vehicle and it is working with international forces to “establish contact and determine the location of our military personnel.” Salvadoran authorities said that helicopters were dispatched to the area but they, too, came under fire as they dispersed armed men in the area. “Multiple attempts to approach by land and air have been made, but these have been hampered by the intensity of the fighting,” the Salvadoran military said. The weapons and ammunition gangs are using are not made in Haiti and will continue to find ways to enter the country, Wien-Weibert Arthus, Haiti’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, told the UN Security Council Monday. “This latest episode is a reminder, as if we really needed one, of the fact that the security challenges in Haiti are complex and complicated,” he said. “We hope that those who are missing will be able to go back to their families unscathed.” Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people, a record, across Haiti in recent years, with more than 5,700 people killed or injured from January to mid-September, and more than 230 others kidnapped, according to the UN. A warning from the U.S. Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, condemned the attack during the UN Security Council meeting on Haiti. “We believe the four men survived, but they do remain unaccounted for,” he said. “We will bring you home.” Waltz said that gangs attacked the armored vehicle with “hundreds of bullets and explosives.” “To the gangs and gang leaders who carried out this cowardly attack, if you think you’re going to intimidate this coalition into retreat, you have made a terrible mistake,” he said. The gang suppression force said in a statement that it’s assessing the situation and has advised residents where the attack occurred to remain indoors. “Gangs are testing the gang suppression force,” Jack Christofides, the force’s special representative, said at the UN Monday as he noted that attacks against the force have recently increased. He warned that gangs have carried out reprisal killings in some areas following operations by Haitian and international forces, and that they have pushed deeper into places including the community of Kenscoff and the Artibonite region. “The reality is that we cannot be everywhere at once,” Christofides said. Haiti prepares for an election despite violence The area where the armored vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitelhomme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the UN and the US. Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said that while some gangs have been under pressure since the suppression force was deployed, “others want to show that they can strike back.” “If these soldiers are indeed being held, the groups gain (an) edge to negotiate and to pressure the security forces,” he said. In September 2025, the UN Security Council authorized the 5,550-member force to replace a former Kenya-led multinational force that struggled with a lack of funds and resources as it tried to help Haiti’s National Police quell gang violence. The gang suppression force has more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti, including soldiers from Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala. “The force is making a difference with what it has,” Christofides said, adding that authorities have started to see early signs of reduced gang influence and control in certain areas. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops. It comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade and showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince. Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the UN special envoy to Haiti, said at Monday’s meeting that electoral preparations “have reached an unprecedented level of progress.” He said that more than 35 parties and political groups have registered, along with 3,500 candidates. Among them is former Haitian President Michel Martelly, who was sanctioned in November 2022 by Canada and in August 2024 by the US, which accused him of facilitating drug trafficking and sponsoring multiple gangs.

cnn.com.title: Democratic senator sparks controversy over comments on investigating the Trump administration
cnn.com.text: Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin is drawing criticism from President Donald Trump and other prominent Republicans after suggesting congressional investigations could deter recent graduates from joining the Trump administration. The controversy stemmed from Slotkin’s remarks at a University of Chicago event last week, when she was asked how Congress could reassert its role as a check on the Trump administration. Slotkin said if Democrats regained the majority in Congress, they should look to pass major domestic bills and use their oversight powers to focus on “signature” examples of corruption by the Trump administration, targeting not just the president, but also aides who did his “bidding.” “I wanna look at these signature cases and not just focus on the president but on the people who enabled him,” the Michigan Democrat said. “I want young people coming out of school to say, ‘Should I go work for the Trump administration?’ … I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want. And so let me avoid participating in that.’ I want that deterrence message sent.” The remarks sparked backlash from Republicans, including Trump, who on Monday called Slotkin a “lowlife who’s ruining her state.” “What they’re doing is really discouraging people from going into politics. No, a weaponized government of Democrats, that’s what they’ve done,” Trump said when asked about the senator’s remarks. Sen. Mike Lee accused Slotkin of threatening young, politically inclined Americans. Mike Davis, the head of a conservative legal group, accused her of trying to scare young people away from government and wrote she should “learn about the Second ​Amendment, sweetheart.” Slotkin said Davis, in those comments, was suggesting she be shot, and that it amounted to the mobilization of “death threats” against her and her staff “for sport.” Davis later said, “Elissa Slotkin can pretend she’s the victim all she wants, but she expressly called for the arrest of political opponents to deter their young supporters from public service. That is textbook fascism.” The controversy over the comments comes in the final sprint to the midterm elections with Democrats increasingly optimistic they could win the House and potentially even the Senate. Both parties are already bracing for what is expected to be an outpouring of congressional investigations into the Trump administration if Democrats prevail. A group that identifies itself as the University of Chicago’s “leading student-run conservative & libertarian publication” clipped a portion of Slotkin’s comments in an X post, which has been viewed over 7 million times. In response to that clip, Lee wrote, “It is absolutely disgraceful to threaten young Americans for participating in politics and serving their country.” Slotkin said in response on X that the Utah Republican was “lying about what I said,” and wrote, “spare us the manufactured outrage.” The Michigan senator noted in her post and in an interview with CNN that she was the target of Trump’s Justice Department, which investigated her and other Democratic lawmakers after they posted a video urging service members and intelligence officials to disobey any illegal orders from the administration. “My point is, do not get yourself involved in illegal activity,” she said Monday evening on “The Lead.” “It’s the same thing I was talking about a year ago. Whether you’re the uniformed military or a civilian in government, if you’re being asked to do something by the president or his team that’s illegal, you have a responsibility to reject that. That is my point.” Other Trump administration officials, including Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor, have chastised Slotkin’s comments. “This is incredibly disappointing and unprofessional coming from a US Senator - endorsing political prosecutions to dissuade patriotic Americans from serving their country,” he wrote. “In contrast, we at @USOPM believe in recruiting the best and brightest early career prospects.” This story has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Russian satellite makes possibly unprecedented approach to another spacecraft without permission
cnn.com.text: A rare move by a Russian-made satellite may have brought it within less than a mile of a commercial Earth-observation satellite that may be used to provide national security services to countries such as Ukraine. It’s not clear what, exactly, the Russian satellite, called Kosmos 2612 or Cosmos 2612, intended to accomplish with its close approach. But the behavior was consistent with rendezvous and proximity operations, or maneuvers carried out in orbit that are designed to bring two spacecraft together, said orbital monitoring services company LeoLabs, which tracks space junk and activity in Earth orbit, in a statement. “While the intent remains uncertain, the behavior warrants continued monitoring,” LeoLabs added in the statement. While rendezvousing or docking two vehicles together happens all the time in space — Kosmos 2612’s actions could mark the first time that one spacecraft approached another without permission, noted Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and space analyst, in a post on social media. The observation satellite, called Iceye-X36, is operated by Iceye, a multinational company with offices in the United States, Finland and several other countries across Europe and Asia. The company said in a statement Monday, “We are aware of the situation and tracking it closely. Our constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience.” A spokesperson declined to comment further. Iceye-X36 uses synthetic aperture radar, or SAR, technology, which “enables high resolution imagery to be created night or day, regardless of weather conditions,” according to NASA. Potential objectives Iceye’s satellite constellation has been used to support “the Ukrainian Armed Forces with persistent situational awareness on tactical timelines,” according to a January news release that detailed an expanded agreement between the company and Ukraine. It was not immediately clear whether ICEYE-X36, specifically, was used to support Ukrainian military operations. Iceye declined to comment. Signs that Russian military spacecraft may have been seeking to close in on Iceye-operated satellites have emerged since May, when four Russian-controlled satellites adjusted their orbits to align with Iceye-X36, according to a June report from The Royal United Services Institute, or RUSI, a UK-based defense and security research organization. Then, on October 15, the Kosmos 2612 satellite made a swift approach to Iceye-X36, closing its distance from 350 kilometers (217 miles) to less than 5 kilometers (3 miles) by early morning on October 16, according to LeoLabs. Kosmos 2612 then appeared to hold its distance, “making small adjustments” to “maintain a close relative position” throughout the weekend, LeoLabs said Monday. “Analysis indicates that it approached to within roughly 500 meters during part of the event — however, it’s important to note that exact separation estimates carry uncertainty because of the repeated maneuvers and challenging tracking geometry,” LeoLabs said. CNN has reached out to the Russian Ministry of Defence and Aerospace Forces and Russia’s space agency, Roscosmos, for comment. By Monday, the Kosmos 2612 satellite had begun to move away from Iceye-X36, LeoLabs said. The maneuvers that the Russian vehicle demonstrated could have been used to “inspect, characterize, shadow, or potentially interfere with another spacecraft,” according to the company. “While this event, and the capabilities demonstrated, do not establish hostile intent,” LeoLabs said, “It does, however, demonstrate capabilities that could support intelligence collection, on-orbit inspection, coercive signaling, interference, or preparation for future counterspace operations.” RUSI’s report also detailed several potential objectives that Russia may have by making a close approach with one of Iceye’s satellites. The maneuver could be an intimidation tactic or an attempt to interfere with Iceye’s operations through “jamming,” an interference technique that uses radio noise to prevent satellites from communicating. “The range of options for the protection of the ICEYE satellite are currently limited,” the RUSI report states, “and the defence and protection of satellites presents a famous dilemma.”

cnn.com.title: ‘Tariff Man’ finally found tariffs he doesn’t like
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump loves tariffs so much that during his first term, he nicknamed himself “Tariff Man.” Trump tripled down on tariffs during his second term, lobbing them on friends and enemies alike, in an attempt to revive American manufacturing, crack down on illegal drugs and even to protest an alleged “witch hunt” against an ally in Brazil. After spiking tariffs last year to the highest level since the Great Depression, Trump posted photos of himself headlined “Mister Tariff” and “The Tariff King.” But when it came to keeping sky-high tariffs on Russia, Tariff Man balked. On Friday, Trump ignited bipartisan uproar when he signed an executive order that waived new sanctions and tariffs on Russia two days before they would go into effect. Those penalties were contained in a bill Trump signed into law in September that was named after Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator from South Carolina. The executive order suspends tariffs of up to 500% on US imports from Russia and 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil and natural gas. In other words, Congress built a new economic weapon to use against Russia’s war machine, but Trump has decided not to fire it — at least for now. “This eviscerates any real enforcement of the Lindsey Graham sanctions act,” said Ed Mills, Washington policy analyst at financial firm Raymond James. Mills noted that the move falls within a “pattern” for Trump, who similarly left Russia off the list of countries facing sweeping tariffs in April 2025. “The timing of the announcement is telling. Friday news dumps are done for the actions you don’t want noticed and politically you don’t want to defend,” Mills said. “This is certainly not the closing argument the GOP wanted weeks before the midterms.” The tariff pause helped ease intense pressure in the energy market — but only slightly. Oil futures dipped Monday morning as traders bet that fewer sanctions on Russia will mean more energy supply. And by early Monday afternoon, Brent crude, the world benchmark, flirted with five-month highs around $110 a barrel. “Russia is already selling crude oil to China, India, Turkey and elsewhere while they have been limiting exports of refined fuels,” said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. “The waiver may make it easier to sell oil to a wider range of customers, but whether it leads to additional supplies reaching the market is another question.” The executive order was met by praise from Kirill Dmitriev, head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, who hailed it on X as “an important and truly historic moment.” ‘Capitulating to a Russian dictator’ Multiple Republicans broke with Trump over the decision to scrap the Russia sanctions, including Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who is filling her late brother’s seat and running for a full term. “I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia to end the war and get the gas prices down because I don’t trust (Russian President Vladimir) Putin and I don’t trust Russia,” she said. Outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis blasted the move as “beyond irresponsible” and slammed Trump for “capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day.” Trump officials defended the decision to waive Russia sanctions. Over the weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the executive order gives Trump time to “study” the global economic impact of the sanctions. “The problem is that these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries — India, for example, and others,” Rubio said. “I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy.” Highest tariffs in nearly a century The decision was a surprise to some analysts, given Trump’s embrace of tariffs. Mills said many expected Trump might opt to only lightly enforce the Graham Act sanctions, but not to explicitly pause the tariffs altogether. Last year, Trump spiked US tariffs on imports to the highest level since the 1930s, according to John Iselin, associate director of economic analysis at The Budget Lab at Yale University. Although US tariffs have since eased — due to a series of pauses with China, a Supreme Court decision against Trump’s global tariffs and other developments — they are still higher than at any point between the 1940s and 2024.

cnn.com.title: Saudi Arabia cancels next week’s ‘Davos in the Desert’ conference after series of Houthi attacks
cnn.com.text: In a major setback for the kingdom’s economic ambitions, Saudi Arabia has canceled a major conference scheduled for next week in Riyadh amid a wave of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants. Known as “Davos in the Desert,” the Future Investment Initiative will now take place on an undisclosed date in 2027, according to a statement from the conference shared via email with CNN’s Becky Anderson. Normally, the annual event showcases Saudi Arabia’s financial muscle and growing role on the world stage. Wall Street leaders including JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon and BlackRock boss Larry Fink were all scheduled to speak at next week’s event. However, the FII decided to cancel the October 26-29 conference in the wake of a series of Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital, including a deadly missile strike earlier this month on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. The decision comes after a series of Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and other strategic sites, prompting a number of countries to issue travel warnings.  Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have exchanged near-daily missile, drone and air strikes in recent week, with the conflict escalating sharply.Some boards of directors may have balked at sending their CEOs into Saudi Arabia in the midst of the deadly battle with the Houthis. “This decision has been taken to ensure that our milestone tenth edition delivers the full scale, quality and impact that our partners, members, speakers and delegates expect,” the FII Institute, which runs the conference, said in the statement.Organizers said the new dates in 2027 for the event “will be communicated very soon” and all registrations and partnerships “remain valid.”The cancellation of this year’s event is a blow to Saudi Arabia’s efforts to diversify the oil-rich country’s economy away from oil and natural gas.The deteriorating security situation undermines decades of effort to attract Western capital to the Middle East and may herald a period of investment uncertainty that would be detrimental to the whole region.

cnn.com.title: The rioting across France is a symptom of a much larger public and political crisis
cnn.com.text: “We have a mess on our hands, to put it bluntly,” French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said Monday. If anything, he might be guilty of understatement. After widespread rioting at the weekend – estimated to have cost several hundred million dollars in property damage and theft – France faces a toxic mix of urban rebellion, political drift and economic crisis. The disorder at the weekend occurred in major cities across the country, leading Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to offer his resignation because of the police’s failure to contain the rioting. There was rampant looting in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and other cities, while the city hall in Limoges, which survived two world wars, was badly damaged by fire and its clock spire collapsed. The violence at the weekend, which led to some 2,400 arrests, followed weeks of protests by French students angry about crumbling schools, a lack of teachers and dismal job prospects. More than 6,000 arrests were made during the school protests that began at the start of the fall term and more than 100 schools were damaged. More demonstrations are scheduled for next weekend. In November, labor unions plan to strike. France faces a winter of discontent in the run-up to a presidential election next spring. The far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is leading in the polls. Political drift In a national televised address Sunday, President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence but did not set out ideas to deal with it or seize the initiative. Instead, he warned of politicians seizing on the chaos for political gain – before leaving France for a three-day visit to the Gulf states. Lecornu similarly deployed the blame game. After far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the government of “opening the door to chaos” with its policing tactics, Lecornu shot back: “You cannot call for an end to the violence while providing excuses to those who commit it. This is YOUR political responsibility.” Le Pen, who is standing in the presidential election for the far-right National Rally party, has sought to inject the issue of migration into the debate, blaming the violence on delinquents from France’s banlieues, poor urban areas where much of the country’s migrant population lives. “Our country is caught in a vice…between violence and powerlessness,” she said, suggesting only her firm hand could restore order amid Macron’s “chaos.” The president of her National Rally party, Jordan Bardella, poured fuel on the fire, demanding that “Antifa militias, far-left extremist groups and Black Bloc groups” be designated as terrorist organisations.” Black Bloc groups wear matching or similar black clothing along with face masks during protests to hide their identity. Analysts say this political fragmentation, which led to the paralysis of parliament after snap elections called by Macron in 2024 backfired, is likely to persist – and is at the core of France’s deepening crisis. The political center in France has evaporated, allowing the National Rally and Mélenchon’s far-left France Unbowed party to harvest growing public exasperation, while Macron’s successive prime ministers have been unable to pass a budget through Parliament. The multitude of candidates in the center, “most with relatively few supporters, will ultimately help secure the second-round election for one of the two contenders who represent the greatest danger to democracy in France,” wrote Robert Zaretsky, a professor of modern French history at the University of Houston, in an essay for the Atlantic. Debt and déclinisme The current crisis has polarized an already deeply divided society. Besides the shock and anger at the weekend’s mayhem, there is an air of defeatism. In a recent Ipsos-BVA poll, 85% of respondents said that France was in decline, and 98% were dissatisfied with the present state of the country. Whoever governs France next will have shrinking room for maneuver, even if they can stitch together a stable coalition. The French economy is stagnating. Farmers were hit by an extremely hot and dry summer, while global energy prices stoked inflation. Tourism remains a strong earner for France, but the videos of violence on the streets circling the globe in the past two days may deter some travelers. French businesses are wary of the drift and indecision. Investment has fallen about 1% in the first half of this year amid climbing interest rates. Above all, there is the debt. “France carries one of the highest government debt burdens in Europe, and political deadlock means we expect its debt level to continue rising,” researchers at Oxford Economics said in July. France will have to issue a record high of €340 billion in medium- and long-term bonds next year, according to analysts. Its debt as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP) rose to 119% in the second quarter of this year, double the European Union’s target. Jittery investors sent the country’s 10-year government bond yield up to 4.9% on Monday. Its reputation in bond markets is not helped by Mélenchon’s plan to freeze or wipe away the French sovereign bonds held by the Bank of France. “Political fragmentation may persist well after the 2027 elections, meaning that France’s next government will continue to kick the public-finance can down the road,” said Oxford Economics. This would “prolong the existing climate of high uncertainty, weighing on confidence and domestic demand.” The man most revered by the French, General Charles de Gaulle, once declared that “France cannot be France without grandeur.” De Gaulle had soaring ambitions for the country’s global role and independence. But during his long presidency he also told an aide: “I keep the theater going as long as I can and then, after me, have no illusion, things will go back to where they were.” De Gaulle stepped down a year after the 1968 riots that shook France – events that some commentators are likening to today’s shock. When he became president, Macron was seen as the antidote to what the French call déclinisme (a word that first appeared in the French Larousse dictionary in 2016.) “He delivers an extremely positive, constructive message, full of hope for the future. He shows that there is also another France,” wrote one commentator. A decade later, Macron’s approval rating is hovering at about 15 to 17%, according to multiple polls Déclinisme is still very much on the lips of a citizenry that is demanding more from a beleaguered state that has less.

cnn.com.title: The (very red) pattern of Trump’s 2026 campaign rallies
cnn.com.text: A new Washington Post-ABC News poll over the weekend featured a telling stat. Other recent polls have generally shown voters prefer Democrats over Republicans for Congress by close to 10 points on the all-important “generic ballot.” But when President Donald Trump is invoked — i.e. choosing between a Democratic-controlled Congress that could act as a check on Trump, versus a GOP-controlled Congress that could pass his agenda — that gap balloons. Registered voters preferred the blue side by 19 points, 58%-39%, in the Post-ABC News poll It’s clear from those numbers why Republicans in swing areas would be reluctant to campaign with Trump — and why he’s hitting such red territory. With the president’s midterm travels now in full swing, a number of patterns have emerged: 1) He’s campaigning overwhelmingly in red states that voted for him by double digits in 2024, and 2) when he does campaign in more competitive areas, it’s generally for candidates in red states who are struggling — and seem to need to roll the dice on Trump driving up turnout among a dejected GOP base. There are exceptions to both, and Trump’s travel schedule is evolving. But that’s about the shape of it. Vice President JD Vance has traveled to many of the same places as Trump — sometimes going to more politically challenging areas before the president does. It’s certainly a far cry from when Trump said during the Republican midterm convention last month that he would travel to all 35 of the biggest “swings” in the country. NPR calculates he’s been to less than one-third of them. Trump’s focus on red states The first pattern is unmistakable. Trump’s decision to use his limited time before the election to travel to dark-red states like Oklahoma, Alabama, Tennessee and Kentucky raised plenty of eyebrows But it’s not just those states. Since the GOP’s midterm convention, the nearly 20 states that Trump has visited or is planning to visit this week voted for him by 14 points, on average. That list includes as many states that voted for him by about 30 points (the four states named above) as presidential swing states (Arizona, Georgia, Michigan and North Carolina). Including New York — the lone state Trump lost in 2024 that he’s visited recently — Trump has traveled to or is planning to travel to only five states that didn’t vote for him by double digits. The candidates who will campaign with him seem to need help That doesn’t mean that every Republican in key races has avoided campaigning with Trump. But the ones who have appeared with him generally seem as though they could use a boost. Those in better shape and in swing-to-blue-leaning states haven’t welcomed him or have been scarcer when Trump comes around, including skipping his rallies. Thus far, the two bona-fide presidential swing states where Trump has rallied with the Senate hopeful are Georgia and North Carolina. But in both cases, the polls and the two parties’ ad spending suggest those seats are likely lost to the GOP. The other key GOP Senate candidates who have rallied with Trump or will rally with him in the coming days either come from states he won by at least 16 points (Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts, South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham and Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall), or come from double-digit Trump states but have trailed in more quality polls than they’ve led (Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan). Polls in those states are sometimes within the margin of error and have no clear leader, but the Republicans have trailed in some of the other polls. There is no sign yet of Trump campaigning for Senate candidates in blue-leaning states like Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire. He travels to Iowa and Michigan this week, but we don’t yet know who will attend. The story is similar in governor’s races. Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo and Georgia GOP nominee Rick Jackson have both campaigned with Trump in competitive, marquee races. Trump will also go to Florida this week to stump for Rep. Byron Donalds in a red state. (Donalds recently made headlines for scrubbing his website of Trump mentions.) But the other gubernatorial candidates to appear with Trump are Republicans who have sometimes looked more like underdogs — in Alaska, Arizona and Ohio. And there is no sign yet of Trump campaigning with hopefuls in Maine, New Hampshire, Oregon and Wisconsin. And when Trump visited Texas to campaign with Paxton earlier this month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — who has polled better than Paxton — very notably didn’t appear. The absentees Absences have been a trend too. Sometimes when Trump shows up, the GOP candidates just … don’t. That was true not only of Abbott, but also a bunch of New York GOP officials including vulnerable Rep. Mike Lawler when Trump visited that state, a pair of key House candidates in Arizona last week, and another GOP House candidate in Kentucky (who, like Donalds, scrubbed his website of Trump mentions) on Saturday. And when Vance visited Iowa last month, GOP Senate nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson didn’t attend — and Vance barely mentioned the Senate race. A big question for this week is who shows up when Trump visits Iowa on Thursday and Michigan on Sunday. In Michigan, former Rep. Mike Rogers has gone further than most top GOP Senate candidates to distance himself from Trump, including recently on Trump’s trade war with Canada. The president’s visit will take place on the Canada border in Port Huron, which could make for some difficult optics for Rogers. In Iowa, Hinson has also sought distance from Trump on issues including the Iran war, importing foreign beef and, most recently, importing Russian diesel fuel. And as noted, she skipped the Vance event. But she also comes from a redder state, and she has suggested she’d welcome Trump to Iowa — including when he put her on the spot during an Oval Office event in late September. That could be a dilemma that awaits other Republicans. What happens if they’d prefer Trump not come, but he does anyway? He’s made clear he doesn’t like Republicans giving him the cold shoulder, nor does he appreciate the narrative that he’s a liability. But that new Post/ABC News poll number speaks volumes. By showing his face in crucial states and making himself and his agenda the issue, Trump often appears to be doing his party no favors.

cnn.com.title: Finland gripped by national broadcaster’s puppies live stream
cnn.com.text: It’s dark outside. The news cycle is relentless. But Finland’s national broadcaster has a solution: Adorable puppies, available any time, night or day. Yle has been drawing millions of people to its website with “Pentulive” – Finnish for “Puppy Live” – a 24/7 live stream of Hilkka, a Lagotto Romagnolo dog, and her brand-new litter of puppies as they sleep, play and suckle enthusiastically. Hilkka gave birth to the two females and four males on October 10. The webcam was switched on shortly after, and the puppies will remain in the spotlight until they leave for their new homes in December. Given that puppies need up to 20 hours of sleep a day, the action can be limited, which may explain why “Pentulive,” now in its sixth season, has been labelled “slow TV” – a concept first trialed in Norway in 2009 with the Norwegian public broadcaster’s airing of a seven-hour train journey. Nonetheless, viewers who tune in to the home of the anonymous breeder have been promised the chance to witness some of the “puppies’ milestone moments,” according to a Yle press statement: from opening their eyes to learning to walk and having their first playtime outside. Despite Finland’s tiny population – just under 5.66 million – the “Pentulive” webpage had 6.5 million page views last year, according to Yle, and its social media channels attracted 20 million views. And based on viewing figures so far, this year’s puppies look set to outperform. One of the world’s northernmost countries, Finland is preparing to usher in its long, dark winter. Temperatures can drop as low as -50°C (-58°F) and in parts of the country north of the Arctic Circle the sun does not rise above the horizon for weeks on end. So it is hardly surprising that residents enjoy a cozy distraction from the bitter conditions outside. The puppy-cam was first launched in 2021 by Yle science reporter Pirjo Koskinen as part of a series on canine science. She told CNN in an email that the idea was, in part, “to shed light on a dog’s crucial first few weeks,” adding: “What happens at the breeder’s – much like with human children – influences the rest of the dog’s life.” Escape into the ‘puppy bubble’ Distraction from the harsh reality of daily life is part of “Pentulive“‘s appeal, Koskinen believes. “It is all about caring, love, and nurturing – all those positive aspects of humanity that often get pushed aside by a constant stream of unpleasant news,” she said. “‘Puppy Live’ offers comfort and relaxation amidst the rush of everyday life; it’s a wonderful escape from the human world into a ‘puppy bubble.’” Sonja Mutanen, a doctoral researcher studying media and animals at the University of Eastern Finland, explained its particular appeal to Finns. “For many viewers, these live streams are a much-anticipated highlight of the dark Finnish winter months,” she told CNN. “This kind of feel-good content can foster a sense of belonging and emotional well-being, which is important during late autumn and winter when people tend to stay at home more.” Live streams offer something different Miiamaaria Kujala, adjunct professor of comparative cognitive neuroscience at the University of Helsinki, said in an email to CNN that a live feed affects us in a completely different way from the short reels that are now commonplace on social media. “The live stream offers something that appears to be missing from many of the modern busy lives: something real, genuine and fragile,” she said. “Pentulive is life-paced: It contains very calm periods and unexpectable action periods. As a live feed, it likely provokes more intense emotional responses from the observers … but it is also immensely calming to observe a sleeping puppy.” It also provides a “sense of continuity as it follows the puppies growing older,” she said, adding: “They’re not just random animals, you learn to know them individually.” This is the second litter for 5-year-old Hilkka, who is currently on leave from her role as a “school dog,” where she provides emotional support for pupils. So far, the fluffballs have only been given nicknames by their breeder, but on Saturday they will be officially renamed. The viewing public will narrow down a selection of names, from which the puppies themselves will “choose” – by sitting in a circle of sealed envelopes and snuffling at the one that appeals.

cnn.com.title: Kenyan cult leader found guilty over 190 children starved to death in the hope of ‘meeting Jesus’
cnn.com.text: The leader of a Kenyan Christian cult has been found guilty of the murder of 190 children through an organised system of enforced fasting and abuse. Paul Mackenzie was on Monday convicted along with about 30 other suspects at Mombasa High Court over the deaths of 191 people, all but one of them children in Shakahola forest in eastern Kenya. Prosecutors have dubbed the trial one of Kenya’s “most consequential” criminal cases ever. The court found the deaths resulted from an “organised system in which religious teachings and an established hierarchy were used to direct and enforce deadly fasting among Mackenzie’s followers,” the office of the director of public prosecutions in Kenya said. “Fasting was implemented sequentially, beginning with children, while guards controlled movement and prevented followers from escaping,” the office said in a statement. Mackenzie also discouraged modern medicine and formal education, the court heard. Mackenzie, who is in his early 50s, and his co-accused were charged with the murders in 2024 after hundreds of children’s bodies were exhumed from Shakahola forest where Mackenzie and his associates were accused of running a death cult. Authorities started digging up bodies in Shakahola forest in April 2023. So far they have recovered 429 bodies. Further charges could follow. Mackenzie, who ran the Good News International Church, was accused of instructing his followers to starve themselves and their children to death so they could reach heaven and meet Jesus, CNN previously reported. Postmortem findings cited by Lady Justice Diana Kavedza on Monday indicated that some victims died from suffocation, neck compression or head injuries, rather than starvation alone. Mackenzie’s attorney Lawrence Obonyo told reporters Monday the defense team planned to appeal, saying his client maintained that he hadn’t forced anyone to fast and that the victims’ actions were voluntary. Search for justice In a lengthy ruling lasting more than eight hours on Monday, the judge described how Mackenzie used sermons and written materials to persuade followers that the outside world was evil, and that they could only find salvation by moving to the forest. Evidence extracted from his phone, including WhatsApp messages, showed communications with followers before they relocated to Shakahola, according to the judge. She said followers were persuaded to abandon their homes, families and livelihoods. The judge also described how those who resisted Mackenzie’s directive to fast were forced to comply. “Children were restrained, denied food and punished for attempting to eat or escape,” the director of public prosecutions said. CNN previously reported on families searching for relatives who had disappeared into Shakahola forest. Rodgers Shibutse, a Nairobi resident, said he found his mother’s remains among those exhumed in February 2024. Shibutse told CNN on Monday that Mackenzie had caused immense pain and that he wanted him sentenced to life in prison. Mackenzie and his co-accused will be handed their sentence on November 6. Asked whether that would bring justice for his mother, Shibutse said: “Not 100% justice, but at least the government has done something.”

cnn.com.title: Whiskey rebellion over 1868 law on home distilleries heads to the Supreme Court
cnn.com.text: When John Ream got into brewing beer at home nearly two decades ago, starting out was as easy as opening the kit his wife bought for him as a gift. But the Ohio engineer’s plans ran dry when he tried to switch to making whiskey. That’s because a 160-year-old federal law bars Americans from making distilled spirits at home. Ream could have faced jail time if he followed through and was caught, and risk losing his home. Instead of pouring himself a stiff drink, he sued. “Brewing is a nice blend of science and art, and being able to combine different flavors together,” Ream told CNN in an interview, adding that he did not intend to sell his creations. “I would like to take the same skills that I’ve learned and try my hand at distilling.” The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to decide if the federal government may bar people from distilling liquor at home in an appeal filed by the Trump administration after the 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the prohibition, “while venerable,” violated the necessary and proper clause of the Constitution. The justices technically held Ream’s separate appeal, which followed a decision from the 6th Circuit that upheld the federal ban. But Ream’s case – and his ability to distill at home – is sure to be influenced by the outcome of the Justice Department appeal. The Supreme Court will likely decide the DOJ case next year, and then send Ream’s appeal back to lower courts for additional review. The government’s appeal dealt with a Texas group called Hobby Distillers Association and individual members that wanted to distill spirits at home. One of them received a letter from the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, part of the Treasury Department, threatening a $500,000 fine. Ream’s lawyers, who are also challenging the law in the DOJ case, say the outcome of the case could have broad implications beyond making booze. The ban was enacted in 1868 ostensibly to limit rampant tax evasion by commercial distillers. But under that theory, Ream argues, the government could ban any number of activities at home – baking, sewing, remote work – simply by taxing it and citing evasion as a justification. The government collected $6 billion in revenue from the tax in 2024. A trade group representing distilled spirit industry said that it “appreciates the enthusiasm” of home distillers, but warned of the risks of making liquor at home. “The distillation process can be quite dangerous, including risk of explosion, burns, fires, and more,” said Courtney Armour, chief legal officer at the Distilled Spirits Council. “Furthermore, if not produced properly, the finished product can cause blindness or death.
