In a home distilling setting, these dangers would not just be limited to the individuals engaging in the production but also their neighbors in the surrounding area.” Helped cover Civil War costs Federal law bans the making of distilled spirits in any “dwelling house,” shed or yard. The Justice Department said the provision was intended to head off evasion of federal excise taxes that were levied on distilled spirits for much of the nation’s history and were revived in the mid-19th century to help pay for the cost of fighting the Civil War. There’s no dispute that Congress has the power to levy the tax. The Justice Department argues that lawmakers’ authority to ban home distilleries flows from the Constitution’s necessary and proper clause, which gives Congress broad leeway to pass laws required to carry out its enumerated powers. “Congress restricted home distilling because a distiller can more easily conceal a distilling operation or thwart necessary inspections — thereby evading the requisite tax — if the still is located in a dwelling-house or connected structure,” the Trump administration told the justices in court papers. But Ream and a group of would-be distillers argue that the biggest problem with tax evasion at the time was not home distillers but commercial distributors who found it cheaper to bribe revenue agents than pay the federal tax. They say that the prohibition on homemade whiskey was really a sop to the temperance movement in exchange for lowering the tax. “There’s not much in the record that supports their theory that the home distilling prohibition had anything to do with tax evasion,” said Robert Alt, president of The Buckeye Institute, which is representing Ream and the others challenging the ban at the Supreme Court. “This prohibition seemed to be probably a political logroll,” he said, so that lawmakers could avoid looking soft on liquor as they made other changes to the way the excise tax worked. Ream also raised a broader challenge to the ban, questioning the government’s effort to justify it under Congress’ power to regulate interstate commerce. Holding off on Ream’s case suggests the justices weren’t yet ready to address that separate argument. While the Justice Department notes the government’s long history of taxing liquor, several conservative groups pointed out that there is also a healthy history of the founding fathers distilling whiskey, brandy and other spirits at home. People visiting Mount Vernon in Virginia can tour George Washington’s distillery and even purchase bottles produced at the site. As president, Washington moved to quell the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794. By the time he died a few years later, his estate operated one of the largest distilleries in the nation. It is a point that several of the conservative justices, who have sharpened the court’s focus on the founding era, could note during arguments. When the court heard arguments earlier this year in a challenge to a federal law that permitted police to disarm regular drug users, Justice Neil Gorsuch led a soliloquy about the founders’ drinking habits. “John Adams took a tankard of hard cider with his breakfast every day. James Madison reportedly drank a pint of whiskey every day,” Gorsuch told the attorney representing the Trump administration in March. “Are they all habitual drunkards who would be properly disarmed for life under your theory?” Penalties for violating the home distillery ban are severe. They include criminal fines and up to five years in prison. A violator’s home would also be subject to forfeiture. Two federal appeals courts reached different outcomes after reviewing the home distillery ban. The Louisiana-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals decided that, “while venerable,” the prohibition violated the necessary and proper clause. But the Cincinnati-based 6th Circuit came to the opposite conclusion, and it brushed off the idea that its decision would logically allow the government to ban other types of activities at home. That’s because, the appeals court said, alcohol is essentially in a class by itself. “Indeed, rules concerning alcohol more generally are unique as to the evasion that often accompanies them,” the 6th Circuit wrote. “From excise taxes, to Prohibition, to the use of fake IDs to obtain alcohol (itself almost a rite of passage for some generations), to moonshiners even today.” This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: US-Ukraine relationship worsens amid Trump and Zelensky’s mutual distrust
cnn.com.text: The relationship between Ukraine and the United States is facing increasing strain over intelligence sharing, sanctions, Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy and the path to peace. There also appears to be deepening mutual distrust between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky. Trump on Monday accused Zelensky of not knowing what he was talking about and suggested it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.” Over the weekend Kyiv launched one of its biggest drone attacks this year on Russia, hitting a key oil terminal, in defiance of Trump’s demand that Ukraine stop hitting Russian refining plants. The White House is trying to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices in the US ahead of crucial midterm elections, as diesel prices are at a record high. Last week Trump called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace” and said Zelensky was more difficult to deal with than Russian leader Vladimir Putin. In an interview on Sunday, Zelensky hit back, saying it was “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face,” an apparent reference to Trump’s relationship to Russia. Trump again criticized Zelensky on Sunday, claiming in a Truth Social post that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.” The relationship now seems to be at its lowest ebb since the explosive meeting at the White House 18 months ago. Zelensky has consistently said he is open to peace negotiations if Ukraine’s security can be guaranteed. The Ukrainian president said he spoke to US envoy, Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Sunday as part of “nonstop communication” to work towards the goal of peace. Zelensky added later he was hoping to meet the two “maybe in Norway in the coming days.” CNN has reached out to the White House for comment on the meeting. “We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer,” Zelensky posted on X. “Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end,” Zelensky added on Monday. Zelensky also spoke to Pope Leo XIV on Monday, according to the Vatican. The pope spoke to the Ukrainian president just days after a phone call with Putin in which he expressed his concern about the “grave humanitarian situation” in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where Ukrainian authorities say around 2,000 civilians are stuck without access to food or basic medicine. Trump has defended recent concessions to Russia on sanctions, which have included a waiver to allow Russian diesel exports and another exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress. “I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote in his Sunday post. In an interview Sunday with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Zelensky said the waivers strengthened Putin’s war against Ukraine while Moscow was failing on the battlefield. There is growing anxiety in Kyiv and Europe that the Trump administration will make further concessions to Moscow in an effort to get Putin to agree to a peace deal. Zelensky told “Meet the Press” that the US siding with Russia would be a “historic mistake.” He said he wanted to trust Trump and hoped he would change his attitude to Putin. Asked if Trump was an ally of Ukraine, Zelensky said: “I hope so.” On Monday, Zelensky appealed directly to the US Congress, holding an online meeting with a group of lawmakers from both parties. He described the current situation as “the most difficult situation from the very beginning of this war” and saying that it appears as if “some political decision has been made to slow down support for us.” Ukraine is also perturbed by reports of a possible three-way meeting involving the US and China next month on settling the conflict – without Ukrainian involvement. “I think there’s been talk of a meeting. I don’t know if anything’s been finalized,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said during a visit to Uzbekistan Monday. Trump said on Monday that he’d consider a trilateral meeting with Putin and the Chinese leader Xi Jinping — but said that the sitdown would focus on denuclearization, not Russia’s war with Ukraine. But Ukraine criticized the idea, arguing such a meeting would not help peace but “would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Monday. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandizement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” Sybiha wrote on X. The Kremlin said Monday that “no concrete proposals or agreements – neither regarding the meeting itself nor its potential agenda and content – have been discussed or put forward by anyone.” Attacks persist Defying Trump’s demands, Ukraine is keeping up long-range strikes into Russia. One target at the weekend was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal. The terminal can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year. Ukraine’s Fire Point company, which makes the drones used in the attack, said there was a fire on the terminal’s grounds following the strike. A logistics center in St. Petersburg was also attacked, according to Ozon, a Russian distribution company, as well as a data center for the Russian VKontakte social media platform. One person was killed and five wounded in the attacks, with residential homes damaged as well, according to local authorities. A week ago, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such an agreement. Ukraine briefly halted such attacks, but Russia never stopped pounding Ukraine’s energy plants and cities. “Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ​ago, Russia has ​deliberately ‌attacked ​Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors ⁠76 times,” Zelensky ​wrote on X Sunday. On Monday, Zelensky said a Russian drone attack in the Kharkiv region killed six people, including three children. Sharing a blurred photograph of one of the victims – a small child in a stroller – Zelensky said the horrific image showed “the truth about this war.” “Lives must be protected. Ukraine needs air defense. You can’t think about making money with Russia as long as it continues its asinine war,” he said on X. Accusations have also flown over the cuts in US satellite intelligence provided to the Ukrainian military. Zelensky repeated on Sunday that changes in the Starlink system owned by billionaire Elon Musk was limiting the speed of its short-range and battlefield drones, describing it as a “message from the American government.” Musk said last week that the systems are owned and controlled by the US government, meaning that only the government could decide to place limits on their speed or usage. The Trump administration has denied it ordered the service restricted. On Monday, Trump said he didn’t know who it was that restricted it, but would “like to find out.” Similarly the Trump administration has pushed back on accusations from Kyiv that intelligence on incoming ballistic missiles is not being shared. Zelensky said on Monday that Kyiv had received no advance warning of ballistic missile attacks on Sunday night – something he claims has occurred multiple times in the past week. “Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners.” US satellite networks are critical in providing the Ukrainian military with warnings of incoming missiles. Russian ballistic missile attacks are aimed at crippling civilian life and destroying essential infrastructure. “I don’t know where he’s getting these things or why he’s saying these things to the press,” Rubio told ‌reporters Monday. “You should go back and ask him. There’s been no pause.” “What he should be focused on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That’s what he should be focused ​on,” Rubio said of Zelensky. Kyiv and Washington see very different paths to that goal. CNN’s Daria Tarasova, Anna Chernova, Julia Benbrook, Jennifer Hansler, Christopher Lamb, Kristen Holmes and Ivana Kottasová contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Supreme Court backs Pentagon decision to throw out plea deals for 9/11 alleged conspirators
cnn.com.text: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to review former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin’s decision to cancel plea agreements with Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other defendants accused of plotting the 9/11 terror attack. By denying the appeals, the high court left in place a decision from an appeals court last year that found Austin, who worked for former President Joe Biden, “indisputably” had authority to cancel the agreements, which had taken the death penalty off the table for the three alleged conspirators. The decision puts the case back in the hands of military courts that have for years struggled to set a trial. The agreements had prompted a backlash from some groups representing 9/11 victims and their families. In separate appeals, Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi, and Walid Bin ‘Attash argued that the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit overstepped its authority by siding with the government in the case. “The practical effect of today’s denials of certiorari is to clear the way for the inexorable pre-trial proceedings in these cases to continue,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN legal analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center, who filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging the justices to take up the appeals. “It would be one thing if a trial were reasonably likely in the near future, but even the current summer 2028 trial date is entirely unrealistic given how many issues remain to be resolved.” Trials against Mohammed and the others have been delayed for years as multiple presidential administrations have tried to determine how to handle the issue of the torture of individuals at CIA prisons, and the question of whether evidence obtained through torture was admissible in court. The pretrial agreements were announced in 2024 after more than two years of negotiation. The agreements required that the accused plead guilty to all charges against them and undergo a public sentencing hearing in which they would be required to answer questions by family members and survivors of the September 11, 2001, attack. Austin abruptly revoked those agreements two years ago, asserting that such a significant decision “should rest with me.” The Trump administration has continued to defend Austin’s decision to revoke the deals. A military judge overseeing the trials of the three men ruled in 2024 that the plea agreements were “valid and enforceable.” A military appeals court ruled against Austin weeks later. The agreements had prompted a backlash from some groups representing 9/11 victims and their families. Justice Brett Kavanaugh recused himself from consideration of the case. This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: Priest killed by falling crucifix during live streamed Mass
cnn.com.text: A priest has been killed by a falling crucifix at a church in Ecuador as he performed a mass that was being live streamed online. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died on Saturday at the Perpetuo Socorro church in the city of Guayaquil, southern Ecuador, according to a statement from the city’s archdiocese, published on Facebook on Monday. Video of the incident shows Sánchez leading the mass when a large wooden cross that was standing on the altar behind him falls over and hits him on the head. Shouting can be heard from the congregation, and several people enter the frame and rush toward the priest. On Sunday, the church held a eucharist in memory of Sánchez, led by Cardinal Luis Cabrera, archbishop of Guayaquil. “We are grateful for all of the condolences from around the world, and especially for your prayers for the eternal rest of the soul of Patricio Sánchez,” the statement reads. According to CNN affiliate Ecuavisa, the priest was preparing to lead a wedding ceremony when the tragedy occurred. Police have not commented on the incident so far, Ecuavisa reported. CNN has reached out to the Archdiocese of Guayaquil for comment.

cnn.com.title: Mars’ two tiny moons shouldn’t exist. A new mission has launched to reveal their secrets
cnn.com.text: Mars’ largely unexplored moons are getting their moment in the spotlight now that a first-of-its-kind mission has taken flight. The red planet has many unsolved riddles, but the Japanese-led Martian Moons eXploration project will focus solely on two of the biggest curiosities orbiting nearby. Phobos and Deimos have long baffled scientists, who have been eyeing the small, lumpy moons for clues about the early days of Mars. “This is kind of like one of the major outstanding mysteries of solar system formation, the origin of Phobos and Deimos, so we really do need a mission like MMX to figure this out,” said Dr. Daniel Glavin, senior scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and participating scientist on the MMX mission. Previous Mars missions have observed the peculiar pair whenever convenient. Orbiters circling the red planet have snapped images of the rocky bodies over the years, while rovers including Curiosity and Perseverance have captured some fantastic “googly eye” eclipses when Phobos moved between Mars and the sun. But even after decades of observations, scientists still don’t know how Phobos and Deimos came to be. “What are these little space potatoes? We can’t explain Phobos or Deimos right now. They shouldn’t exist, but they do,” said Dr. Abigail Fraeman, research scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California. “They’re super weird, they’re super small and they’re super puzzling.” MMX lifted off aboard an H3 rocket from the Yoshinobu Launch Complex at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan’s Kagoshima Prefecture at 3:41 p.m. ET Monday (4:41 a.m. JST Tuesday). The risky robotic mission is an international collaboration — including scientific instruments from NASA, the European Space Agency, France’s National Center for Space Studies and the German Aerospace Center — that aims to collect more than 0.4 ounces (10 grams) of material from Phobos and return to Earth in 2031. The detailed observations and samples captured by MMX might reveal the missing pieces to Phobos and Deimos’ origin story — and could even unveil secrets about the red planet itself. If the samples contain pieces of Mars, MMX could potentially be the first mission to successfully bring back Martian material to scientists on Earth in a race alongside China. Landing on an enigmatic moon American astronomer Asaph Hall discovered the red planet’s unusual moons in 1877. He named them after the two mythological sons of the Roman god Mars: Phobos, meaning fear, and Deimos, signifying dread. Phobos is a doomed moon, drawing 6 feet (1.8 meters) closer to Mars every 100 years. Scientists expect the lumpy rock to crash into the planet in roughly 50 million years or break up into a rocky ring that stays in orbit. The object’s defining feature is Stickney crater — a gaping cavity, about 6 miles (9.7 kilometers) wide, that takes up approximately half of the tiny moon’s surface. Thousands of meteorite impacts have also scarred Phobos over time. Meanwhile, more distant and diminutive Deimos is slowly spiraling away from Mars. The moon has a smoother surface than Phobos but is still heavily pockmarked and covered in a perplexing amount of dust. Scientists are weighing two leading hypotheses about how these oddballs came to orbit around Mars. One concept suggests that a large object slammed into Mars, launching rocky material that coalesced into Phobos and Deimos, Glavin said. The other hypothesis purports that the two moons are asteroids that came too close to Mars and were drawn in by its gravity. “None of our data fit either hypothesis correctly,” said Fraeman, who is also a participating scientist on MMX. Japan’s expedition to the enigmatic moons could find new data that supports one of the existing hypotheses or illuminate an entirely different formation backstory, Fraeman added. The mission will primarily focus on scouting and visiting Phobos, the larger and closer of the two moons to Mars, but along the way it will also take images of Deimos to help scientists better understand similarities and differences between the fraternal moons. Carrying a small rover named Idefix, the MMX spacecraft — a stack of three modules for propulsion, exploration and returning to Earth — will spend about a year traveling to Mars and then orbit Phobos for about three years. A suite of instruments aboard the spacecraft’s lander, called the exploration module, will enable scientists to gather a variety of data, including measurements on terrain, minerals, chemical elements and space radiation. Two Super Hi-Vision cameras will take the highest-definition images of Mars and its moons in 4K and 8K. The spacecraft will first deploy the Idefix rover, developed by the German Aerospace Center and France’s National Center for Space Studies, in early 2029. The robotic explorer will make initial observations that will help mission scientists and engineers determine sites for MMX’s four-legged lander to collect samples directly on Phobos. The rover will drop from about 131 to 328 feet (40 to 100 meters) down to the surface of Phobos; the tiny moon’s weak gravity should cushion its fall and enable the rover to bounce before sticking its landing. After autonomously releasing its wheels and solar panels and maneuvering into an upright position, Idefix will embark on a 100-day mission. The gravity on Phobos is so weak that Idefix, which weighs roughly 55 pounds (25 kilograms), will only weigh about 0.5 ounces (15 grams) during its surface operations. The drink crate-size rover will scout out areas of scientific interest and potential safe landing spots. The mission team will then select two separate sites for the MMX lander to touch down. Images taken by current orbiters show that Phobos appears to have one lighter side and one darker side — almost as if it has two different types of surfaces, Glavin said. That’s why the plan is to collect a sample from each of these two regions — on the side of Phobos that faces Mars and the opposite side facing away from the planet, said Dr. Tomohiro Usui, a scientist at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA, who has worked on the mission for 10 years. “We’re going to choose a first landing site and then do some landing operations, and after that we’re going to lift off and get back to orbit,” Usui, professor in the department of solar system sciences at Japan’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, told CNN. “It takes another several months for the search of the next landing site. Landing operations are very risky.” The MMX lander has two different ways to collect rocks and dust from Phobos. A coring sampler will drill down 0.8 inches (2 centimeters) and store the subsurface material in a tube aboard the spacecraft’s sample return capsule. A separate pneumatic sampler will use pressurized gas to kick up surface material and collect it in a tube. After the samples have been stored aboard the MMX lander, it will lift off, make observations of Deimos and begin the journey back to Earth in 2030. Insights gained from MMX’s tour of the Martian moons could even aid with the planning of crewed missions to Mars in the future, Usui said. Revealing Martian secrets The MMX lander is like a Swiss army knife of many different components, providing scientists various ways to try to decode the mysterious origins of Phobos and Deimos. Ahead of the samples returning to Earth, researchers will be able to get a sneak peek at initial remote-sensing data beamed back in real time from MMX instruments such as the Mars-moon Exploration with GAmma-rays and Neutrons spectrometer, or MEGANE. MEGANE data could reveal signs of volatile elements, or chemical elements with low boiling and melting points, such as hydrogen, sodium and chlorine on Phobos and Deimos, for example. These elemental composition measurements could provide key clues that lend credibility to one origin hypothesis over another, said David Lawrence, planetary scientist at the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory and science lead for MEGANE. “If you had a giant impact, what happens is the materials get very hot, and you will cook off these volatile elements,” Lawrence said. “In contrast, a lot of asteroids that we see have higher abundances of these volatile elements.” Fraeman, who focused part of her doctoral thesis on Phobos’ composition, will do a combined analysis of MEGANE data and observations captured by the MMX InfraRed Spectrometer, or MIRS. The spectrometer will use near-infrared light to measure minerals, organic matter and water-related substances on Phobos. Even though the Martian moons are mission priorities, scientists anticipate that MMX’s data will also reveal previously unknown aspects of Mars’ past. “If Phobos is made from bits of Mars that were thrown up and then recoalesced, that could give us some important new clues about the composition of the planet and what it was like when it was much younger,” Fraeman said. Even if the rocky neighbor doesn’t contain remnants of Mars, Phobos would be equally intriguing if it’s a captured asteroid or comet — which could have transported water and other volatile elements from the edge of the solar system to Mars’ vicinity, Fraeman said. If Phobos and Deimos were enriched with water and organics, “that could have been a seed for life on Mars,” Glavin said. “That’s what I’m particularly interested in: the origin of life. Are we alone? Did it happen on Mars?” he added. “Studying the samples from Phobos and analyzing Deimos as well is part of that whole story.” Glavin has worked on previous sample collection missions, like OSIRIS-REx, which returned an unexpected wealth of organic material from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu. For MMX, his team will look for amino acids, the molecules that form proteins, and other chemical building blocks of life in the Phobos samples as well. “Amino acids seem to be literally everywhere we look in the solar system,” Glavin said. “What we’re going to be looking at is differences in the number and complexity of amino acids, but also their relative abundances, which can tell us about their origin.” Phobos and Deimos likely have existed for billions of years, which means the moons might be witnesses of Mars’ evolution. Given its proximity, Phobos has served as a little dustpan, collecting material that has swept away from the planet’s thin atmosphere. “There could be pieces of Mars that have landed on the surface of Phobos, much like pieces of Mars have landed on Earth,” Fraeman said. “When we bring samples back from Phobos, there could be little bits of Mars mixed in there.” MMX is not the only craft racing toward the red planet. China’s Tianwen-3 mission, which aims to launch in 2028 and return samples directly from Mars back to Earth, is also expected to return in 2031. “The early 2030s could really be banner years of explanation for Mars,” Glavin said.

cnn.com.title: Tensions flare at court hearing on Trump’s golf course renovation after president says construction will begin ‘immediately’
cnn.com.text: One of the tensest showdowns between the Trump administration and the federal bench in Washington, DC, came to a head on Monday in a marathon court hearing over President Donald Trump’s efforts to overhaul a public golf course that has been the subject of months of litigation. Trump early Monday doubled down on his plan to close and renovate the golf course in Washington, DC, saying construction would begin “IMMEDIATELY” despite a judge’s order to provide three days’ notice ahead of any construction. Trump wrote in a Truth Social post that the government does not “need an approval” to proceed with the construction. “Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY! The finished product will be World Class, and bring income and great prestige back to D.C.,” he wrote. By the end of the day, Trump was still fuming about it. Just before midnight, the president posted on Truth Social: “’Trash Island,’ Washington, D.C., the nickname for the broken and dilapidated Golf Course that is the subject of frivolous litigation in the United States Court System, before a judge that seems not to want Greatness for our Capital or our Nation (but who knows?), has been badly managed for so many decades that it is a completely nonviable and unsafe Project.” He said his plan “will turn Trash Island into an Island of Beauty and Success!” But, Trump’s dream of renovating the East Potomac Golf Course is already the subject of a legal fight as preservationists and golfers seek to stop the president from changing the public park. The case may seem relatively minor compared to some of the other sweeping legal battles of Trump’s second term. But the litigation has demanded the attention of several top attorneys from the Justice Department, who have sought to defend the actions government officials who are overseeing the course and have tried distinguish them from the president’s public statements about his intentions for the grounds. US District Judge Ana C. Reyes, who is overseeing the case, issued an order last week that requires the government to give at least three days’ notice before making any “irreparable modification” to the course. Reyes and the third-highest ranking Justice Department official, Associate Attorney General Stan Woodward, sparred repeatedly over the information she was demanding from the administration. The question in the case, since last Monday, had largely been about the administration removing, with less of a day’s notice to the court, of 400-plus trees from the park earlier this month. But the hearing on Monday quickly turned into a clash over what Trump wrote on social media, the Justice Department’s ability to defend separate assertions made by the National Park Service in court, and how far the federal trial-level court can go to demand answers from the executive branch. “I don’t know what to do, when I keep getting different stories,” Reyes told Woodward as the hearing began with a heated moment. “I have, on the one hand the president of the United States saying to the American people … there is a final plan,” Reyes said hours later in the same hearing Monday. “I have you all telling me, witnesses saying what they’re saying, there is no final plan … which is it?” Robert Stander – a DOJ attorney who was handling the bulk of the administration’s legal arguments – struggled to answer the question directly and Reyes rejected his attempts to compare the social media posts to an executive order that was just the start of an agency’s work on a project, rather than a final decision. Woodward returned to the line of questioning at the end of the hearing and told Reyes there was “no plan to close the course, as those words have their literal meaning.” He told the judge that asking Stander, a lower-level attorney that did not go through Senate confirmation, to contradict the president put his colleague in a “difficult” position. Reyes is considering whether to issue a longer-term order limiting what the administration can do to the course, including cutting down more trees. Last week, Reyes presided over a testy hearing in which she said she was “furious” with the administration for removing hundreds of trees without proper notice. The government claimed the removals were routine maintenance unrelated to any plan to renovate the golf course. Reyes ordered that no more trees be cut down before October 26. The Justice Department on Friday filed a motion asking for Reyes’ removal from the case, accusing her of having a “disdain for the Trump Administration.” Reyes over the weekend denied that motion and refuted the government’s claims against her. In his Monday post to Truth Social, Trump disparaged Reyes a “crazed lunatic.” The golf course is one of several renovation projects Trump is working on in Washington. The president’s desire to turn the public course into a professional course – a renovation that could cost between $20 million and $49 million – has angered those who fear it may take away a public and affordable place to play golf in the nation’s capital. Administration officials express ignorance to Trump’s intentions Amid the tense exchanges between DOJ and the judge were hours of testimony from government officials charged with oversight of federal public grounds – testimony that turned the proceedings into a grueling drag through bureaucratic procedures of the National Park Service. Multiple government officials who oversee the golf course expressed ignorance to Trump’s latest assertions about the future of the course. The acting director of the National Park Service, Jessica Bowron – who signed off on this month’s move to cut down the 400-plus trees – said she was not aware of plans to close East Potomac Park next month, nor had she been in any discussions about renovating the course. She and other officials say their work on the removing the trees was carried out under a directive that they implement recommendations from 2019 for making the course look more it did when it was first built, in a proposal known as the Cultural Landscape Report. Reyes has said that she believed that explanation was a pretext for giving the administration cover to start the renovation. She quizzed officials Monday on the “coincidence” that the administration suddenly rushed to implement a seven-year-old proposal – specifically, only its recommendations to cut down certain trees – just as Trump was demanding work on his overhaul to begin. Greg Wischer – a political appointee at the Interior Department who has coordinated Trump’s directives for “beautifying” Washington, DC – testified that he came across of 2019 landscape recommendations as part of research in recent months for what his agency could do to “clean up” the course. He suggested that those “clean up” efforts were separate from the Trump-ordered redesign. DOJ assertions of privilege prevented him from answering several questions about key meetings and conversations that preceded the tree removals. But his testimony revealed that for months he has been receiving “conceptual proposals” for renovating the course from famed golf course designer Tom Fazio and his son Gavin. Wischer first saw the rendering posted by Trump on Sunday last week, according to his testimony, when Gavin Fazio texted it to his personal phone. Later in the hearing, Reyes asked Stander whether there was a contract with the Fazios to redo the course and asked the other attorneys at the defense table when Stander said he did not know the answer. Woodward stood to clarify that there was no such contract. This story has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: So you say you hate ‘surveillance pricing’
cnn.com.text: “Surveillance pricing” sounds very, very bad. Consumers think that companies are tracking their search history, location and income to charge more for groceries and other purchases. Naturally, lawmakers are trying to crack down on this supposed nightmare. In Colorado, the legislature passed a bill this summer to ban companies from using customers’ personal data to set individualized prices. The concern is that two people could be charged different amounts for milk based on what the data spits out about their willingness to pay. But Colorado Gov. Jared Polis saw a big problem with the bill. “Many Coloradans won’t get discounts on items they buy if I were to sign this,” Polis said in a June letter. “It would punish differentially lower prices, not just higher prices.” He vetoed it. Americans are channeling their rage over high prices, AI and giant companies gathering their data into the issue of “surveillance pricing.” A growing number of cities and states are responding with legislation to reel in companies’ use of customers’ personal data to set prices, especially at large grocery stores and fast-food chains. Some bans also target electronic shelf labels at stores. Unions have backed these restrictions on electronic labels because they fear the technology will eliminate the need for workers to change thousands of paper tags in stores each week. But the tech is more neutral, and Polis’ veto exposed a contradiction with the growing backlash to the practice: the same algorithm that companies use to charge more also can deliver lower prices, reduce food waste and create other benefits for consumers. Broad state and local bans cut off the possibility of lower prices and other tech that delivers benefits, economists, attorneys and marketing experts say. “Some of the surveillance pricing laws are not only unlikely to protect consumers, they may even harm them,” said Jean-Pierre Dubé, a marketing professor at the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business. Evidence also shows that neither “surveillance pricing” nor electronic shelf labels increase overall prices. “There is essentially no change in pricing behavior after these digital labels are installed,” a study tracking more than 180 million price records at grocery stores last year found. Dynamic pricing on steroids The debate around “surveillance prices” often blurs two different practices: dynamic pricing, which adjusts prices based on supply and demand and other market conditions, and personalized pricing. Dynamic pricing has existed for decades. Happy hour, lunch specials and end-of-season clearance sales are familiar examples. Consumers also encounter dynamic pricing when they buy plane tickets online or order Uber rides. There is little evidence that dynamic pricing raises prices overall. In some industries, including airlines and restaurants, it has actually enabled companies to offer lower prices. Airlines have long used dynamic pricing to offer lower fares to travelers who are flexible on their travel dates or willing to fly at off-peak hours. A large restaurant chain that used an algorithm to adjust food delivery prices found that it helped smooth out orders throughout the day, according to a 2023 Harvard University study. The algorithms slashed prices during slow hours to attract customers who would otherwise dine elsewhere, bringing the average price down across the day. Lower prices weren’t the only benefits of dynamic prices. In the grocery industry, research from the University of San Diego in 2023 found that dynamically pricing perishables cuts down food waste by 21%. But as AI has expanded companies’ ability to personalize prices across more industries, the practice has gradually been described in more nefarious terms such as “AI surveillance pricing” and “price discrimination.” Economic populists such as Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders blame “surveillance pricing” for driving up prices, claiming AI will make things worse. Lindsey Owens, the CEO of progressive economic think tank Groundwork Collaborative, gained traction for her warnings about the opaque ways corporations use customers’ personal data to rip them off. Owens pointed to a patent Walmart received in 2023 for technology that can remotely deploy dynamic price changes to electronic shelf tags: “If a customer has tuna fish, they may be offered a different price for mayonnaise,” the patent says. Facing public uproar, Walmart last month defended its practices and told customers: “We don’t set different prices based on who you are or the time of day.” Walmart has little incentive to abandon its business strategy of stable, consistent prices, said Ioannis Stamatopoulos, a professor of operations at the University of Texas at Austin who has studied dynamic pricing. The company relies on a model known as everyday low prices — rather than sales and coupons — to draw shoppers. Rapid price fluctuations would alienate Walmart’s customers, Stamatopoulos said. “They would rather keep you happy and coming back instead of risking your continued business for a few opportunistic cents,” he said.

cnn.com.title: ‘I want to get that sculpture out of there’: Donors fear the worst for Kennedy Center’s art
cnn.com.text: At the height of legal and political tumult at the Kennedy Center last summer, board members discussed moving the iconic eight-foot, 3,000-pound bronze bust of President John F. Kennedy from the Grand Foyer while the main building closed for renovations. They reasoned the move to a newer building would not only secure the artwork but ensure the campus remained a living memorial to the 35th president, according to sources familiar with the board discussions. What they didn’t know – but would soon find out – was that the bust is bolted into the foundation of the building, multiple feet underground, and moving it wouldn’t be logistically feasible. So, it will remain in place, sources say, and be shielded during construction. The fate of the bust, which was commissioned and gifted by the Kennedy family, underscores the haphazard efforts in recent months to catalog and protect the treasures in the Kennedy Center. The building houses hundreds of irreplaceable pieces of art and antiquities – including tapestries, sculptures and chandeliers – that have been donated or loaned by other countries and benefactors. Worried donors, artists and their family members have been calling and emailing the Kennedy Center for months, asking about what’s being done to protect the artwork, whether their pieces will be temporarily moved, and if they’ll one day be returned, according to half a dozen people who spoke to CNN on the condition they remain anonymous. Some donors are suggesting arrangements for their pieces to be moved to museums and other places – away from the Kennedy Center. And some told CNN they feared speaking out publicly while the artwork they care about is still inside the center. “I want to get that sculpture out of there,” said one person who donated a piece to the center. Apprehension over the collection began to fester late last year when officials devised a plan for permanently removing artwork that envisioned possible “disposal” through various means, including “return to country of origin, transfer or exchange with another institution, public sale, or destruction,” according to internal documents reviewed by CNN. Then, President Donald Trump, who is chairman of the Kennedy Center board, repeatedly stoked fears about the artwork with threats of demolishing the performing arts center, the removal last month of a major outdoor sculpture from the center’s grounds and the addition of a gold-leaf portrait of himself. Kennedy Center officials now say the proposal CNN reviewed was never envisioned as a sweeping purge of artwork. They insist the “cornerstone of the collection – historic international gifts given to the Center for its opening – remains intact” and that the institution is exploring adding further works. Many of the pieces were given as gestures of goodwill and in commemoration of John F. Kennedy. On the day of his assassination, the American sculptor Robert Berks began work on what would become the bust that was installed on the day the institution opened in 1971. Officials also tell CNN that all artwork will be “fully safeguarded” during the renovation. Some pieces will be temporarily relocated, they said, if necessary to ensure they’re protected and that safety is maintained during construction. And some pieces won’t be moved. For instance, an iconic starburst Lobmeyr crystal chandelier, a gift from Austria that’s 60 feet wide and illuminated by more than 3,200 bulbs, is expected to stay during the renovation. A plan for the bronze bust of Julius Rudel outside the Opera House, the first artistic and music director of the center, is being discussed. “We remain in regular contact with the foundations and entities who have donated art to the Center,” a Kennedy Center spokesperson told CNN. Meanwhile, Trump’s renovation plans – and his efforts to put his name on the facade – are still the subjects of a court fight. Officials say the REACH, a smaller venue on the Kennedy Center complex, will still serve as a temporary living memorial to JFK. A ‘disjointed’ response With the Kennedy Center’s doors temporarily closed and officials readying for a two-year renovation, art donors and enthusiasts are scrambling to understand what’s happening and fearing the worst – from artwork becoming collateral damage during construction to being accidentally thrown away. Josef Palermo, a former curator at the institution, described the Africa Lounge being cleared out in one day. The room housed dozens of works donated by African nations, including 12-foot double doors carved from a 700-year-old tree in Nigeria. “Walking into it when it was hollowed out and darkened and my heart really sank,” Palermo told CNN in an interview. “The room was completely stripped bare.” The room is now being used for storage. The Kennedy Center says the African room art remains on site and that preservation efforts are underway. “There is a major concern that a lot of this artwork is being pushed around the center,” one person close the Kennedy Center who works with several donors said. The institute has seemed open to finding a way to accommodate suggestions for artwork to be displayed elsewhere, according to several people who spoke to CNN. But these conversations are happening in an ad hoc manner, they said, often driven by donors and families of the artists, and not being initiated by the institution. “It is a little bit disjointed response,” the person close the Kennedy Center said. “Responses on this have been very inadequate or not clear, or you know ‘everything is safe and sound, rest assured’ kind of thing,” the person said – but donors are “not given any detail in any way.” The system for cataloguing art inside the Kennedy Center had been disorganized, sources say. Adding to the disarray this year, the center’s finances tanked, scores of staff were laid off and changes were made to the interior decor. At the same time, archival materials have been used as decorations in different offices throughout the building. When the center underwent layoffs this spring, some sources said that staff inadvertently took home mementos, such as such as signed Kennedy Center Honors posters that are technically part of its archives. Some gifts and valuable assets, including the spare crystals for the chandelier from Austria, are housed in a fire- and flood-proof storage facility at the center. The arts institution also rents a storage facility in Virginia and just renewed the ten-year lease. That’s where some of the remaining marble, donated by Italy, that makes up the white facade of the building is kept. And earlier this year, the Kennedy Center hired a lead archivist, Olivia Herschel, to oversee and manage its catalogue of artwork. Now, seven months later, the center said in a statement to CNN that “for the first time in our institution’s history, the collection has been comprehensively cataloged, marking a significant step in the preservation efforts of new leadership.” Herschel also has become an unofficial liaison with donors and artists seeking answers. Sources who spoke to CNN say they’ve been in touch regularly and were given assurances they will be told of any developments with the artwork. While sources describe her as engaged and respectful, they also question how much power she has to deliver on her assurances given the dynamics under the Trump administration. The center declined to make Herschel available for an interview. Historical givings The idea of a national cultural center that showcased the best of American music, art and drama started to take shape after World War II under President Dwight Eisenhower, who signed a law to create a national performing arts space on the banks of the Potomac River in 1958. The space was envisioned as an “artistic Mecca … that would be open to visitors from every land.” Kennedy – a devoted patron of the arts – carried Eisenhower’s vision forward. First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy helped lead efforts to raise money for the center and in 1962, during a televised fundraiser, the president told the nation why he believed the center would be invaluable. “Today, as always, art knows no national boundaries,” he said. “The poet, the artist, the musician, continues the quiet work of centuries, building bridges of experience between peoples.” “Art is political in the most profound sense,” Kennedy added. Less than a year later, he was assassinated. At the time, Ralph Becker, the general counsel for the center, was tasked with helping to coordinate donations from foreign dignitaries. He later wrote that he began having discussions about renaming the institution in Kennedy’s honor within hours of the president’s death. World leaders began flooding Becker with requests to donate artwork to the center after Kennedy’s assassination. Italy supplied the marble to form the facade of the building from the famed Carrara mountains – the same mountains that produced the marble for Michaelangelo’s David. Canada provided the curtains for the Eisenhower theater; France donated tapestries by Henri Matisse, and India created 20 specially designed planters for the Grand Foyer. Norway supplied 11 chandeliers for the concert hall, and Tunisia donated a reproduction of a 3rd century mosaic for the rooftop terrace. Uncertain future With the future of the Kennedy Center building in limbo, sources who spoke to CNN wondered about the long-term plans for the artwork and whether Trump will replace it with pieces more to his liking. Palermo, now a whistleblower, has said that he was told last year to remove all the outdoor art, including the abstract “Blue” sculpture, because Trump wanted “all new art for the reopening.” The abrupt removal of that work in September seemed to confirm concerns, even as the Kennedy Center said deinstallation after seven years was “common practice.” Kennedy Center officials tell CNN that there are no other planned or imminent changes to the artwork currently on display. But this month, with no public announcement, the Kennedy Center convened its first “visual arts committee” – a panel of staff and board members who will aim to curate and expand public installations of performing and visual arts. The committee will manage the addition of visual art through rotating displays that will be open to the public — like the recent addition of gold-leaf portraits on temporary loan to the REACH featuring Trump and Elon Musk.

bbc.com.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
bbc.com.text:
- Published
President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.
Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."
While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.
The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.
So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims.
1. US economy growing
The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.
The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.
And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.
That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.
The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.
It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.
Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.
The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.
Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office.
2. Inflation picked up
Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.
The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%.
That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.
Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.
While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.
The price of a gallon of diesel in the US, external - a fuel used not only by drivers but also widely in agriculture and industry - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.
The price of some grocery staples , externallike beef and coffee have risen since Trump returned to office, though the price of eggs has fallen.
And some US retailers have warned, external that rising energy prices caused by the Iran war will make producing food more expensive and raise prices at the till.
3. Household income growth held back
Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump.
The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external.
However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households:
- Trump's tax cuts
- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans
- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war
ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.
The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.
ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external.
4. Job creation slowed down
Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs", external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border.
Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month.
But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency, external.
And the number of Americans employed in manufacturing, external - 12.6 million in September 2026 - is slightly lower than it was when Trump's second term began.
However, the US unemployment rate remains relatively low, external at 4.2%, which is broadly where it was when Trump returned to the White House.
Part of the reason for this is Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation programme, which has reduced the size of the available US workforce, external and means a lower number of jobs need to be created each month to stop unemployment rising.
5. Borrowing costs rising
US government borrowing has increased in Trump's second term, partly driven up by his significant tax cuts.
The federal government deficit - the gap between its revenues from taxes and its spending - was $2 trillion in the year to September 2026, external. That's equivalent to around 6%, external of US GDP.
And the US deficit is projected to rise to above 8% of GDP by 2030, external.
That high rate of government borrowing is itself helping to boost US GDP growth.
The IMF has warned that excessive US government borrowing, external, which it uses to bridge the deficit, and its rapidly rising national debt are raising the risk of a future financial crisis in America. This would have a deeply damaging impact on most American households.
The growing deficit is also one of the reasons the US government gets charged more to borrow money in financial markets.
The 10-year US government bond yield has risen sharply since Trump returned to office in January 2025 and is now above 5%, the highest rate since the global financial crisis in 2007.
That increase in the market cost of US government borrowing also puts upward pressure on the interest rates on mortgages available to American households.
The interest rate on a new 30-year US mortgage has risen to 7.4%, external per year, up from 6.9% when Trump returned to the White House.
That's added to problems in the US housing market, making homes less affordable for new buyers. It has left many existing owners reluctant to move because doing so would mean giving up their cheaper mortgages, which they took out at lower rates, external and cannot take with them to a new property.
Data graphics by Erwan Rivault.

bbc.com.title: Canadian tourist found guilty of animal cruelty after stealing Las Vegas flamingo from enclosure
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A Canadian man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he took a flamingo from its enclosure in Las Vegas and brought it back to his hotel room during an alcohol-fuelled bender.
Mitchell Fairbarn, who was visiting the US city, took the Chilean flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino in March.
Videos shown at his trial showed a smiling Fairbarn carrying the bird by the neck as he took a lift to his room. He testified that he had drunk 30 to 40 beers before the incident and said he never meant to harm the animal. He faces nearly five years in prison.
Animal experts testified the flamingo had feathers torn out and suffered blood loss due to Fairbarn's actions.
A lawyer for Fairbarn said his actions were intended as a harmless prank, and blamed alcohol for his "bad decisions".
"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," said his lawyer Josh Tomsheck, external.
"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."
His lawyer added he had received death threats since his arrest.
Testifying in his defence, Fairbarn, 34, said he thought it would be "funny" to take the bird.
He said he had been up drinking all night and had just gotten off a call with a colleague when he made the decision to abscond with the bird.
The Flamingo Las Vegas, located along the famous Las Vegas strip, features a wildlife habitat inside its hotel and casino that is free to walk through. It features a flock of Chilean flamingos, other birds, fish and turtles.
During the trial, the jury heard from 14 witnesses and reviewed more than 112 pieces of evidence, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
It took a jury around five hours to convict him on felony and misdemeanour animal abuse charges.
Fairbarn has been unable to leave the US since his arrest. He remains on house arrest in Las Vegas, with a sentencing hearing due to take place in December.
A veterinarian for the state said that Peachy has largely recovered since the event but has a now has a more anxious demeanour around humans.

bbc.com.title: 'Our worst nightmare': Threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
bbc.com.text:
- Published
As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.
Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.
He was briefed by federal police – whose counter-terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Witnesses saw the suspect do a U-turn before striking the MP and then reversing to ram her again, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has said.
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese has been emotional when he has spoken about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.
Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.
In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.
Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.
Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.
"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.
Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's domestic spy agency Asio, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.
"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the federal police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.
In the wake of the attack, a range of MPs have described wearing disguises in public, locking their office doors, and scanning every crowd for potential threats.
Women in politics are particularly scared, said Victorian state MP Georgie Purcell, who shares part of her electorate with Haines.
"Being a woman in politics changes the way you move through the world. We consider where we park our cars, the route we drive home, if we hold public events," she said in a statement.
"For many of us, the news... is our worst nightmare".
Coalition Senator James Paterson told News24: "I'd like to say that I was surprised… but I'm not at all surprised."
There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.
"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

bbc.com.title: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.
The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence.
"The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen".
A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation.
The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack."
In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait.
A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters.
Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas.
Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range.
"The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested.
"In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop – completely unrelated to the protests, he said.
"Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said.
Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem.
Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her.
"In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."
The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.
She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it.
"When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said.
"They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."
At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down.
"We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.
Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said.
"I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.
Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

bbc.com.title: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.
It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds.
"The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds."
Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity".
Speaking in the House of Commons on Monday, Carney said the fire was "driven by ferocious winds".
"The fire jumped nearly a kilometre less than a minute to where the soldiers were gathered," he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known.
Carney said the injuries occurred "in the space of a few minutes".
The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases.
Carney confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.
He said the troops were preparing to be sent to Latvia and were training to join the Canadian Armed Forces' Global Response Task Force, "which can deploy within hours anywhere in the world Canada needs them".
Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition.
Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.
Tributes are being paid to the servicemen who died.
Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, wrote on Facebook that it was "with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father".
Wong received a tribute from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, of which he was part. The regiment was "deeply saddened", it wrote in a Facebook post of its own. It sent "heartfelt condolences to [the group's] families, friends, and fellow soldiers".
The mother of Goulding, Sonia Monk, said her late son was an exceptional athlete and a natural leader. "He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up," she told CBC. "He really was the light of my life."
Canadian PM Carney said on Monday that Goulding was known as "a generous and deeply loyal friend".
Lykkemark, Carney said, "was known for his gift for lightening a hard day, his quick wit - he dreamed of a career in law enforcement".
"These were sons, brothers, partners, friends, young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause," Carney said.
In recounting Saturday's events, Rutland told reporters that members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range.
He told reporters that officials knew about the fire on the base for several hours, but it was decided that training "could carry on for a certain amount of time".
"I spoke to my commander last night, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them," Rutland said.
He added it was not yet known what exactly caused the fire.
Some witnesses said they had heard explosions, fuelling speculation that oil and gas infrastructure may have been hit and sparked the fire. But Rutland said authorities "do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure".
The Canadian Armed Forces has said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBC said.
According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month.
Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries.
About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.
The fire erupted just before Albertans voted to decide whether the province should separate from Canada.
Defence minister David McGuinty declined to comment on Saturday when asked whether it would impact the election.
"This is not the time to speak about that issue at this stage," he said.

bbc.com.title: US church on frontline of battle against drug known as 'tranq'
bbc.com.text:
US church on frontline of battle against drug known as 'tranq'
America has been fighting the War on Drugs for decades, but the drug cartels, the suppliers and the dealers appear to be always one step ahead of the authorities.
President Trump has declared the cartels, "terrorists" and labelled fentanyl, the powerful synthetic opioid, a "weapon of mass destruction".
But the drug supply is changing, with other deadly synthetics being added to the mix, including strong animal tranquillisers, known on the streets as "tranq".
While overdose deaths are falling, the potency of the new drugs has recovery workers worried. For some the answer might lie in reducing demand, giving users support and helping them end their addiction.
BBC international correspondent Quentin Sommerville and camera journalist Darren Conway travelled to Columbus, Ohio to find out more.
Read more on this story: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis.

bbc.com.title: Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.
Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.
He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch.
El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.
El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.
The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.
Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.
One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."
Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.
Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire.
A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.
However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.
While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.
Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.
