A third election in March 2020 gave Likud 36 seats to Blue and White’s 33, and produced a Netanyahu-Gantz unity government that collapsed within a year. In March 2021, Likud won 30 seats to Yesh Atid’s 17, but an eight-party coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid that also included Ra’am, an Arab party, ended Netanyahu’s 12-year run. It lasted a year.
Netanyahu returned in November 2022, with Likud on 32 and Yesh Atid on 24, at the head of what has been described as Israel’s most right-wing government. Polls now show neither bloc clearly reaching 61.
Israel’s prime ministers
The state of Israel has had 14 prime ministers since its foundation in 1948. Netanyahu is by far the longest-serving, with 19 years in three separate stints: 1996 to 1999, 2009 to 2021 and from 2022 to now
Only David Ben-Gurion, who led the country from 1948 to 1954 and again from 1955 to 1963, comes close.
Whatever happens on October 27, Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in.

aljazeera.com.title: US Supreme Court to hear case on race in school admissions
aljazeera.com.text:
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about the role of race in admissions to selective Maryland middle schools after a group of parents claimed policies discriminated against Asian students in favour of Black and Latino students.
The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear the parents’ plea on four academically rigorous “magnet” schools in Montgomery County, a suburb on the outskirts of Washington, DC, in the neighbouring state of Maryland.
The high court said it would weigh whether the parent group has enough evidence of discrimination for the case to move forward.
Lower courts previously dismissed the case because Asian-American students were not underrepresented at the specialised-curriculum schools compared with the pool of students that applied.
If the Supreme Court rules for the parent group, the Association for Education Fairness, it could revive the lawsuit.
The court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months and rule by June.
‘The Pandemic Plan’
The Montgomery County school district’s selection process was introduced in the 2021-2022 school year during the COVID-19 pandemic.
It screens all students for academic potential, and then implements a lottery to randomly assign students from that pool to receive enriched instruction at either a magnet school or a local school.
The suit alleged that the screening process makes it harder for Asian-American students, who the challengers said are clustered in “high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools”, to enter the lottery pool.
Part of the process ranks a student’s performance by comparing the student’s test scores against those of other students whose family incomes are at a similar level.
“Under the applicant pool benchmark, the government can set specific racial targets, hit them, and avoid even an inquiry into discriminatory intent,” so long as it has not explicitly called out race in its process, they wrote in their appeal to the Supreme Court.
Previously thrown out
The case was thrown out in 2022 by US District Judge Paula Xinis. She noted that the percentage of admitted Asian-American students exceeded the percentage of Asian Americans among all applicants to the magnet schools.
Xinis also found no evidence that the lottery policy was implemented with discriminatory intent.
The school system has consistently argued the new admissions policy, called the “Pandemic Plan” due to the timing of its release, is race-neutral.
“The Pandemic Plan is a colorblind lottery,” lawyers wrote in a brief asking the Supreme Court not to take up the case. “Nothing about the Pandemic Plan, its history, or its purpose is offensive to the Constitution.”
Supreme Court justices will now consider whether a group claiming to be targeted by a race-neutral policy must show it was disproportionately harmed to prove intentional discrimination.

aljazeera.com.title: Japan launches historic mission to bring back Mars moon samples
aljazeera.com.text:
Japan launches historic mission to bring back Mars moon samples
Japan has launched a five-year uncrewed mission to collect samples from Phobos, one of Mars’ two moons, and return them to Earth by 2031. If successful, it would be the first mission to bring back samples from a moon of Mars for scientists to study.

aljazeera.com.title: Fourteen dead in illegal Colombian gold mine collapse
aljazeera.com.text:
Fourteen dead in illegal Colombian gold mine collapse
Search efforts have been halted in Colombia after an illegal gold mine collapsed in a remote part of the country. Fourteen people were killed and several others were injured. The mine is surrounded by dense rainforest and only reachable by boat or plane.

aljazeera.com.title: ‘Deliberate’ car ramming of Australian MP an isolated incident, police say
aljazeera.com.text:
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) have said the alleged targeting of independent lawmaker Helen Haines appeared to be an “isolated incident” and there were no known further threats associated with the attack.
Haines was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her office in Wangaratta, about 200km (124 miles) northwest of the state of Victoria’s capital, Melbourne, on Monday, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called a “deliberate” act.
The 65-year-old underwent surgery overnight, with Australian media outlets reporting on Tuesday that she has lost a leg and remains in critical condition in a Melbourne hospital.
The suspect is in police custody, an AFP statement released on Tuesday said. Local media identified the driver as a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, Victoria.
Federal and state police were working “to identify potential charges”, including “the offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment”, the statement said.
The prime minister said on Tuesday that the vehicle had performed a U-turn before hitting the MP.
“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone just skidding off the road,” Albanese told the ABC national broadcaster.
The prime minister said the alleged attacker’s motive remained unknown.
Bystander intervened
A former nurse, Haines is an independent federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi and is known for her socially conscious policy positions on the environment and transparency.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told ABC Radio that witnesses said Haines was struck twice by the vehicle before a bystander intervened.
Ricky Jefferies ran from his barber shop, restrained the attacker and removed a knife from him after initially believing the incident was a car accident, Australian media reported.
“I heard a loud bang with no brakes. It was crazy; I just ran out to the front to see what’s happening,” Jefferies told reporters outside his shop.
“I didn’t realise the seriousness of the situation initially, and once it became relevant, I just did what I could and what others were already trying to do.”
Threats and abuse
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said she was shocked by the “deeply disturbing attack” and wished Haines a full recovery in a post on X.
The attack comes after the federal police documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation’s politicians in recent years. Politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security.
Albanese said on Monday that “the temperature has increased in recent times”.
Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.
She has been praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.

aljazeera.com.title: Angel Reese scores 30 as Dream stun Valkyries to go level in WNBA Finals
aljazeera.com.text:
Angel Reese scored 30 points and had 16 rebounds as the Atlanta Dream stymied the Golden State Valkyries in a stunning win in the WNBA Finals to level the series 1-1 in San Francisco.
Allisha Gray added 18 points as the Dream took full control at both ends in the second half, winning 79-65 on Monday night to even the best-of-seven series before it heads to Atlanta.
Rhyne Howard set a Finals record with six steals, while Jordin Canada contributed 13 points, 10 assists and seven rebounds as the Dream earned the franchise’s first Finals victory after going winless in three previous trips. They now head home, having salvaged a split in front of the boisterous “Ballhalla” crowd at Chase Center.
“This environment is tough to play in. Shoutout to the fans. Shoutout to my team, though,” Reese said after the game. “We came and fought. I mean, that Game 1 was tough for us. But we moved on.”
Reese became the third player with at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a Finals game, joining Jonquel Jones of Connecticut in 2019 and Breanna Stewart of Seattle in 2020.
“She was definitely way more aggressive; she had a great game,” Valkyries centre Kiah Stokes said. “We let everyone kind of have their way.”
Game 3 is Wednesday in Atlanta, where the next two games were moved to the NBA’s Atlanta Hawks’ State Farm Arena so more fans could attend.
It holds more than 17,000, as opposed to the Dream’s regular home, Gateway Center Arena, which accommodates only 3,500.
Chase Center holds 18,064 and has sold out every game since the Valkyries began playing last year.
Gabby Williams finished with 14 points on 3-for-15 shooting after she was the only Golden State player to score in double figures with 26 points in Game 1, going 7 for 24 from the 3-point range.
“We shot terribly,” point guard Veronica Burton said. “We missed shots that we make all the time.”
Foul trouble almost did in the Dream this time, but Reese simply would not have it. She went scoreless in the second half of the opener, but delivered the big baskets and key defensive stops two days later, finishing 10 for 16 from the floor while dishing out three assists and blocking two shots.
“We watched film and saw the things that we messed up on. When I said that they didn’t do anything to mess us up, it was literally just us,” Reese said.
“And we can see that tonight. And we’re gonna carry that over in Atlanta. Atlanta, y’all better pull up and pop out; I’m looking forward to it.”
Atlanta scored 24 points off Golden State’s 19 turnovers to hand the Valkyries their first loss in regulation since a 73-70 defeat at Chicago on August 21.
The Dream had just eight points off turnovers in Game 1, but returned to the defensive formula that advanced Atlanta this far.

aljazeera.com.title: PSG vs Barcelona: UEFA Champions League – Yamal, Torres, predictions, teams
aljazeera.com.text:
Who: Paris Saint-Germain vs Barcelona
What: UEFA Champions League, match day 3
Where: Parc des Princes, Paris, France
When: Tuesday, October 20, at 9pm (19:00 GMT)
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up and live updates from 16:00 GMT.
One of the most eagerly awaited Champions League matches of the season will be played against the backdrop of turmoil on the streets of the French capital as holders Paris Saint-Germain host Barcelona on Tuesday.
The fate of the match has been subject to debate as the French government seeks to control the violent protests gripping the country.
However, once the match gets under way at the Parc des Princes, fans can expect a mouthwatering battle between the Champions League’s top two teams as the back-to-back holders welcome five-time winners.
Boasting a perfect record across all competitions, Spanish giants Barca are arguably one of Europe’s best teams this season.
PSG too have been nothing short of lethal – the Parisians lead the UCL points table and have scored a whopping 10 goals in two games.
There will be plenty of star power on display when the match kicks off as the dazzling duo of Ferran Torres and Ousmane Dembele will headline the star-studded home side.
Lamine Yamal, who is enjoying one of the best starts to a La Liga season for a forward, will be joined by Raphinha for Barcelona.
Here’s everything you need to know ahead of PSG vs Barcelona:
How have PSG played this season?
After seven matches, PSG are second in Ligue 1 with 14 points, behind Lyon on goal difference. They have won four times, drawn twice and lost once in the French top division.
How have Barcelona played this season?
Barcelona are five points clear at the top of La Liga table with nine wins from nine. Their blistering attack has scored 39 league goals.
What happened in the first and second Champions League rounds?
Two-time holders PSG thrashed Slovan Bratislava 6-1 in their UCL opener at home before beating Manchester City 4-2 in a thrilling away fixture.
Barcelona thumped Feyenoord 5-1 at home and bounced back from a goal down to smash Galatasaray 4-1 away.
Those results keep PSG top of the table and Barcelona second, with both on six points.
Will PSG vs Barcelona go ahead amid the protests in France?
Despite the violent protests and nationwide arrests, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the match will not be postponed or cancelled.
Lecornu said on Monday that he had asked regional authorities to impose “partial” and “localised” curfews in some cities to protect businesses after weekend demonstrations spilled over into some of the worst street violence in recent years.
“These curfews must be local and partial. It is out of the question to put all of Paris under curfew.”
At the same news conference, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters there were no plans to cancel the match.
Police have arrested at least 2,400 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during nationwide demonstrations that attracted hundreds of thousands of people to denounce rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
PSG vs Barcelona: Predictions
Opta’s supercomputer has given PSG a 39.7 per cent probability of winning, while Barcelona have a 37.7 per cent chance.
There are 22.6 per cent odds for a draw.
PSG vs Barcelona: Head-to-head
(Only in the Champions League)
- Matches: 15
- PSG wins: 6
- Barcelona wins: 5
- Draws: 4
PSG vs Barcelona: Form guide
(Last five matches across all competitions; latest game first)
PSG: W-W-W-W-W
Barcelona: W-W-W-W-W
Who are the top players to watch?
Ferran Torres and Ousmane Dembele (PSG): Torres, who joined PSG after four seasons at Barcelona, is their leading scorer with seven goals in all competitions, including an opening day Champions League hat-trick. Dembele has had an all-round impact with six assists and four goals.
Raphinha and Lamine Yamal (Barcelona): With 14 goals, Raphinha is the most prolific striker in European club football this season. Such is his dominance that even a brief injury absence did not take away his top spot. Yamal, on the other hand, has been unstoppable in his own way – the 18-year-old winger’s nine goals and 10 assists make him a once-in-a-generation talent.
Team news and predicted lineups
PSG
PSG suffered a major blow shortly before Tuesday’s trip when left-back Nuno Mendes suffered a thigh injury during their 3-1 Ligue 1 victory at Strasbourg on Saturday.
Mendes will be unavailable for the “next few weeks”, according to the team who are also without Senny Mayulu with a similar issue.
Predicted starting XI:
Matvey Safonov; Achraf Hakimi, Marquinhos, Willian Pacho, Lucas Digne; Warren Zaire-Emery, Vitinha, Fabian Ruiz; Maghnes Akliouche, Ousmane Dembele, Desire Doue
Barcelona
Barcelona have been strengthened by the return of striker Raphinha and midfielder Frenkie de Jong.
Raphinha picked up a knock on recent international duty with Brazil and missed Barca’s wins over Getafe in the league and Galatasaray in the Champions League. Dutch international De Jong has not featured this season due to a knee issue sustained during the World Cup.
Both were on the bench in Barca’s last game, a 5-2 win over Real Betis, with Raphinha coming on as a second-half substitute.
However, defenders Eric Garcia and Jules Kounde are sidelined. Garcia will spend between “three to four weeks” out with a thigh injury, while right-back Kounde suffered an ankle sprain and will miss the game against PSG.
Predicted starting XI:
Joan Garcia; Xavi Espart, Pau Cubarsi, Gerard Martin, Joao Cancelo; Fermin Lopez, Rodri, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Raphinha, Anthony Gordon

aljazeera.com.title: Man claims arm broken in violent ICE arrest
aljazeera.com.text:
Man claims arm broken in violent ICE arrest
Video shows a man screaming in pain as ICE agents pin him down during an arrest in Long Beach, California. The family of Ricardo Gonzalez say he is a US citizen, and that ICE agents broke his arm during a wrongful arrest.

aljazeera.com.title: Four dead as torrential rain batters eastern Spain
aljazeera.com.text:
Four people have been killed as torrential rainfall sweeping eastern Spain triggered severe flooding, evacuations and shelter-in-place orders for tens of thousands of people, authorities said on Monday.
The downpour from Storm Adam, which started on Saturday, dumped as much as 700 litres of rain (185 gallons) per square metre in 24 hours in some areas of the Valencia region.
Floodwaters have since isolated several towns along the Mediterranean coast, while rivers have burst their banks and streets have turned into torrents, leaving scenes reminiscent of the catastrophic flooding that killed more than 230 people in the Valencia region two years ago.
The storm is confirmed to have killed four people: two in the coastal resort of Oliva, a third at a beach in Sagunto, and a fourth who fell into a swollen stream in Catalonia.
Winched to safety
On Monday morning, 800,000 residents were under shelter-in-place orders, but that was reduced to 87,000 in eight municipalities by late afternoon.
Security forces carried out more than 400 rescues in the Valencia region, according to government representative Pilar Bernabe.
People stranded on rooftops have been winched to safety amid widespread evacuations.
The storm, which also lashed the Balearic Islands and Catalonia, prompted authorities to order about 100 municipalities to remain indoors for several hours on Monday.
Most restrictions were lifted by early afternoon as conditions improved, the regional government said.
‘It’s a disaster’
In Els Poblets, northeast of Alicante, cars and vans were piled on top of one another from the force of the water, as residents tried to salvage what they could from their homes.
“The village, well, it’s a disaster. Some people have lost everything all over again, just like in 2007, when exactly the same thing happened,” resident Javier Fornez said.
More than 2,000 people were evacuated, mainly in Oliva, and authorities carried out nearly 100 rescues in Valencia and Alicante on Monday, the Civil Guard police said.
The mayor of Pego, Enrique Moll, told public regional broadcaster A Punt radio on Monday that several people were still waiting to be evacuated by helicopter from their roofs. All access routes to the town were blocked, he added.
The deputy mayor of Oliva, Salvador Llopis, told state broadcaster TVE on Monday that emergency services were rescuing trapped residents, particularly elderly people stuck inside their homes with water up to their waists.
National weather agency AEMET announced on Friday that last month was mainland Spain’s hottest September on record, after registering its warmest summer between June and August.

aljazeera.com.title: The human cost of surging US air strikes in Somalia
aljazeera.com.text:
Mogadishu, Somalia – Nearly a year after a suspected US strike in southern Somalia left shrapnel embedded in her son’s body, Maryam Haji Abdi Guled still feels compelled to accompany him to school.
She fears another child might push him while playing, disturbing a fragment of metal lodged near his hip. Doctors have warned that removing it could leave him paralysed.
“I hold his hand, take him to school, and I bring him back myself. I watch over him,” she told Al Jazeera.
Her son, Abdiqadir Salah, was seven when he was injured during a November 2025 military offensive involving United States air strikes and Somali ground forces around Jamaame, in Somalia’s southern Jubaland state.
Maryam is among several survivors interviewed by Al Jazeera in recent months who say family members were killed or seriously injured during the offensive. Their accounts describe deaths, displacement, lost livelihoods and injuries that continue to shape their lives.
Their testimonies come as US air operations against armed rebel groups in Somalia have intensified sharply under President Donald Trump.
Public records from the US Africa Command (AFRICOM) listed 84 strikes in Somalia through September 2026, while the New America Foundation, which independently tracks the campaign, documented 88 over the same period.
The US military has acknowledged conducting air strikes in the area on November 14 and 15, 2025. But it disputes allegations that its aircraft caused civilian casualties.
AFRICOM told Al Jazeera it had completed an assessment of reports that US operations killed between 10 and 12 civilians and destroyed homes and businesses in Jamaame. It concluded that the information reviewed did not meet the military’s “more likely than not” threshold for determining that US air strikes had caused the reported harm.
That finding does not establish that US strikes caused no harm. Rather, AFRICOM said the evidence did not establish that US operations were more likely than not to have caused the reported casualties and damage.
Al Jazeera asked whether investigators had spoken to survivors, relatives of those killed, hospital staff, local authorities or other witnesses. AFRICOM did not say whether they had done so.
The command said the assessment could be reopened if new information emerged that might change its findings.
The conclusion contrasts with accounts from families who say they witnessed the bombardment and with independent monitoring reports documenting civilian deaths and mass displacement during the offensive.
For those who lost loved ones or were left caring for seriously injured relatives, whether they will ever obtain justice remains unresolved.
A morning of bombardment
Maryam remembers the morning aircraft appeared over Jamaame. She was preparing breakfast after her children returned from school when they heard a roar overhead. Aircraft had become so common that the family no longer regarded the sound as unusual.
“The aircraft never leave us, night or day, and we have become accustomed to them,” she said.
Her children ran outside towards the noise. Maryam followed, intending to bring them back inside before the family fled. Then a munition struck nearby, followed by another explosion near the front door. More bombardment followed around the house.
Maryam believes the attack on her home was carried out by US drones that had been circling over the town before the bombardment.
Ugaas Ahmed Ugaas Said Ali, a Bimaal clan chief who remains in regular contact with families affected by the attacks, said the suffering extended far beyond those who had managed to leave Jamaame.
“Maryam is one of the fortunate people who has been able to obtain medical care. There are many injured people left in the town from that offensive who haven’t been able to make it to Mogadishu,” he said.
The costs that remain
Maryam recalled one munition hitting the ground without exploding, while other strikes killed people nearby. Amid the explosions, she became separated from her children. Three of her six children were wounded, including Abdiqadir, who suffered the most serious injuries.
It took her a day and a night to reach medical care in Mogadishu. During the journey, which lasted more than 24 hours, her son bled and struggled with pain.
Her experience was one of several reported during days of fighting in and around Jamaame.
According to Jubaland authorities, Somali government and regional forces, including the US-trained Danab commando unit, launched operations against positions held by the armed group al-Shabab in villages surrounding the town.
The authorities said at least 56 al-Shabab fighters were killed and 20 captured. Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.
AFRICOM declined to disclose how many strikes were conducted or which munitions were used, citing operational security.
Witnesses interviewed by Al Jazeera said the bombardment came without warning. Three people – two who said they had lost family members, and another whose home was destroyed – declined to speak on the record, citing concerns about their safety.
Ali said residents were afraid to discuss losses caused by air strikes and government offensives because they feared reprisals.
A monitoring network led by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) documented 12 civilian deaths during fighting and air strikes around Jamaame between November 16 and 18, 2025.
The figures cover different phases of an offensive involving both air strikes and ground fighting, making it difficult to establish which forces were responsible for individual deaths.
The UNHCR-led network also recorded 22,800 people fleeing Jamaame and surrounding villages between November 16 and 18, describing the displacement as “rapid and widespread”.
It reported damage to shops and storage facilities, restrictions on civilian movement in al-Shabab-controlled areas, and signs of psychological distress among those who had escaped.
For Ali Aden Borrow, a 52-year-old farmer from Jamaame, the offensive devastated his family. He was away from home when he received a telephone call telling him that his wife had been hit.
She was nine months pregnant and trying to gather their children to escape the fighting when debris from what Ali described as an air strike struck her neck. She and her unborn child died.
Their three surviving children, two girls and a boy, eventually went to live with their grandmother. Ali has since moved between villages and Kismayo, Jubaland’s de facto regional capital, searching for work and trying to support them.
The cost of food, transport and other necessities has left him in debt. He said the family had received little outside assistance.
Another farmer, Nuur Ali Nuur, was working his land when his wife was injured during the same period of fighting. He told Al Jazeera that debris from an air strike struck her lower body and right hand, leaving her paralysed from the waist down.
Their youngest daughter, who was still breastfeeding, was also slightly injured. Neighbours helped transport his wife to hospital while Nuur struggled to care for their five children.
He said he could not afford to take her promptly to better-equipped medical facilities and still owed money for her treatment. Even the journey towards Kismayo depended on persuading a driver to accept payment later.
Anna Zahn, the US-based archive lead at Airwars, said the consequences of air strikes could last for years. Injuries were often under-reported in Somalia, where treatment could be costly and prolonged.
“In fact, the medical care that is needed may not even be available because the very same strikes that caused the injuries could’ve damaged the infrastructure needed – roads, cars, hospitals, factories – to provide advanced and sustained medical care,” Zahn said.
Earlier research in Jubaland by the peace organisation PAX documented chronic injuries, lost livelihoods, displacement and psychological trauma following alleged US air strikes. Researchers said they could not establish the target status of those involved in most of the cases examined.
What did the US investigation establish?
Al Jazeera presented AFRICOM with the accounts of Maryam, Ali and Nuur, including the reported deaths of Ali’s pregnant wife and unborn child, the injuries that left Nuur’s wife unable to walk, and the shrapnel wounds suffered by Maryam’s children.
AFRICOM did not provide the underlying evidence supporting its assessment. It said its investigations draw on intelligence and operational reporting, much of which is not publicly available. It also did not say whether investigators had obtained testimony directly from the affected families.
Zahn said some strikes announced by AFRICOM generated no local reporting that researchers could find. In other cases, witnesses described harm that could not be confidently attributed to a particular force.
She added that AFRICOM had largely stopped routinely disclosing the number of fighters killed or injured in individual strike announcements from early 2025, reducing the information available for independent comparison.
AFRICOM has previously revised its findings on civilian casualties in Somalia, acknowledging deaths caused by its operations after initially reporting that no civilians had been harmed.
The command said that when an assessment establishes that US military operations more likely than not caused civilian harm, it considers appropriate and feasible responses, alongside measures intended to prevent similar incidents.
Those responses may include acknowledgement, an apology or compensation, depending on the circumstances. US legislation makes up to $3m available annually for discretionary payments to people killed or injured, or whose property was damaged, during US or coalition military operations.
Decisions also take account of factors including advice from the host government and potential risks associated with distributing payments.
Speaking in Mogadishu in July, AFRICOM commander General Dagvin Anderson said there had been occasions when US forces made mistakes and “provided reparations”. He also said the command investigated all credible reports of civilian harm.
Questions over targeting
On September 13, 2025, AFRICOM carried out a strike near Badhan in northern Somalia that it said killed Omar Abdullahi, a local clan elder travelling as part of a convoy. The command later identified him as an al-Shabab arms dealer.
Puntland’s Criminal Investigation Department subsequently said Abdullahi had no criminal record and was not under investigation.
Somalia’s Defence Ahmed Moallim Fiqi contested the killing in parliament, saying Abdullahi could have been questioned rather than targeted.
AFRICOM told Al Jazeera that its civilian-harm assessment of the strike did not meet the “more likely than not” threshold for attributing civilian harm to US operations.
Asked whether it still considered Abdullahi an al-Shabab arms dealer, what evidence supported that claim and whether the targeting decision had been reviewed, AFRICOM did not directly answer.
AFRICOM distinguishes between deliberate strikes, which are subject to multiple layers of review, and defensive strikes against imminent threats.
Its broad definition of combatants includes people deemed to provide material support for hostilities. This raises questions about how such determinations are made and how the criteria affect the risk of civilians being targeted.
The US says its strikes are conducted in coordination with Somalia’s federal government. Somalia’s Defence Ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
That cooperation has become increasingly important as Washington expands its air campaign against al-Shabab and the ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated armed group in northern Somalia.
An expanding air war
Zahn said the number of strikes during Trump’s second presidency had nearly reached the total carried out throughout his first term, at roughly four times the rate recorded under former US President Joe Biden.
Airwars data analysed for a separate investigation documented at least 216 civilians killed or wounded in US strikes in Somalia between 2007 and the end of May 2025.
That figure represents only the casualties the organisation was able to document, not an estimate of the full toll. It also predates the offensive around Jamaame.
US air operations in Somalia date back nearly two decades, when Washington began conducting strikes against suspected al-Qaeda-linked fighters in 2007. The campaign has since expanded into sustained military support for Somali forces fighting al-Shabab and, more recently, the ISIL affiliate in Somalia.
Under Trump, the US has loosened restrictions on who can authorise air strikes. The administration’s 2026 “counterterrorism” strategy says greater approval authority was returned to military commanders shortly after Trump took office, reversing the more centralised procedures used under Biden.
Anderson has welcomed the increased operational flexibility, saying it allows faster responses and more rapid air strikes as additional US military assets become available.
Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud also acknowledged the change during an appearance at the Council on Foreign Relations in September 2025.
“During the era of President Trump, it is bigger and much easier than before,” he said of US military support.
US officials argue that al-Shabab remains a direct threat to American interests. During his US Senate nomination process in 2025, Anderson described the group as al-Qaeda’s largest, wealthiest and most lethal affiliate. He said both al-Shabab and Somalia’s ISIL affiliate aspired to attack the United States.
Yet the expansion of US air operations has not eliminated al-Shabab, which has repeatedly regained territory after offensives by Somali and allied forces.
David Sterman, a senior policy analyst at the New America Foundation, said US operations under Trump initially concentrated on the ISIL affiliate in northern Somalia in early 2025, but gradually shifted back towards the south during 2026, historically the main focus of the campaign against al-Shabab.
Ahmed Suleiman Hussein, a national security official, wrote on X in May that government research had found that civilian harm from air strikes could generate grievances that al-Shabab and the ISIL affiliate might exploit for propaganda and recruitment.
Somalia has since adopted a national civilian-protection policy, which Hussein said needed to be consistently incorporated into “counterterrorism” operations.
A family unable to return
For Maryam, the Jamaame offensive has reshaped almost every part of her family’s life. After her children were injured, she initially fled into the countryside, but there was no hospital capable of treating Abdiqadir.
She eventually made the roughly 24-hour journey to Mogadishu, at times carrying him against her body because his injuries left him unable to sit or stand without severe pain.
“He was bleeding in the car and it was a rough road,” she said.
Once in the capital, Maryam moved between hospitals, searching for treatment. Doctors warned that removing the shrapnel lodged near Abdiqadir’s hip could kill him or leave him paralysed, she said.
At several hospitals, she was asked to sign documents absolving medical staff of responsibility if surgery caused further harm.
“I said, ‘No, I will not sign. Bring my son out to me,’” she recalled.
At another hospital, doctors recommended amputating his leg, which she also refused. In September 2026, after a fundraising campaign by the British newspaper The Guardian helped cover his treatment, Abdiqadir underwent surgery in Mogadishu.
Doctors removed two pieces of shrapnel but left another in place because of the risk of paralysis.
“He is currently able to play and move, and we can’t take this risk,” Maryam said.
She has remained in Mogadishu to keep him close to medical care, unable to resume the farming and livestock work that once supported her family in Jamaame.
“I cannot return there now. This child will not get medical care there, and the situation that we fled yesterday is still there, it is even possible that something worse could happen,” she said.

aljazeera.com.title: Zelenskyy seeks answers to why SpaceX Starshield defence is failing
aljazeera.com.text:
Zelenskyy seeks answers to why SpaceX Starshield defence is failing
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Starshield speed restrictions are disrupting early warning air defence systems. Starshield is the Pentagon-controlled military arm of Space X’s Starlink system. The US government has not explained the cause for the restrictions.

aljazeera.com.title: Beyond money: Why young Tunisians are considering emigration
aljazeera.com.text:
Tunis, Tunisia – For Maher Qassem, the phrase “beyond money” sums up why he is considering leaving his country.
After years of working in the media and trying to secure a stable life for his family, he is now thinking of starting over abroad. Buying a home and planning for a better future have given way to more immediate concerns: covering monthly expenses and meeting mounting financial commitments.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Qassem says almost his entire salary goes towards loan repayments, rent and his son’s education. At times, he adds, he has been unable to help his sick mother pay for medication and treatment.
Qassem is among many young Tunisians who see little meaningful change in their daily lives. Seven years into President Kais Saied’s rule, he worries about his son’s prospects and the quality of life the country can offer future generations.
Others, however, continue to trust the president.
Tunisians remain divided between those who believe the past several years have failed to deliver the change they hoped for and those who still believe reform is possible. These contrasting views unfold against a backdrop of persistent economic difficulties.
No change
Ghaith remembers the excitement surrounding the 2019 presidential election and the expectations raised by Saied’s victory. He was 19 at the time, had little interest in politics, and did not vote. But he recalls the hope that accompanied the president’s election.
Seven years later, Ghaith says, little has changed in his own life.
The cost-of-living pressures that existed then remain, he tells Al Jazeera, while ordinary citizens continue to face recurring difficulties obtaining some essential goods and services.
He is also frustrated by the authorities’ communication with the public. Tunisians want clearer answers about government policies and the results they are expected to deliver, he says. They also want accountability and a clear vision for the future.
For Qassem, the reasons for leaving extend beyond economic hardship. He believes working as a journalist has become more difficult, too.
Not everyone has lost faith in the president.
Mohamed Amine, a taxi driver in his 30s, voted for Saied in the most recent presidential election and remains convinced that he can improve the country’s situation.
The president is “sincere in his intentions” and wants change, Amine tells Al Jazeera. He believes, however, that various obstacles have hindered Saied’s reform programme.
It is too early to judge the outcome, he says. The president should be given more time.
Unemployment and emigration
Unemployment, particularly among young people and university graduates, remains a major challenge in Tunisia.
According to the National Institute of Statistics, the unemployment rate stood at 14.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026, with approximately 622,000 people out of work.
The situation is more severe among younger Tunisians. Unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 reached 35.4 percent, while the rate among university graduates stood at 26.6 percent. Among female university graduates, it was 35.6 percent, compared with 14.2 percent among men.
The desire to leave is widespread. A study by Afrobarometer, an independent African research network that conducts public-opinion surveys across the continent, found that around two-thirds of young Tunisians had considered emigrating.
The proportion who said they thought about leaving “a lot” rose from 38 percent in 2018 to 51 percent in 2024. Among young people considering emigration, 59 percent cited better job opportunities as their main motivation.
The findings point to frustration among a section of Tunisia’s youth and growing concerns about the prospects for professional and social stability at home.
The loss of skilled workers
The desire to leave extends beyond young people seeking their first jobs. Tunisia is also losing qualified professionals trained in the country.
Kamel Sahnoun, head of the Tunisian Order of Engineers, said at a press conference organised by the professional body that approximately 6,500 engineers left Tunisia in 2022 alone. The figure compares with an annual average of about 3,000 in 2013 and 2014, highlighting the scale of the departure of skilled workers.
The healthcare sector is also losing professionals.
Figures from the Tunisian Agency for Technical Cooperation show that 1,839 healthcare and paramedical professionals were recruited to work abroad in 2023. Another 1,022 were recruited during the first nine months of 2024, followed by 1,244 in 2025.
The figures, alongside international demand for Tunisian expertise, reflect the search for better working and living conditions abroad.
Beyond the economy
Hamza, a 26-year-old software engineer working for a foreign company, earns what he describes as a good income. Yet he is seriously considering leaving Tunisia.
“It’s no longer just about money,” he tells Al Jazeera.
His decision is shaped by several factors, including his lifestyle, his dealings with the administration, uncertainty about the future and the country’s broader economic situation.
Ramadan Ben Omar, a researcher specialising in migration, says the reasons people leave Tunisia have become more complex.
The motivations are no longer purely economic, he tells Al Jazeera. They also include the search for greater freedom, opportunities to participate in public life and the chance to build a better future.
Increasingly, he says, young people see emigration as a life project in its own right, rather than simply a way to improve their income.
Ben Omar also points to border areas such as Ben Guerdane, where accumulated economic and social pressures have prompted more young people to consider leaving through regular or irregular migration routes.
The question of the future
Maher has packed his bags for a new beginning in France. Hamza is weighing the decision despite his professional success. Ghaith is disappointed after years of waiting, while Mohamed Amine continues to believe in the possibility of reform.
Their contrasting experiences reflect a country grappling with economic difficulties and political uncertainty. For some, the prospect of a better life lies abroad; for others, hope for change at home remains.
The question facing Tunisia is whether it can offer its young people enough reason to stay.

aljazeera.com.title: Saudi Arabia cancels 2026 ‘Davos in the Desert’ amid Houthi attacks
aljazeera.com.text:
Saudi Arabia’s Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference has been postponed until next year, according to a statement on the official website, as deadly strikes by the Iran-backed Houthis against the kingdom continue.
The annual event was due to start next week on October 26 and run through October 29, with a date next year to be announced “very soon”, the statement released on Tuesday said.
FII Institute chief executive officer Dr Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud said the decision “comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates”.
“Because this is our landmark tenth edition, we want to ensure it delivers the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect and truly deserves,” she said.
Informally dubbed “Davos in the Desert”, a nod to the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Switzerland, the state-backed conference showcases the kingdom’s ambitious investment plans in a bid to attract billions of dollars needed to fund its economic transformation away from hydrocarbons towards tourism, sport and technology.
Expected speakers included: Alphabet & Google’s president and chief information officer, Ruth Porat; Goldman Sachs Group chairman and CEO David Solomon; and BlackRock chairman and CEO Laurence Fink, according to the FII website.
Fighting between a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis has escalated in recent weeks.
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, have hit military, energy and civilian infrastructure across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s international airport, killing at least 18 people and injuring hundreds more.
Government staff to work from home
Government agencies in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, have told employees to work from home, one worker and two consultants told the AFP news agency, as the city comes under repeated attack from the Houthis.
The Kingdom Centre, a 99‑storey tower in downtown Riyadh that houses the International Monetary Fund’s regional office, also requested workers stay away until further notice.
On Sunday, an employee of a government agency in the capital received a message saying, “It has been decided to implement remote work from Monday to Thursday this week”. The message added: “We ask everyone to continue their activities as normal.”
Companies based in the King Abdullah Financial District, which hosts offices of major United States firms, have also asked employees to work from home, according to other sources.

aljazeera.com.title: ‘Release Epstein files’, protester interrupts JD Vance’s speech
aljazeera.com.text:
‘Release Epstein files’, protester interrupts JD Vance’s speech
A protester demanding the release of the Epstein files interrupted US Vice President JD Vance at a North Carolina rally for Republican midterm candidates. After claiming illegal border crossings had fallen to zero, Vance joked that the protester was one who had slipped through.

aljazeera.com.title: Rashida Tlaib demands arrest of Israeli soldier tied to Hind Rajab killing
aljazeera.com.text:
United States Representative Rashida Tlaib has called for her government to arrest the commander of an Israeli military unit believed to be responsible for the killing of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in Gaza.
In a social media post on Monday, Tlaib pointed to reports that Israeli soldier Sean Glass was present in the US. She emphasised that the US had a legal responsibility to probe his involvement in Rajab’s death.
“As a party to the Genocide Convention and the Geneva Conventions, our government is obligated to arrest and investigate him for these war crimes and acts of genocide,” she wrote.
As part of her post, Tlaib shared a report from the Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF), which tracks Israeli soldiers suspected of war crimes in Gaza.
The group said it has filed an emergency request for the US Department of Justice to arrest Glass.
“Sean Glass commanded the ‘Vampire Empire’ Company implicated in the killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab, members of her family, and the medics sent to rescue them. HRF’s investigation places him and his troops in the direct vicinity of Hind’s vehicle during the killing,” the group said in a statement.
“Today, Glass walks free in the United States. HRF demands that the US authorities arrest him and bring him to justice.”
The five-year-old’s killing on January 29, 2024, triggered global outrage and became a symbol of Israel’s targeting of Palestinian civilians and children during its genocidal war on Gaza.
Rajab and her family were attempting to leave Gaza City when their vehicle came under Israeli fire.
Her family was killed in the gunfire. Rajab called emergency services, appealing to rescuers, “I’m so scared. Please come!”
Recordings of her telephone call made international news. But both Rajab and the rescue team that tried to reach her were ultimately killed by Israeli forces.
The car Rajab was in was riddled with 335 bullet holes, which Israeli authorities initially blamed on a firefight with Palestinian fighters.
An investigation by the group Forensic Architecture found no evidence of an exchange of fire and concluded that only Israeli forces had been present in the area at the time of the incident.
Israel has opened a probe into the killings, but such investigations are seen by Palestinians as a means of dodging accountability and buying time until outrage over an incident dissipates.
Experts at the United Nations and other human rights watchdogs have declared Israel’s assault on Gaza to be a genocide. At least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, including at least 21,000 children.
The US has continued to bolster Israel with diplomatic, military and economic assistance despite evidence of routine war crimes by Israeli forces in Gaza and elsewhere.
It has also denounced the International Criminal Court (ICC) for seeking the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant on charges of war crimes.

aljazeera.com.title: Hegseth meets Netanyahu in unannounced Israel visit
aljazeera.com.text:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an undisclosed visit to Israel, according to Axios.
The meeting between the hawkish ally of US President Donald Trump and the veteran Israeli premier facing a knife-edge election occurred on Monday, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.
The Reuters news agency could not immediately confirm the visit. The Pentagon and Israel’s embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and there was no immediate indication of what they discussed.
Trump endorsement
President Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social on Sunday to endorse Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election, the first vote since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks in 2023 and Israel’s genocidal campaign in Gaza began.
Trump praised the prime minister for being an ally of the US in its war on Iran. He added that Netanyahu had his “Complete and Total Endorsement”.
“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump wrote.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls suggest.
US Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.
“I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterms,” Vance, who travelled to Budapest and endorsed Viktor Orban in Hungarian elections earlier this year, said in an interview with digital media outlet 2WAY.
“I’m not anti-endorsing him, but I’m not pro-endorsing him; I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

aljazeera.com.title: Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded in Uganda
aljazeera.com.text:
An exiled vocal critic of the Rwandan government has been found decapitated near Kampala, south-central Uganda, according to a police spokesperson, in a case which remains under investigation.
Ugandan police said on Monday they were investigating the “murder of a male adult (around 50), whose head was cut off, and up to now, the head has not yet been recovered”, spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke told reporters, adding that the body had been identified by relatives as Robert Kabera.
The body was found in Luwala, a village near Kampala, and the killing likely took place late on October 16 or early on October 17, police added.
Robert Kabera, a former sergeant who fled Rwanda several years ago, was living in Uganda. The former soldier was not critical of the government during his time with the military, but grew increasingly opposed to Rwandan President Paul Kagame.
Kabera had a YouTube channel, “Major Robert TV”, with 144,000 subscribers. He featured a song praising opposition figure Victoire Ingabire, a rare voice of dissent in Rwanda who had been repeatedly imprisoned.
‘A witch-hunt’
In Uganda, “Robert had no issues with anyone”, his brother, Victor Agaba, told the AFP news agency.
“Our problem comes from home… The army created a criminal case against him. It was a witch-hunt,” he said.
Kabera was declared a fugitive after leaving Rwanda and accused of corrupting a minor, charges he denied.
Rwandan authorities have been accused of assassinating opponents of President Kagame, who has governed the country since coming to power in 2000. The Rwandan president took the reins in the aftermath of the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed, primarily from the minority Tutsi community.
Kabera is not the first opposition figure in exile to be assassinated.
In 2021, a former lieutenant in the Rwandan army, Revocat Karemangingo, was shot dead in Mozambique, where he was suspected of secretly supporting an opposition force.
Outspoken opponent Seif Bamporiki was shot dead in South Africa the same year, while a former Rwandan intelligence chief turned critic, Patrick Karegeya, was strangled in his South African hotel room in 2014.
Former general Faustin Kayumba Nyamwasa, who co-founded the Rwanda National Congress (RNC) opposition party with Karegeya and lives in exile, has survived several assassination attempts.

aljazeera.com.title: Iran war live: Trump says US hits Iran hard ‘economically and militarily’
aljazeera.com.text:
Iran war live: Trump says US hits Iran hard ‘economically and militarily’
Chinese Premier Li Qiang condemned US-Israeli attacks on Iran as ‘blatant aggression’, saying they came during talks and without UN Security Council consultation.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi emphasises that Iran and Russia are currently maintaining their closest strategic relationship in history following talks with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in Tehran.
US President Donald Trump says the United States continues to hit Iran hard “economically and militarily” while praising Russian President Vladimir Putin for “laying off Iran” and doing “nothing” in the conflict.

aljazeera.com.title: Mahmoud Khalil takes deportation fight to the US Supreme Court
aljazeera.com.text:
Pro-Palestine activist Mahmoud Khalil has petitioned the United States Supreme Court to review a court ruling that could pave the way for his re-arrest and deportation.
On Monday, Khalil’s lawyers filed an emergency application to the high court, seeking an immediate stay of a decision from Philadelphia’s 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals.
That court had ruled that federal law should have prohibited lower courts from ordering Khalil’s release from immigration detention in June 2025.
Instead, the appeals court said that Khalil’s detention should have been weighed first in an immigration court — a system overseen by the executive branch of the US government — and not in district court, which is part of the judicial branch.
In March 2025, Khalil became the first student protester known to be targeted for his pro-Palestinian views under the second administration of President Donald Trump.
A permanent US resident and former Columbia University graduate student, Khalil was arrested inside the student housing complex where he lived with his wife, a US citizen.
The push to deport Khalil has become a flashpoint in the debate over free speech on US campuses.
His petition to the Supreme Court could result in a major legal showdown that determines whether federal courts can intervene when noncitizens face retaliatory detention for speech protected under the First Amendment of the US Constitution.
Khalil’s lawyers have asked the Supreme Court to rule that noncitizens do indeed have the right to sue if immigration officials detain them as a reprisal for exercising free speech.
“If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech,” Khalil said during a news conference on Monday.
Trump campaigned for re-election in 2024 in part on a pledge to crack down on the pro-Palestinian student protest movement, which had erupted in 2023.
Columbia University in New York became an epicentre for such activism. Khalil, who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, had served as a spokesperson for the protest groups.
The Trump administration, however, has characterised pro-Palestinian activism as a threat to US foreign policy interests. It has argued it has the legal right to deport noncitizens who engage in such protests as a result.
After his arrest, Khalil was quickly moved to immigration detention centres in New Jersey, then Louisiana, where he remained in custody for more than three months.
Khalil faces deportation to Algeria or Syria if the 3rd Circuit Court’s decision holds.
In May, the 3rd Circuit narrowly voted six-to-five against reconsidering his case, but its decision will not go into effect until Khalil has exhausted his appeals.
He has fought his deportation both in the immigration court system and in the federal district court system, where he has filed a habeas corpus case. Both cases remain ongoing.
In April, the Board of Immigration Appeals denied his appeal in the immigration court system and issued a final order of removal in his case.
On Monday, faculty and staff at Columbia University held a silent vigil outside one of the school’s gates to protest what they described as “abducted students”, taken by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Placards with portraits of Khalil and fellow student protester Mohsen Mahdawi, among others, were hoisted into the air. Demonstrators called for solidarity with the students facing deportation and pushed for Columbia University to reopen its gates to the public after their closure during the protest movement.

aljazeera.com.title: Colombia illegal gold mine collapse kills 14 people
aljazeera.com.text:
The collapse of an illegal gold mine in southwestern Colombia killed 14 people and injured seven others, local authorities said on Monday.
The accident took place in the rural Chambero sector of the Santa Barbara de Iscuande municipality, located in the department of Narino.
Search and rescue operations have concluded, Narino Governor Luis Alfonso Escobar said.
Jorge Tovar Castillo, a disaster response official in Narino, said that an additional 12 to 15 miners have been reported as missing following the accident.
He said that municipal authorities were handling the response but added that communication had been difficult.
Santa Barbara de Iscuande is surrounded by dense rainforest and can only be reached by boat or small aircraft.
In a message on X, Escobar said the gold mine was an “informal” mine.
Informal and unregulated mining is common in rural parts of Colombia, where operations often lack adequate safety infrastructure, leading to frequent fatal accidents.
“At this moment our priority is to save lives, accompany families and guarantee an opportune response to this painful tragedy,” Escobar wrote.
In August, 13 people died in a similar mining accident in the municipality of Policarpa, also in Narino.

aljazeera.com.title: Tehran rejects any role in plot to kill leaders of German Jewish groups
aljazeera.com.text:
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has summoned Germany’s ambassador after a court in Hamburg found two men guilty of plotting to kill two leaders of Jewish organisations at Tehran’s behest, accusing Berlin of leveling “baseless political allegations”.
The decision to summon envoy Axel Dittmann came after Germany summoned the Iranian ambassador, Majid Nili Ahmadabadi, on Monday over allegations that Tehran was behind the plot to assassinate the two pro-Israel public figures.
“Levelling security-related accusations against Iran has long been a tactic employed by the Zionist regime and certain Western nations,” Iran’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement broadcast by official news agency IRNA.
“Attempting to provide a judicial face to baseless political claims not only fails to lend any credibility to such allegations but also undermines the standing of the German judiciary itself,” the statement added.
Hamburg conviction
Berlin’s allegations stem from a court case involving two men, a Danish national and an Afghan national, who were convicted in a Hamburg court on Thursday for planning to target the president of Germany’s main group representing the Jewish community and the head of the German-Israeli society.
The German Foreign Ministry said on X that the Iranian ambassador had been summoned, adding Tehran would not be allowed to “threaten our free society”.
“The malicious assassination attempts against Josef Schuster and Volker Beck will have legal consequences,” it added.
“We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and on those who defend it anywhere, and certainly not in Germany.”
The Dane, partially identified as Ali Hassan S, was jailed for eight-and-a-half years. The Afghan, who was recruited as his accomplice, was sentenced to four-and-a-half years.
Iran’s intelligence service steered the two men, the court said. The pair were arrested in Denmark last year and extradited.
In sentencing the men, the judge said they were guilty of “terrorist activities orchestrated by Iran”.
At the time they were charged, the Iranian embassy in Berlin released a statement rejecting what it called “unfounded allegations made at the behest of Iran’s enemies”.

aljazeera.com.title: Children among six killed in Russian drone strike on Ukraine park
aljazeera.com.text:
Children among six killed in Russian drone strike on Ukraine park
A Russian drone strike on a park in Ukraine’s north-eastern Kharkiv region has killed six people, including three children. The attack comes amid growing concerns over Ukraine’s air defences and Donald Trump’s moves to import Russian diesel.

aljazeera.com.title: Trump: ‘Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon’
aljazeera.com.text:
Trump: ‘Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon’
US President Donald Trump blamed immigrants for the unrest in France following a weekend of protests and looting, claiming Paris would soon become a ‘Muslim city’. He criticised French President Emmanuel Macron for not closing France’s borders.

aljazeera.com.title: Egyptian parliament delays vote on military support for Saudi Arabia
aljazeera.com.text:
Egypt’s parliament has delayed a vote on authorising its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia, which has come under increasing attack from the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen.
The vote has been adjourned to October 26, the House of Representatives said on Monday. The move prolongs the debate over Egypt’s role in the Yemeni conflict.
The opposition Egyptian Social Democratic Party said it had told its lawmakers to abstain.
The party said parliament had not been given enough information about the mission’s objectives, duration, cost, or the risks to Egyptian troops.
However, the party, which holds nearly a dozen seats, said most of its lawmakers support the measure, according to two members of parliament who spoke to the AFP news agency.
The parliament has been tasked with authorising President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to approve any request from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance amid attacks on the kingdom by Yemen’s Houthis.
The call for support came after the Iran-backed rebel group attacked Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco last week. Saudi authorities say 13 people were killed in the October 10 attack on the airport.
El-Sisi said on Saturday that Egypt would take “any measure” needed to protect its Gulf allies.
“I’m not talking about confronting or attacking anyone,” el-Sisi said. “We’re talking only about defence.”
After approval from the National Defence Council, chaired by el-Sisi, Egypt’s constitution requires a two-thirds parliamentary majority to send troops on a combat mission abroad. The council gave its approval on Sunday.
Egypt’s rocky economy
The Grand Imam of al-Azhar urged Arab and Muslim leaders on Sunday to mediate Egypt’s parliamentary decision and avert further bloodshed.
Saudi Arabia holds an important role in financing Egypt’s rocky economy. It is due to deposit $5.3bn into Egypt’s central bank this month, plus $267.39m in interest.
Egypt’s EGX30 stock index fell early on Monday amid concerns about possible military involvement but recovered to close 0.4 percent higher.
Nematallah Choucri, head of research at HC Securities, told the Reuters news agency that geopolitical developments are the main driver of recent market losses.
Egypt is also affected by the shortage of oil and gas exports from the Middle East due to the United States war on Iran and fighting in Yemen.
Egypt’s economy is heavily dependent on remittances from Egyptians working in the hydrocarbons industry in Saudi Arabia.
Suez Canal threat
Political analyst and Gulf studies expert Thomas Bonnie James told Al Jazeera that the Houthi security threat to Saudi Arabia also threatens the Suez Canal, which Egypt’s foreign minister says has lost about $11bn since the Houthis launched attacks in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in solidarity with Gaza in 2023.
James also said Egypt does not want to be seen as the regional ally that “stood aside while others defended the kingdom”.
Turkiye and Pakistan have made their own pledges after activating the Mecca defence pact with Riyadh, signed in August, amid the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East.

aljazeera.com.title: 160 people reported killed in escalating drone attacks across Sudan
aljazeera.com.text:
Sudan army accused of drone strike on livestock market
A wave of drone attacks across Sudan has killed more than 160 people in recent days, according to medics and rights groups.
Drone attacks on Khartoum killed three children on Monday, according to Emergency Lawyers, a group that monitors violence against civilians in Sudan’s civil war, while more than 160 were reported to have been killed in western regions since Friday.
The attacks were blamed on both the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and government forces, They have been fighting since 2023, but the increasing use of drones in recent months has caused growing numbers of civilian casualties.
The deadliest recent attack was near a market on Sunday evening in Al-Dibab town in the southwestern state of West Kordofan, which is controlled by the RSF. Residents and medical workers said a drone attacked a transport hub where villagers had gathered after a market day to find rides home, killing 80 people.
Another 47 wounded people were taken to the nearby town of Al-Mujlad, where 30 later died from their injuries, a medical source said, according to the AFP news agency.
The RSF’s self-declared administration, known as Tasis, and Emergency Lawyers accused the army of carrying out the attack.
Dams attack
In eastern Sudan, a military source said on Sunday that air defences intercepted several RSF drones targeting the Atbara and Setit dams in Gadaref state, about 420km east of Khartoum. There was no immediate comment from the RSF.
Early on Monday, another drone attack hit the RSF stronghold of Nyala, the capital of South Darfur. Medical and RSF sources said 17 people, including seven RSF officers, were killed and 23 wounded.
An RSF drone attack on Friday hit a gathering of displaced people in Sudan’s Blue Nile province on the border with Ethiopia, killing 41 people, Emergency Lawyers said.
The group condemned the attack, calling it a humanitarian tragedy.
The United Nations condemned the deadly attacks on Monday.
“We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting central services,” Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told reporters.
At least 59,000 killed
The current war in Sudan began in April 2023 when the military leader, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as Hemedti, fell out over plans to fold the paramilitary into Sudan’s army.
In June, Hemedti was sentenced to death in his absence for war crimes.
However, the fighting, now in its fourth year, continues and has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED. Aid groups say the actual toll is likely higher.
The UN says about 13 million people have been forced from their homes, creating what aid groups call the world’s largest humanitarian crisis.
Across Sudan, 33.7 million people, including 17.3 million children, urgently need food support this year. An estimated 825,000 children face severe, acute malnutrition, according to the UN.
The United States on Friday urged the UN Security Council to push for a humanitarian truce and expand an arms embargo on Sudan, but China and Russia opposed widening the embargo.

npr.org.title: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
npr.org.text:
Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
EDMONTON, Alberta — Voters in Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, results showed early Tuesday, delivering a victory for Prime Minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity amid U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and annexation threats.
The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.
With more than 1 million votes counted, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation.
"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.
Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. More than 1.35 million Albertans, or 43% of eligible voters, cast advance or special ballots. Albertans were deciding whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could have lead to a second vote on separation.
Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.
Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said Albertans have long been mistreated by Ottawa.
"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us and not return anything."
Taylor MacIsaac, another Wainwright voter, backed separation.
"I think it'll be good for Alberta to separate personally, as a very conservative individual that grew up in rural Alberta," she said.
Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than health care.
With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, "It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we're fighting among ourselves."
Jake Graham, 35, of Calgary, attended a Carney rally wearing maple leaf pants and a Canada hockey jacket. He hopes the vote ends the debate.
"I hope this squashes this for a long time to come and that it's clear and decisive, that these grumblings disappear for a while and we can be a united Canada," he said.
Despite the proposal's apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that will not disappear.
Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. "Vote like Canada's future depends on it because it does," he told a rally Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, even though she opposes independence. She cited a poll showing just 22% support for separation, a figure she said was still too high.
Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said.
Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.
Separatist advocate Jeff Rath said he would be thrilled if 30% of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as leader of her governing United Conservative Party and said the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party.

npr.org.title: DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalate
npr.org.text:
DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalate
The Justice Department announced on Monday it was charging 28 noncitizens with election crimes in California, signaling a further escalation over the state's voting system that looks like it will continue through Election Day and beyond.
The DOJ also filed an emergency request in federal court to stop California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls whom the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." The state has asked for specific information on how the federal government came to its conclusions, but has not received it.
"This Department of Justice will not look the other way while noncitizens vote in federal elections," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said at a press conference on Monday announcing the election crime charges. "Unfortunately the same can't be said for California and L.A. County."
Noncitizen voting has never been found to be a widespread problem in American elections, but the Trump administration is devoting significant resources to uncovering the ineligible voting that does occur. The DOJ has been announcing handfuls of new charges almost every day as early voting gets underway in many states.
The Justice Department's latest request in federal court is a continuation of a saga that began this summer with President Trump's primetime speech on election integrity. It took a major turn last week with the delivery of a flash drive to Los Angeles County that contained 20,000 names and a 48-hour deadline to investigate them. Local and state officials declined to do so, and the federal government sued.
McCotter escalated the dispute further on Friday by warning California officials in a letter that they could be criminally prosecuted for knowingly processing ballots "cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens." President Trump wrote on Truth Social that evening: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"
Taken together, the threats have local officials and election experts worried that the adversarial posture of the Justice Department towards California portends more actions to come aimed at delegitimizing results in this fall's midterms.
"There's a few things to be worried about," said Rick Hasen, an election law expert who runs UCLA's Safeguarding Democracy Project. "One is the risk of disenfranchising eligible voters. The other is the risk that it further undermines voter confidence in the electoral process by making it seem like [noncitizen voting] is a major problem when it is not. And the third risk is that this is going to be used as some sort of pretext to try to seize ballots or interfere after the election is over."
Dana Lewis, the Republican county recorder for Pinal County, Ariz., said local officials nationwide are watching and communicating about what's happening in California, the same way they did when the FBI raided an elections office in Fulton County, Ga. in January.
If those officials are administering a race this fall that is close or contested, they feel they could be next, she said.
"When this impacts another jurisdiction, you automatically have to feel that," Lewis said. "If it's happening in Georgia, if it's happening in Colorado or California, we're all watching."
New criminal charges against noncitizens in California
All 28 people charged in California on Monday are green-card holders, and all appeared on the list of 20,000 names the DOJ gave California officials last week, according to DOJ officials.
A number of them do not appear to have actually voted, and some registered to vote more than 20 years ago. Many are accused of making false statements in their naturalization applications, which ask whether applicants previously registered to vote or claimed U.S. citizenship.
Previous research has shown that when noncitizen voting and registration occurs, it is also often the result of bureaucratic error and not intentional fraud. New Jersey revealed this summer that a software glitch at the DMV registered more than 6,000 people to vote even though they had indicated they were noncitizens.
Bill Essayli, the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for California's Central District, downplayed that possibility on Monday, however.
"It's not something that just happens to you," Essayli said. "They either attested to it when they got a driver's license, or they went out of their way to file a voter registration form, and they swore under oath that they were a citizen."
In the past seven weeks, the Justice Department has charged 113 noncitizens across 20 states with voting and registration crimes, officials said at Monday's press conference.
UCLA's Hasen said the charges seem to be meant to make noncitizen voting "look like a bigger issue than it is."
"Given that there's over 20 million registered voters in California, this is quite a small number of allegations," Hasen said. "And we don't know how many of these allegations will even pan out. And so even if all of these were in fact people who were illegally voting, it's a drop in the bucket compared to the number of voters in California."
Recent polling suggests a sizable portion of the American public thinks immigration enforcement will be present at voting locations this fall, despite federal law banning armed federal agents from the polls. Non-white voters are more likely than white voters to say they fear voting could put them at risk of being questioned by immigration authorities despite being citizens.
In an interview earlier this fall with NPR, Los Angeles County's top voting official, Dean Logan, alluded to those worries.
"Given everything leading up to this election, what we're trying to remind voters is the best way to secure the election is through your participation," Logan told NPR. "Don't be distracted by the litigation. Don't be distracted by the mis- and disinformation. If you have questions, let us know, let us answer them. But don't let this keep you from voting," he said.
"Because if you're not voting, none of the rest matters, right?"
An unprecedented demand by DOJ
The Justice Department's request that a federal judge block California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots from the list of 20,000 "likely noncitizens" it gave state officials last week is unprecedented and an especially unusual request given that voting is already underway.
California officials have argued that complying with the Department's demand to set the ballots aside would be unlawful and noted the DOJ has not confirmed that the voters on the list are noncitizens.
"The extraordinary measures you demand are contrary to both federal and state law," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber wrote to the DOJ's McCotter on Oct. 13.
"Withholding ballots from some duly registered voters and segregating and refusing to tabulate voted ballots submitted by others, is an unprecedented suspension — and even denial — of voting rights," she wrote.
