theguardian.com.title: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles
theguardian.com.text:
Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s King Charles to Aung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation.
A presidential spokesperson said on social media that home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment.
Photos showed the Nobel Peace laureate smiling in a wood-panelled room, a paper calendar on the wall behind her.
Suu Kyi, 81, the daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San, has spent much of her life in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. She is now serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw, the capital.
Over her lifetime, the country’s military rulers have been cautious about locking Suu Kyi away in prison due to her beloved domestic status and international prominence, particularly in Britain, where she lived and married an Oxford academic. Most other political prisoners languish in jail.
Despite winning a 2015 election, she was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the independent conflict monitor ACLED. Since then, Suu Kyi’s whereabouts and health have been difficult to determine until an International Committee of the Red Cross visit in August.
Coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has been making efforts to rebuild regional and international diplomatic ties.
Kim Aris, Suu Kyi’s son who lives in London, said in a statement that he welcomed Charles’s gifts but warned their delivery should not be exploited by the regime.
“We must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy,” he said. “My mother’s fundamental human rights continue to be violated.”
Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington considers a genocide.
The former commander-in-chief has recently conducted several regional visits to rebuild bilateral ties with neighbours, after the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) regional bloc barred him from its summits for not following an Asean-brokered peace plan.
During his most recent trip to Malaysia this month, the leader was given an official welcome and honour guard. Min Aung Hlaing earlier visited Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.
Phil Robertson, director at the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates (AHRLA) group, said the Suu Kyi book photo op was part of Myanmar’s “quest for global legitimacy”.
“The bottom line is Asean has grown tired of arguing with Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s intransigent military leaders and having nothing to show for it, and they desperately want to move the bloc on to other, more cheery issues,” he said.
“So as the Asean dominoes fall to the Myanmar charm offensive, they just want to make their regional capitulation look good – and that requires Myanmar to play its part by trotting out Suu Kyi at occasional intervals to receive their latest beneficence.”
Min Aung Hlaing has also made efforts to reach out to Donald Trump’s administration, saying in a September interview with Time magazine that “it would be ideal if the US could cooperate with us”.
Weeks later, Reuters reported that the US and Myanmar officials had held talks in Naypyidaw and Tokyo, in part to shut down scam centres that target Americans, but which could be broadened to exploitation of Myanmar’s mineral deposits.
The US state department has said it is re-examining “the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country”. China has become Myanmar’s key global partner.
Myanmar has always denied the accusations of genocide, and Suu Kyi, who held the role of state counsellor at the time of the atrocities, defended the country at the international court of justice, disappointing many in her global support base.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

theguardian.com.title: Royal Exchange boss unveils new plays two years after damaging censorship row
theguardian.com.text:
A theatre boss has promised to channel the “pioneering spirit of Manchester” and be “brave and fearless” as she unveiled a new season of work, two years after a deeply damaging censorship row.
Selina Cartmell, the artistic director of the Royal Exchange in Manchester, revealed details of 2027-28 productions that include a retelling of the Munich air disaster and a modern Stockport-set version of the ancient Greek myth Phaedra.
Cartmell took over at the theatre two years ago, during what was one of the biggest crises in its 50-year history.
A production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream was cancelled in a dispute over one of the production’s songs, which referenced transgender rights and contained the phrase “free Palestine”.
There were accusations of censorship, although an independent review did not find that but did highlight “significant leadership failures”. The play’s director, Stef O’Driscoll, talked of a growing “fear-driven decision-making in the arts”.
Cartmell told the Guardian it had been “a very challenging time” for the theatre, and the board at the time took “full responsibility”. All the review recommendations were now in place, with “artists firmly back at the centre of the theatre”, she said.
“It was an incredibly complex and difficult period of our time, but we are absolutely, as a theatre, moving forward into the next chapter.”
Cartmell said she was interested in northern stories with an international reach, adding that risks would be taken – “all part of the pioneering spirit of Manchester”.
She said the theatre would reopen its 100-seat studio space next year, which has remained closed since the Covid pandemic.
She said the closure had been a “real loss to Manchester” and reopening it would allow the theatre “to nurture local talent and to tell really urgent stories”.
The first studio show since March 2020 will be Talking to Boys, by Abbi Greenland, which explores “what happens to one woman’s mind through 14 conversations with the men in her life”.
The reopening will coincide with a weeks-long closure of the main 750-seat in-the-round space for refurbishment, including the seats, which have been in place for 30 years.
Season highlights in 2027 will include the world premiere of a new play by Olivier and Tony award-winning Simon Stephens, The First Blue Thing.
Directed by Cartmell, it is a reimagining of the Greek myth of Phaedra – a princess who falls in love with her stepson, leading to terrible consequences – and will be set in Stephens’s home town of Stockport.
There will also be a new production of Guys and Dolls, and A Midsummer Night’s Dream with the soul singer and West End star Beverley Knight.
In 2028, 70 years after one of the defining moments in the history of Manchester – the Munich air disaster – the theatre will stage the world premiere of an adaptation of David Peace’s novel Munichs.
Munichs brings to life the story and aftermath of the air crash that killed 23 out of 44 passengers, including eight Manchester United players, three of its staff and eight journalists.
It has been adapted for the stage by Ben Power and will, Cartmell said, explore the “religion of football” and how a club, a community and a country were all changed by events on 6 February 1958.
The Royal Exchange is one of the UK’s leading regional theatres and has a proud history, Cartmell said, “of doing things differently, dancing to their own drum beat.
“I think Manchester has that spirit as well, that punky, edgy feeling of going: right, we need to take risks. We need to act with courage. We need to be brave and fearless. And this is the moment … Manchester, as we know, is going through an extraordinary moment in time.”

theguardian.com.title: Public support for founding principles of NHS is falling across UK population
theguardian.com.text:
Public support for the NHS’s founding principles – that it is free to use, available to everyone and tax-funded – has fallen over the last five years, research has shown.
Backing for all three pillars dropped between 2021 and 2025 across the UK population, except for a small rise in millennials’ support for the NHS being funded from taxation.
Experts said the sharp rise in economic hardship and changes in attitudes towards migration during those years could help explain the drop in support.
With healthcare swallowing up ever more public spending as the UK contends with an ageing population, and the government is under pressure to spend more on defence, social care and the special educational needs system, that decline could make it harder for ministers in future to justify raising the NHS budget.
The King’s Fund thinktank analysed British Social Attitudes survey data on attitudes towards the NHS’s founding principles among five age groups: gen Z (born 1997-2012), millennials (1981-1996), gen X (1965-1980), boomers (1946-1964) and those born prewar.
Support for the NHS being free of charge and available to everyone has fallen in recent years across all five groups. While large majorities still agree that it should be available to everyone, the decline in that belief was particularly striking. The proportion of those born before the second world war who think that declined from 87.1% in 2021 to 73.2% last year – a 13.9 percentage point fall. Among boomers it fell from 83.1% to 71.2% – down by 11.9 percentage points.
Support for the NHS being free of charge was also down, but by smaller proportions, and it remains a belief shared by between 85% and 92% of the population.
However, the analysis also revealed the emergence of what the King’s Fund called “a generational fault line in attitudes to NHS funding”, with gen Z holding different views from other age groups.
Support among gen Z for the NHS remaining tax-funded fell by 11.2 percentage points from 2021-2025 – a bigger drop than among gen X, boomers and the prewar cohort. Fewer than four out of five gen Z (74.1%) hold that belief, compared with at least 80% elsewhere.
Danielle Jefferies, a senior analyst at the King’s Fund, said that public backing for the NHS’s underlying principles remained strong 76 years after its creation.
“Nevertheless, politicians and the public should not take that support for granted. Our analysis shows a slight fall in support for the founding principles of the NHS over the last five years, against a backdrop of record low public satisfaction with the NHS and growing divisions across different age groups and political perspectives.
“The public’s longstanding support for the NHS is often wrapped up with the country’s identity, so it is hard to unpick exactly why support for the principles might be falling slightly. While there is no single explanation for the recent shift, wider changes in public attitudes may be playing a role.
“For example, the latest British Social Attitudes survey suggests that changing attitudes towards migration may play a role in declining certainty about the principle that the NHS should be available to everyone.”
Economics probably explains Gen Z’s attitudes, Jefferies added.
“Gen Z are coming of age in incredibly challenging economic climate. Analysis from the Institute for Fiscal Studies suggests that younger adults today are economically worse off than previous generations at the same age. They face high housing costs, significant student debt, years of wage stagnation, and were the first generation to come of age in the aftermath of austerity and during the Covid-19 pandemic.
“Against that backdrop, it’s perhaps unsurprising that younger adults are more hesitant about paying higher taxes to fund public services. Add to that that many younger people might be trying to access [NHS] services like mental health support and dealing with long waits, many could feel short-changed,” Jefferies said.
“When living standards have stalled and many are dissatisfied with public services like the NHS, support for paying more tax cannot be taken for granted.”
Long waiting times for NHS care such as A&E, surgery, cancer treatment and mental health help may influence public opinion too.
Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of NHS Alliance, said: “At a time of huge and sustained challenges for the health service, it is natural that people may question the funding model, though it’s worth noting that even in generation Z, a large majority backed the current approach.
“That said, any erosion of support is a concern. The NHS must keep delivering for the public and for patients, and making the case for continued public backing, including through their taxes.”

theguardian.com.title: New Bradford railway station will ‘transform travel across the north’
theguardian.com.text:
A new railway station will be built in Bradford to “transform how people travel across the north”, the government has announced.
The station will be at the heart of the Northern Powerhouse Rail (NPR) scheme, built on the current Bradford Interchange site but allowing through trains between Leeds and Manchester.
With the promise of more frequent and faster services, it is expected to support new homes and jobs for the West Yorkshire city, located alongside its Southern Gateway regeneration project and connecting to the proposed tram to Leeds.
Approval of the station, which is expected to be built by the mid-2030s, has been regarded by northern leaders as a critical sign of political commitment to improving rail links across the north, after long delays in delivering pledged upgrades.
The Department for Transport said that NPR would allow a “turn-up-and-go railway” for passengers from Bradford, with sufficiently frequent trains running across the north for people not to need to check timetables.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “Today marks an important milestone for Bradford with a brand-new station that will transform how people travel across the north.”
The new station, along with the proposed West Yorkshire mass transit network – better known as the Leeds tram – will bring more than £1bn in economic benefits, according to Bradford council.
The mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, said: “Bradford has so much untapped potential, and faster, more frequent trains to Leeds and Manchester, and the transformation of the city centre will help to finally unleash it.”
Henri Murison, the chief executive of the Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said the decision to build a new station at Bradford Interchange represented “a long-term commitment to the city and the wider north”. He added: “Confidence is already building here, and this will help build it further.”
NPR was first promised by the Conservatives in 2014 but no firm funded plans emerged for the proposed railway linking cities from Liverpool to Hull.
The government under Keir Starmer announced in January that NPR would be delivered in three stages, with a funding cap of £45bn, which could be topped up by local contributions.
The scheme will start by improving connections on existing lines around Yorkshire. It also includes plans for a new line between Liverpool and Manchester.
As mayor of Greater Manchester at the time, Andy Burnham had championed a new underground station for Manchester Piccadilly as part of the project, which the Treasury did not approve.
The rail industry is also anticipating more work on improving Manchester-Birmingham links to replace the scrapped HS2 northern leg, another transport issue long pushed by Burnham.
Northern transport links could be improved further after the mayor of South Yorkshire and other leaders announced plans to bring Doncaster Sheffield airport into public ownership.
The combined authority and Doncaster city council are set to buy the airport from Peel Land, hoping to restart freight next year and passenger flights by spring 2028.
The airport’s owners shut down operations in November 2022, regarding it as commercially unviable.
However, South Yorkshire’s mayor, Oliver Coppard, said that, subject to formal approval, a deal was now going through that “puts the future of DSA back in our hands and finally gives one of the biggest and best growth opportunities in South Yorkshire the platform for long-term success that it needs and deserves”.
He said the government’s devolution agenda had allowed them to now act to resume flights to the city, adding: “When the airport closed, almost everything was against us; the owners did not want to sell, we had no legal powers to intervene or stop the airport from closing, and no backing from the government at the time. Today, the sky’s the limit.”

theguardian.com.title: Mother of alleged Alan Jones victim ‘absolutely trusted’ the radio host, court told
theguardian.com.text:
The mother of the youngest alleged victim of Alan Jones has told a Sydney court she “trusted” the 2GB broadcaster and was “comfortable” her teenager was going to spend a weekend at his Fitzroy Falls property.
The young man, known as complainant A, has testified that when he was 17 he was alone at the southern highlands farm when Jones allegedly kissed him, put his tongue inside his mouth and touched him on the bottom. “I felt violated and I felt gross,” he told the court earlier.
Complainant A is one of five men who allege Jones, 85, sexually touched them between 2003 and 2020. All five have now completed their evidence as the trial enters its 11th week.
Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.
A’s mother gave her evidence-in-chief on Tuesday in the Downing Centre local court after her son had spent more than a week in the witness box interrupted by multiple legal arguments.
The divorced mother, who was facing financial ruin and mourning a death in the family, said she “absolutely trusted” Jones as she had read many emails from him in which he said what a wonderful young man her boy was.
“I was just so pleased to have an older mentor in [A’s] life that was interesting and interested in so many things … and saw my son was as intelligent as he is and engaging,” she said.
Jones, who had been corresponding with A since the then 13-year-old asked him for help with his mother’s “dire” financial problems, had never invited her to his home but had invited the teenager on multiple occasions, the court heard.
She said her son had meals with Jones at a local pub and at his Circular Quay apartment but she was never invited.
When her son returned from his two-night stay during the school holidays, the mother said she “knew straight away something was up” because “his mood was different” and he wasn’t sleeping.
“He told me had had broken a plate and he was remorseful about that,” she said. Complainant A earlier told the court Jones was “frustrated, annoyed and angry” when he dropped a $1,500 Versace plate.
Ten days after he returned from Fitzroy Falls her son handed her a “scrawly” note and said “I don’t want to talk about it”, she said as she broke down in tears in the witness box when handed a copy of the note by a court officer.
Her son earlier told the court he wrote a vague account in the note which said he “felt violated at Fitzroy Falls about an incident of a sexual nature”.
She said she read the note and asked her son if he wanted to report the alleged assault to the police. He declined, saying: “I wasn’t raped. It is probably not a big thing in the scheme of it. It will be my word against his and he is a powerful man.”
The witness said she told her son “not to have any contact” with Jones, but she continued to correspond with the broadcaster about issues he had been helping her with, including repairs on her house, which Jones paid for to the tune of $100,000.
Asked why she continued to correspond with Jones, the witness said: “I was scared because I had already asked [A] if he wanted to go to the police” and “nothing with the bank was finalised”.
She said she was afraid Jones could withdraw the assistance he had provided and “that was pretty frightening”.
The witness said she gave her first statement to police several years later, in May 2024.
In December 2025 she found the note and handed it to the detective who was investigating A’s case.
The trial continues.

theguardian.com.title: In ruby-red Kansas, Trump contemplates the possibility of a Democratic win in the state
theguardian.com.text:
The fact that Donald Trump was here at all said more about a looming electoral disaster facing his Republican party next month than anything contained in his dark and discursive 98-minute stump speech.
On Monday, amid raucous chants of “USA! USA!”, the president held his first campaign rally in Kansas for eight years. No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in this ruby-red state since 1932, the year Herbert Hoover was president, Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and the Nazis became the biggest party in the German Reichstag.
Since then Republicans in the state have built one of the longest winning streaks in Senate history, but such is the collapse in public esteem of the president that the midterms on 3 November could be the night that a blue wave engulfs the heart of Trump country.
“You’re really sort of – I hate to say it – you’re sort of tending toward the purple,” the president told about 5,000 supporters in a multipurpose arena outside Wichita, acknowledging that Kansas already has a Democratic governor in Laura Kelly. “That’s why I have to be sure that we get this guy.”
The “guy” concerned was Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican senator facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor. Opinion polls show them running neck and neck. In the third quarter, Hamilton reportedly raised $11m while Marshall managed just $800,000.
Marshall, 66, is an obstetrician-gynaecologist and ex-congressman who has proved a staunch Trump ally, including by embracing his debunked claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Hamilton, 62, founded the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the biggest United Methodist congregation in the country. He opposes Trump’s tariff agenda and what he calls the president’s “erratic leadership”.
Despite Hamilton’s background as a pastor and former Republican, Marshall insisted on Monday that Hamilton was “too woke for Kansas”. Accompanied by Chuck Berry’s Johnny B Goode as he walked on stage, Marshall said: “This is a guy that participates in protests against police. He supports drag shows. He tells us to apologise for the colour of our skin. And in a state with more cattle than people, he tells you to stop eating beef.” The crowd jeered each time.
Trump, 80, is barnstorming the country in what some have called a “desperation tour” aimed at rescuing Republicans from the hole he has dug for them. Critics suggest he might actually be making life harder by nationalising races that candidates would prefer to keep focused on local issues.
By imposing himself in Kansas, at a rally that was disrupted by several protesters, Trump underlined the election as a referendum on his presidency, with the potential to cost Republicans control of both the Senate and House of Representatives just two years after they swept into power.
Farmers in Kansas, a heavily agricultural state, have been hit hard by the consequences of the Iran war: a gallon of diesel costs nearly $6. The president upset cattle ranchers with a plan to reduce import tariffs to lower the price of beef and with aggressive immigration raids that prompted some agricultural workers to stay at home. On Monday Trump announced a new program to provide farmers with $8bn in support to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.
The election will test whether the old playbooks that fuelled his presidential campaigns – hurling insults, stirring bigotry and telling lies – can still work among an electorate weary of the cost of living, foreign wars and government corruption.
Trump launched a tirade against Hamilton, dismissing him as a “radical left lunatic” and a “phoney who’s pretending to be a moderate”. Trump claimed the Democrat supports flooding Kansas with refugees who “go around killing people”, that he used church money to fund “transgender crap”, that he “openly mocks Jesus” and that he believes America is systemically racist.
“He wants you to repent for being born white,” Trump said.
The president also sought to weaponise the recent upheaval in France, pushing the baseless nativist claim that the violence is being led by immigrants. “We’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he said. “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America.”
Trump unleashed bitter attacks on three Muslim politicians: Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. When Tlaib’s name was mentioned, members of the crowd yelled: “Deport her!” Trump falsely claimed that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt. He mockingly warned that, should El-Sayed be elected and sit on the Senate intelligence committee, he would leak information to the enemy.
Supporters roared their approved, thrilled by what they saw as Trump’s transgressive daring. The president, who won Kansas by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, showed he can still draw a crowd in one of the most surprising battleground states in the country.
Earlier, in warm sunshine, a long line of people snaked through fields outside the 5,000-seat multi-purpose arena in Park City, Kansas. There were sights that have become familiar over more than a decade: giant Trump flags, tables full of “Make America great again” caps, spangly “DJT” and “Trump the golden age” jackets, “Alligator Alcatraz” merchandise, “We are all Charlie Kirk now” sweaters and T-shirts that said “Stand for the flag, kneel for the cross”.
One woman wore a sweater that said: “0% liberal.” One man wore a T-shirt that declared: “I love Trump because he pisses off all the people I can’t stand.”
For these supporters, Trump rallies are galvanising and still the best way to get out the Republican vote. Cybersecurity worker Justin Nelsen, 44, said: “It fires us up, it gets us all excited for the cause and allows us to put out there what we want here as the state of Kansas. That’s why I’m here.”
Attendees were aware of the danger posed by Hamilton. Brittany Jones, a 33-year-old lawyer wearing a Stars and Stripes sweater, said: “If you know Adam Hamilton at all you know that he’s a problem and a chameleon and good at saying what he thinks people want to hear, even if he doesn’t believe it. He has shown himself to be not only a turncoat to things that matter to Christians, he has wholly given himself to the local agenda. Even though he claims to be a moderate, there’s nothing moderate about him.”
A Democratic victory here would represent a political earthquake, Jones acknowledged. “It’s seismic. It would be sad for most Kansans when they realise what happened, and some people just aren’t thinking through the consequences, but he has a built-in audience of people who are highly motivated.”
Jones, who had her friend’s three-month-old baby, Hannah, tucked under one arm, said she mostly welcomed Trump’s second term. “Overall I care about the social issues and he’s done a lot to protect girls’ sports, he’s done a lot to protect kids from being put through harmful gender transition procedures. Those things matter to me, they matter to the future of girls all across Kansas and America, and so I’m excited about those things.”
Construction worker Thad Snider, 42, who attended wearing a red “Make America Great Again” T-shirt alongside his mother, said he was not overly worried about the Senate seat falling to the Democrats.
“I don’t think Adam’s as strong a candidate as what the media is trying to sell him as,” he said, pointing to Hamilton’s past political donations to Democrats including Hillary Clinton. “I don’t think it’s going to happen but, if it did happen, it would be very shocking.”
Snider argues that voters faced a stark choice between political parties, describing the Republicans as the “least bad” option because “at least they’re not socialists or communists”. He added that he disagreed with foreign wars and wished Trump had done more on election integrity, but remained loyal to the president. “Any time you turn around a battleship, it takes time.”
That sentiment was echoed by Darrell Claphan, 72, a retired sales worker, who said of Trump: “He’s doing fantastic. He’ll go down in history being the number one president at what he’s done for the country in my lifetime.”
Claphan dismissed opinion polls showing a close race, stating: “Polls have been wrong ever since I’ve been alive.”
Asked how he would react to a Democratic Senate victory in Kansas, Claphan said: “I’d be shocked. But I don’t think it’s going to happen.”

theguardian.com.title: ‘These risks are real’: the threat of AI bioweapons – podcast
theguardian.com.text:
Support the Guardian: theguardian.com/sciencepod
‘These risks are real’: the threat of AI bioweapons – podcast

theguardian.com.title: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
theguardian.com.text:
As Republicans confront mounting political headwinds ahead of November’s midterm elections, Donald Trump is attempting to turn unrest in France into a cautionary tale for American voters, recasting the demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living as evidence of the dangers of immigration and the erosion of western civilization.
At a rally in Kansas on Monday evening, Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” he said.
Nationwide protests in France on Saturday were called over rising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they erupted into looting and clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday, overnight curfews were issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris.
“This is what’s happening to France – they want to happen to our country. It’s never happening here,” Trump declared, drawing loud cheers from the thousands-strong crowd in ruby-red Kansas where the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Earlier in the day, Trump repeated his baseless claim that migrants had “taken over” France, writing on Truth Social that the country’s leaders must “CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!”
The rhetoric echoes France’s far-right National Rally, whose president, Jordan Bardella, described the violence as a convergence of ultra-left extremism and delinquent populations from the suburbs. Trump and Vance have both publicly backed Marine Le Pen, and the unrest has added pressure on Emmanuel Macron six months before an April election to choose his successor.
As Trump set off for the Kansas rally on Monday, the US president told reporters at the White House that he had warned Macron he was “making a big mistake”.
“The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,” he said, adding: “We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
Before Trump arrived on stage in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities, which included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.
The demonstrations in France began weeks ago, when high school students began marching for teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. The CGT, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the movement and called for lower prices, higher pensions and better wages. The anger has since widened to fuel prices, which have climbed since US strikes effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, and other economic grievances.
As the midterms loom, the unrest in France offers Trump a familiar politcal opportunity: the chance to transform a crisis on the other side of the Atlantic into an argument in favor of the hard-line immigration policies that helped propel Trump’s return to the White House.
“If you import the third world, you become the third world,” the official White House X account posted earlier in the day..
JD Vance and array of Republican politicians have lined up to make a similar argument.
Sharing a video that showed the historic city hall in Limoges alight, vice-president JD Vance argued that the rioting was the result of what he called a liberal failure. “Western liberals imported the third world into France,” he wrote on X, adding that the country had “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”.
House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
Not all protests have drawn the same attention from Washington, as young people have taken to the streets across Europe, in Spain, Portugal and Italy, over underfunded schools, housing costs and a wider squeeze on living standards.
Neither has the president commented on protests in Albania, where demonstrators have targeted both the government and a luxury tourism development backed by an investment firm founded by Trump’s close familyson-in-law, Jared Kushner.
But Republicans are eager to keep the attention on France, as they warn of threats to the national identity and seek to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.
The vice president said he hoped Americans were paying attention as they cast their ballots.
“This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” Vance concluded.

theguardian.com.title: At Kansas rally, Trump focuses closing midterm message on anti-Muslim racism – as it happened
theguardian.com.text:
Trump focuses closing message on anti-Muslim racism, with attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib
Donald Trump made anti-Muslim racism a focus of his attacks on Democrats in remarks in Kansas on Monday, with attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, and gratuitous mentions of Barack Obama’s middle name.
“Democrats are the party of Abdul Mohammad El-Sayed,” Trump said of the Michigan Senate candidate.
The president then repeated his riff about what a brilliant move it was for him to stop using El-Sayed’s first name and instead call him “Mohammed El-Sayed”, to better stoke Islamophobia.
“You know, he got very upset because I called him Mohammad. I just felt like it. Somebody said, ‘How did you do that?’ I said, ‘I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want’”, Trump said.
“And actually his middle name is Mohammad,” the president added, before adding: “One good thing if you call somebody from that part of the world Mohammad, you’re about 65% sure to get it right. So if you have any problem with names, just call the guy Mohammad.”
El-Sayed responded to Trump mocking his name at a previous rally by writing on social media: “He says the name just fine when he’s begging the Qataris for a personal jet or the Saudis for funding for his son-in-law’s private equity firm.”
Despite being in Kansas to campaign for Republican senator Roger Marshall, Trump returned again and again to attacks on El-Sayed, and brought up two Muslim congresswoman, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, who are also not from Kansas.
He also lied that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt, a wild claim that is not supported by any evidence at all but is repeated almost daily by the president.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:

Speaking outside Wichita, Kansas on Monday, Trump seemed to back off his threat to ban the sale of jets made by the Canadian manufacturer Bombardier, which employs 1,500 people in Wichita.
Trump also frankly stated that he will only use the power of the federal government to allow year-round sales of gasoline containing higher volumes of ethanol if Kansas voters re-elect Republican senator Roger Marshall.
According to AdImpact Politics, a firm run by Donald Trump’s former campaign manager, Brad Parscale, has reserved $32,000 in advertising time to broadcast ads on behalf of the state of Israel in the Des Moines, Iowa market starting on Saturday, 24 October. According to video posted on social media by one Iowa farmer, an ad making the case for the Iran war, and for US support for Israel, has already started running on the Roku streaming service in the state.
Amid concerns that the Trump administration could use the power of the federal government to intimidate voters from casting ballots against Republicans, the senior federal prosecutor in south Texas released a menacing social-media video, promising to hunt down “crooked local election administrators”.
State of Israel is paying to run TV ads supporting Iran war in Iowa ahead of midterms
According to AdImpact Politics, a firm run by Donald Trump’s former campaign manager, Brad Parscale, has reserved $32,000 in advertising time to broadcast ads on behalf of the state of Israel in the Des Moines, Iowa market starting on Saturday, 24 October.
According to video posted on social media by one Iowa farmer, an ad making the case for the Iran war, and for US support for Israel, has already started running on the Roku streaming service in the state.
“I’ve been seeing these Israeli propaganda ads running for the last 2 weeks in Iowa,” the farmer wrote. “Nothing about candidates, just how Israel is good for us.”
The ad closes with a web address that directs viewers to the website Iowa4israel.com, created by Parscale’s firm, Clock Tower X, and featuring the full video.
Trump says he will not allow year-round sales of gasoline blended with 15% ethanol if Kansas elects Democratic senator
In addition to repeating a huge number of false claims about his presidency is his remarks in Kansas which have just ended, Donald Trump also frankly stated that he will only use the power of the federal government to allow year-round sales of gasoline containing higher volumes of ethanol if Kansas voters re-elect Republican senator Roger Marshall.
To make sure his message was clear, the president then said that he would block the sales if Democrat Adam Hilton wins the seat.
The year-round sale of gasoline blended with 15% ethanol has long been a priority of the biofuels industry.
Currently, gasoline containing 10% ethanol can be sold year-round, but sales of the 15% blend, known as E15, are restricted during summer months because the fuel evaporates more readily in hot weather and contributes to smog.
The Environmental Protection Agency can issue an emergency fuel waiver to allow the sale of E15 in the summer, and did so March in an attempt to lower costs for consumers amid the oil-price shock brought on by Trump’s war on Iran.
As he listed what he called the “goodies” he has granted to the people of Kansas in his remarks in Kansas on Monday, Trump said: “I also gave Kansas a waiver to sell E15 all year round. And with Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year round E15 permanent. But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him.”
In Kansas, Trump says he will drop tariffs on Canadian jet manufacturer key to Wichita economy
Speaking outside Wichita, Kansas on Monday, Donald Trump seemed to back off his threat to ban the sale of jets made by the Canadian manufacturer Bombardier, which employs 1,500 people in Wichita.
Last month, Trump intensified his trade war with Canada by writing on social media: “NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!”
The announcement threatened Wichita’s economy, where the company has invested hundreds of millions of dollars and Bombardier is the third largest aerospace employer.
In his rambling remarks on Monday, the president seemed to suggest that, despite this decision he made, Kansas voters should re-elect Republican senator Roger Marshall, since he had called to try to get Trump to lift the ban on a company whose name seemed to escape him.
“Because of Roger and his phone call, I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straight in a way. Is that right, Roger? I’ll be helping them,” Trump said.
“Because I always viewed them as a Canadian company. You know what I’m talking about,” the president went on, still failing to identify the company or say how, exactly, he was going to “help” them. “But now I find out they have a presence here, and we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas. So we’ll take care of those people.”

The president then repeated his riff about what a brilliant move it was for him to stop using El-Sayed’s first name and instead call him “Mohammed El-Sayed”, to better stoke Islamophobia.
“You know, he got very upset because I called him Mohammad. I just felt like it. Somebody said, ‘How did you do that?’ I said, ‘I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want’”, Trump said.
“And actually his middle name is Mohammad,” the president added, before adding: “One good thing if you call somebody from that part of the world Mohammad, you’re about 65% sure to get it right. So if you have any problem with names, just call the guy Mohammad.”

Despite being in Kansas to campaign for Republican senator Roger Marshall, Trump returned again and again to attacks on El-Sayed, and brought up two Muslim congresswoman, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, who are also not from Kansas.
He also lied that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt, a wild claim that is not supported by any evidence at all but is repeated almost daily by the president.
Trump repeats wildly false claims that inflation is down and schools are performing transgender surgeries
Donald Trump’s ongoing speech to supporters in Kansas is filled with false claims he has made previously at rally after rally. Among the whoppers the president told are that inflation, which is up since he took office and started a war with Iran that has driven global oil prices sky-high, is down.
“We’ve got it cooked, the inflation,” Trump said. “Once that oil comes down, that’ll be the final straw.
Democrats, the president claimed in another wildly false tale that he tells day after day, are in favor of “transgender for everybody - the absolute mutilation of your children, where your son Timmy comes home five days later as Sarah and you don’t even know about it.”
“The worst thing they did to us is allowing 25 million people into our country totally unchecked, totally unfettered,” the president also said, wildly inflating the total number of undocumented immigrants in the United States.
Trump repeats racist false claim that rioting in France is related to immigration
Speaking in Kansas on Monday, Donald Trump repeated his entirely imaginary theory that the wave of protests and rioting in France is being led by immigrants.
In fact, as the Guardian’s Jon Henley reports from Paris, a month-long student protest by over crumbling and crowded classrooms “converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.”
Those largely peaceful protests were hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and set fire to Limoges’ city hall.
Despite on-the-ground reporting on the protests from news organizations across the political spectrum, Trump and Republicans, including Fox News hosts, have insisted that the rioters in France are immigrants.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France, a once great nation that is being conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity,” Trump said, desperate to return to his obsession with nativist resentment and racism.
“They hate, frankly, the Western civilization itself,” the president went on. “And as we’re seeing in Europe, globalists, left-wing politicians have treasonously imported millions and millions of Third World migrants who are totally incompatible with West, and they are incompatible with Western values. They despise everything about France, and they’re destroying that country. And we’re not going to let that happen to this country.”
Protesters disrupt Trump rally in Kansas, where Republican fear losing US Senate seat
Protesters disrupted the first minutes of Donald Trump’s speech to a Republican midterm campaign rally in Kansas, where his party is concerned that his deeply unpopular policies could cost incumbent Republican senator Roger Marshall his seat, in the face of a strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a mega-church pastor.
Protesters quickly disrupted the event, before being led out.
US attorney in Texas threatens to hunt down 'crooked local election administrators'
Amid concerns that the Trump administration could use the power of the federal government to intimidate voters from casting ballots against Republicans in the midterm elections, the senior federal prosecutor in south Texas released a menacing social-media video on Monday, promising to hunt down “crooked local election administrators”.
The prosecutor, Aaron Reitz, is a former chief of staff to senator Ted Cruz, who was appointed US attorney for the southern district of Texas by a panel of federal judges, bypassing the usual Senate confirmation process.
Far from presenting himself as a non-partisan official, Reitz ran unsuccessfully for Texas attorney general this year, finishing fourth in the Republican primary despite promising voters he would use that office “to destroy the left”.
In the video statement released on Monday, Reitz warns that he is on the look out for “crooked local election administrators.”
“They have a duty to prevent illegal voting, and I’m here to make sure they do their job,” Reitz says. “And it means no fraud, accurate voter roles, honest paperwork, secure ballots, and lawful procedures are essential to a fraud-free election.”
“So, let me be clear: if you violate federal election law, I will hunt you down and prosecute you,” Reitz warns.
“Election day is Tuesday, November 3rd,” he concludes. “We’ll see you out at the polls.”
Our colleague David Smith reports from Park City, Kansas, where Donald Trump is scheduled to address a Republican campaign rally, that the president’s false claim that rioting in France is driven by immigrants preceded him.
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally has kicked off with something unusual: riots in France.
With supporters still filing into a 5,000-seat multi-purpose arena in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities. It included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.
That matches current Republican talking points, which seized on the unruly protests to demonise multiculturalism and defend “America first” nationalism ahead of the midterm elections.
As he set off for Kansas, Trump told reporters at the White House that he had warned French president Emmanuel Macron he was “making a big mistake”. Trump said: “The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal … We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
The official White House X account posted on Monday. “If you import the third world, you become the third world.” Vice-president JD Vance and an array of Republican politicians have lined up to make the same argument.
House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS – just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
Trump is in Kansas to rally for Republican Roger Marshall, facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, who has outraised him by a big margin. No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932.
A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.
Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.
Trump's claim 'a million' Ukrainians have been killed contradicted by evidence
Before we move on from Donald Trump’s latest attempt to blame Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the death of “a million” Ukrainians since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, it is worth pausing for a moment to explain that this number, which Trump has been repeating for two years, is false.
While the exact death toll is not known, a study published in July by the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, estimated that “Ukrainian forces have suffered somewhere between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties (killed, wounded, and missing) and between 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities between February 2022 and June 2026.”
The same study concluded that the Russian military “has suffered 1.4 million battlefield casualties and as many as 450,000 deaths since its February 2022 full-scale invasion”.
Despite the evidence, Trump has been wildly inflating the Ukrainian death toll in public comments for two years. On the campaign trail in October 2024, Trump claimed that there were “millions of dead people” as a result of the war in Ukraine at that time.
Four months later, after he returned to the Oval Office, Trump told a national prayer breakfast in Washington that there were “probably 800,000 Russians; 600,000 – 700,000 Ukrainians, young people, just laying on a battlefield dead”.
Two months after that, when Trump was asked to comment on Russia’s Palm Sunday attack on Ukraine, Trump said “This country would’ve never allowed that war to have started if I were president. That war is a shame. Millions of people are dead”.
Last week, Trump attacked Zelenskyy for resisting the Russian invasion, saying: “You’ve lost 30% of your country and you’ve had over a million people killed.”
In August of this year, the United Nations reported that more civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine in July than in any month since March 2022.
Overall, since 24 February 2022, the UN said it has verified that at least 16,874 civilians killed have been killed in Ukraine, including 820 children, and 51,273 injured, including 3,126 children.”
Vance speech disrupted by protester shouting 'release the Epstein files'; he replies with a racist joke
A protester disrupted a speech by JD Vance, the US vice-president, in North Carolina on Monday, shouting “Release the Epstein files! God bless our children!” before being led away.
The protester, who was positioned directly behind Vance during a midterm campaign rally in support of Republican candidates, was seen on a live video stream standing up and shouting about 10 minutes into the vice-president’s speech.
As the man was led away the crowd booed the interruption, and chanted “U!S!A!”
Vance then attempted to joke that the man, a person of color who spoke with an American accent, must be an undocumented immigrant.
“Ladies and gentlemen, I’m going to have to amend something I said earlier. I said that we have had zero illegal border crossings in the United States of America,” Vance said to laughter from the crowd. “But one isn’t bad, right?”
New Reuters poll shows Trump's approval rating dropping to a record low
A new poll by Reuters shows that only 31% of Americans approve of Donald Trump’s performance in office, a percentage point lower than the survey from two weeks ago and a record low for the president.
It comes as Trump embarks on another campaign sprint to help beleaguered Republicans in competitive midterm races.
When asked which party they would vote for if the elections were held today, 47% of registered voters in the nationwide poll picked Democrats, while 35% chose Republicans.
'It's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine': Trump slams Zelenskyy and defends lifting Russian sanctions
Trump again rebuked the idea that his move to waive sanctions for Russia last week was ultimately to hand Moscow a win.
“I’m supporting stopping the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn’t want to stop it, but I want to see people not die.”
In response to Zelenskyy saying that the US president is on the “wrong side of history”, Trump snapped back.
“If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago, and he’d have a million people living from his side,” Trump said. “I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine …. Very little land has moved, but a million people, a tremendous number of people, are dead.”
Ahead of leaving for a campaign rally in Wichita, Kansas, Donald Trump again claimed – without evidence – that the riots throughout France were due to mass migration.
“I told Emmanuel [Macron], you should close up your borders,” the US president said. “I’ve known him for probably eight or nine years. I told him as soon as I met him, I said, ‘you’re making a big mistake’. We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
Attorneys for Mahmoud Khalil, the former Columbia University student who has become the symbol of the Trump administration’s crusade against pro-Palestinian speech, have petitioned the US supreme court to review his case – the final chapter in a months-long legal saga that could determine countless foreign citizens’ ability to challenge their detention by US immigration authorities in federal court.
Khalil, a US permanent resident who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, was arrested in his Columbia housing in March 2025, the first of several foreign students and scholars the Trump administration targeted over their advocacy for Palestinian rights. He was detained for more than three months in an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Louisiana before a federal judge in New Jersey, where he had been briefly held before ICE moved him, ordered him released while his immigration process proceeds.
“This fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country, it’s really about whether anyone in this country can speak out for Palestinians without being punished for it,” Khalil said during a press conference on Monday.
The US departments of state, justice and homeland security did not respond to requests for comment.
The government has cited an obscure McCarthy-era law to argue that Khalil and the other scholars’ pro-Palestinian expression posed a threat to US foreign policy objectives.
So far, no court has fully weighed in on the constitutionality of the law, with legal arguments instead focused on whether district courts have the authority to order people released from immigration detention while their immigration cases are under way. Khalil’s attorneys and immigrants rights advocates warn that if the supreme court rules the district courts lack such authority, that would effectively result in people the government has detained unconstitutionally to languish in immigration detention with no recourse, potentially for months or years.
The justice department announced the arrest of 28 legal permanent residents in California “who are charged in criminal complaints with federal crimes, including that they fraudulently registered to vote in US elections, electoral contests in which most of them cast illegal and fraudulently obtained ballots”. Non-citizen voting is extremely rare, andthe 28 who have allegedly committed crimes, would be an exceptionally small fraction of the 174 million people who were registered to vote in the 2024 presidential election.The arrests come just days after the administration sued the Golden state, to prevent it from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has allegedly identified as “likely” noncitizens.
New polling also shows that a majority (66%) of Americans believe Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself. Looking at that data from the Washington Post and ABC even further, 34% of Republicans believe Trump is enriching himself – a 12-point jump from last September. More here
Meanwhile, Trump heads to Kansas today to kick off a seven-state campaign blitz this week in parts of the country he carried in 2024, as unexpectedly tight races in GOP strongholds stoke fears of sweeping Democratic gains in next month’s midterms. With 15 days until the 3 November vote, Trump’s rally on the outskirts of Wichita aims to shore up the incumbent Republican senator Roger Marshall, who is locked in a dead heat with his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton. He’ll follow up with rallies in the Carolinas, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan over the next six days.
More US representatives reported todaythat their offices had been sent suspicious letters, after the FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service said they were investigating letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country containing an “unknown substance” last week. On Monday, congressman Suhas Subramanyam, a Virginia Democrat, said his office in Leesburg received an envelope “containing a suspicious substance” and staff were “promptly evacuated”. Similarly, in Maine, Democratic representative Chellie Pingree said that her office also received “a suspicious letter consistent with those received by many other congressional and election offices in recent days”.
In a bipartisan call with GOP Senator Thom Tillis and Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite services “remain degraded” and “disruptions to US intelligence sharing” persist, when it comes to the “early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches”. Last week, the two lawmakers called on the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate Ukraine’s disruptions accessing Starshield – the military version of Starlink’s satellite network built for governments and defense agencies – and in a statement today they said that Zelenskyy reiterated his “willingness to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities as President Trump has proposed, but only if [Vladimir] Putin agrees to the same”.
A man who heckled the Democratic candidate for Senate Abdul El-Sayed and demanded he disavow the Muslim Brotherhood at a Michigan town hall is a former aide to the Republican senator Josh Hawley, according to congressional staff records.
At the event on Saturday, an attender who gave his name only as “Tommy” shouted from the crowd, asking whether El-Sayed would disavow the movement. El-Sayed answered: “Sure, yeah, absolutely,” then turned the question around, asking whether the man assumed he wouldn’t.
Tommy said he had simply not heard El-Sayed reject the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist movements. Under Trump the US has moved to designate certain chapters of the group as foreign terrorist organizations.
Over nearly five minutes at the town hall, El-Sayed pointed to how the question shouted by Tommy carried an implication of “dual loyalty”, comparing it with the doubts once raised about John F Kennedy’s Catholicism, and told the room he was running for the Senate and “happen[s] to be Muslim”.
He then asked Tommy whether he would disavow any attempt to read religious doctrine into American law. Tommy said he would not. El-Sayed answered that it was Tommy who needed to understand the constitution, drawing cheers, and the man left the room.
The questioner has since been identified as Thomas Teepell, whose staff records show he joined Hawley’s office as an intern in 2023 and rose to operations director before leaving in February. He then became political director for Philip Sarnecki’s Kansas gubernatorial campaign. Sarnecki lost the Republican primary on 4 August.
Teepell is the son of the Republican strategist Timmy Teepell, a longtime adviser to Hawley and the former Louisiana governor Bobby Jindal. The Handbasket first reported the identification.
The question echoes a line of attack that Republicans have tried to push against El-Sayed for weeks, including when Rogers raised alleged Brotherhood ties during one of their debates.
Zelenskyy tells lawmakers that Starlink services 'remain degraded'; US intelligence sharing disruptions persist
In a bipartisan call with GOP Senator Thom Tillis and Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite services “remain degraded” and “disruptions to US intelligence sharing” persist, when it comes to the “early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches”.
Last week, the two lawmakers called on the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate Ukraine’s disruptions accessing Starshield – the military version of Starlink’s satellite network built for governments and defense agencies – and in a statement today they said that Zelenskyy reiterated his “willingness to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities as President Trump has proposed, but only if [Vladimir] Putin agrees to the same”.
Zelenskyy’s call with Washington lawmakers comes after he said that Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, as my colleague Andrew Roth reports from Kyiv. On Friday, Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia – a move he claimed was to prevent driving Russia “away from the bargaining table”.

theguardian.com.title: Kumanjayi Little Baby: damning report finds ‘heartbreaking’ child protection failures before five-year-old’s death
theguardian.com.text:
A report on the Northern Territory’s child protection sector has detailed “confronting” and “heartbreaking” failures in the lead-up to the alleged murder of Warlpiri girl Kumanjayi Little Baby.
The five-year-old was found dead in April, five days after she was allegedly abducted from a town camp in Alice Springs.
Police then charged Jefferson Lewis, a 47-year-old man who was not a member of the child’s family or known to her mother, with murder. He has been remanded in custody and is yet to enter a plea.
The minister for children and families, Robyn Cahill, tabled the report in NT parliament on Tuesday.
The NT government commissioned the independent review, conducted by former New South Wales police commissioner Karen Webb and senior public servant Greg Shanahan, in the wake of the child’s death.
The report identified a number of priorities, including strengthening the child protection practice framework and its intersection with domestic and family violence, risk assessments and safety planning – including adequately assessing the suitability of adults to become carers.
Cahill said the report showed a “recurrent pattern” of how police worked alongside the department, which allowed children to be placed in the care of adults without a criminal background check.
She said Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family had been known by the department since her mother was pregnant with her, receiving 14 notifications over six years about the little girl’s exposure to domestic and family violence.
“[There were] serious gaps between what the law required of the department, and how the law was applied,” she told parliament. “Gaps in policy, in process, and most critically, gaps in how risk to children was being assessed.
“Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family was known to the department before she was born. Her mother was assaulted at least twice while she was pregnant with her. When she was 17 weeks old, a safety plan was put in place that relied on adults from the family’s network to keep her safe. The review found no evidence that police or background checks were done on any of them.
“It was later established that one of those adults had a long and violent criminal history. Including five counts of threat-to-kill.
“These were the adults trusted to keep a baby safe. How can something as basic as checking if they are safe to be around children not be standard practice?”
The opposition’s protection spokesperson, Chansey Paech, told Guardian Australia that the report failed to address the “root cause” which led to the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby.
“This report does not actually go to the root cause of Kumanjayi Little Baby’s passing, that an alleged violent perpetrator who was released from prison with no accommodation, no housing, no job, no transport, no money, no rehabilitation or supervision, allegedly killed a child,” he said. “None of that is in the report.
“The main issue and concern we have with it as the opposition, is that this government continues to … see child protection in isolation.”
Paech, who was not given time to speak in parliament, criticised the government decision not to refund Darwin’s largest homeless shelter, YiSSA, which closed last week, leaving hundreds of First Nations families without a place to live.
“The CLP talks about caring about children, well, they are effectively evicting kids with their new three-strikes policy, and they have also closed the YISSA facility,” he said. “So we’ve got kids without homes.
“And they’re deploying territory [Department of] Children and Families staff out to run the new Batchelor site rather than being on child protection matters.”
Cahill said the NT government accepted all 45 recommendations made by the report.
The interim report, released in July, said “the review team have not been able to draw a nexus between the matters referred to DCF [the Department of Children and Families] and the circumstances leading to KLB’s [Kumanjayi Little Baby’s] abduction”.
It said the child’s mother had been the victim of domestic and family violence, but that: “Despite repeated indicators of domestic and family violence, the cumulative impact of the violence and its implications for the child’s safety were not adequately recognised, and protective responses were not pursued in a timely manner.”

theguardian.com.title: Helen Haines loses leg after car allegedly did U-turn and struck her twice in Wangaratta
theguardian.com.text:
The man accused of attacking Helen Haines allegedly made a U-turn before ramming the independent MP twice in an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office, causing her to lose one of her legs.
The member for Indi was airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night.
Surgeons were on Tuesday fighting to save Haines’ other leg, as the 65-year-old remained in a critical condition.
A 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota LandCruiser was arrested at the scene. The alleged attacker has been named as Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, Guardian Australia has confirmed.
Police were expected to interview the suspect in the attack on Tuesday, Acting Supt Ashley Mason said.
Anthony Albanese confirmed authorities believed the attack was deliberate.
“Helen Haines represents the best of our political representatives,” the prime minister said on Tuesday afternoon.
“Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity, totally committed to strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria.”
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said witnesses alleged the driver completed a U-turn before the incident.
“What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time,” he told ABC radio.
“A bystander ran towards the scene, got the driver out of the vehicle and held the driver until police arrived.”
Ricky Jefferies, whose barbershop is next door to Haines’ office, ran from his shop to help after hearing the crash.
“I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do,” he told reporters on Tuesday morning.
Jefferies, who returned to work on Tuesday morning, alleged the driver had a knife on him. “He didn’t pull it out,” he said. “Basically just … took it out of his pocket and threw it away.”
Burke said: “I think every Australian is grateful for those moments when a hero like this runs towards the most dangerous place.”
The home affairs minister said the nation’s security agencies and police will be working through what more could have been done to prevent the alleged attack and to help keep others safe.
On Monday, Burke reported that there had been 1,067 reports of harassment or threats against high office holders in Australia in the last financial year, an increase from 951 the year before.
“We already knew that we needed to do more to be able to keep people in public office safe and we have been,” he said.
“While we don’t make public the dollar figures and the exact provision of security for obvious reasons … we had a very significant uplift in the budget.
“There is a direct line between the temperature of debate and things willing people will say, and then when people are willing to take action.”
Albanese has been joined by leaders and parliamentarians from across the country in calling for a calming of political discourse.
The mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant, expressed gratitude to Jefferies for stepping in to stop the man.
“I spoke to the barber this morning and he just shrugged his shoulders. He seemed to just take it in his stride. This was something that he had to do and he did it,” she said.
“He was extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took yesterday … he did an amazing job.”
Wangaratta, the rural city in which the incident occurred, is a tight-knit community in north-east Victoria. At the last census it had a population of about 20,000 people, while the broader local government area had just under 30,000.
Haines was elected to federal parliament in 2019 and has been key to the establishment of the National Anti-Corruption Commission, as well as campaigning for rural health services, telecommunications access and pushing back on misuse of taxpayer funds, or pork barrelling.

theguardian.com.title: ‘I don’t want to be known as a hero’: barber who rushed to help Helen Haines praised by PM
theguardian.com.text:
The Australian prime minister has hailed him a hero for rushing out of his shop to help independent MP Helen Haines after she was allegedly run down in a deliberate attack – but barber Ricky Jefferies says he had “no choice” but to intervene.
Standing on Tuesday morning outside his shop, which is right next to Haines’ electorate office in Wangaratta, Jefferies was almost shy about the whole thing.
“I don’t want to be known as a hero,” the regional Victorian barber repeatedly told the large media pack that surrounded him.
Jefferies spoke about how he had just finished cutting a young family’s hair when a car hit Haines at about 4pm on Monday. When he heard the loud crash, he ran to help.
“A lot of people a lot of people got involved immediately, and they didn’t even check the danger,” he said. “They just ran to help. The driver was still in the car, the car was still on, and … one man sat in front of the moving car,” he said.
“I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do.”
Haines was allegedly rammed twice on Murphy Street in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon, and remains in a critical but stable condition on Tuesday morning. The prime minister alleged it was an attack and it “wasn’t an accident”. Haines’ alleged attacker, who was arrested at the scene, has been named as 43-year-old Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, Guardian Australia has confirmed.
Witnesses have described the driver as doing a U-turn before allegedly ramming Haines against a vehicle, then reversing before doing it a second time, the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said on Tuesday morning.
Jefferies said after getting the driver out of the car, he held the man down. He said he told him he couldn’t leave but that the man would be alright, in an attempt to calm him while others helped Haines.
He also alleged the man had a knife on him.
“He did have a knife. He didn’t pull it out. Basically just … took it out of his pocket and threw it away,” he alleged.
Jefferies, who was back at work cutting hair at 7am on Tuesday, said he didn’t stop to think about the danger, only that his wife might be upset if he got hurt.
“[I just thought] my wife will be disappointed if I’m injured,” he said. “My family is everything, and my community is second to that.
“I was just trying to not get injured and not let anyone else be injured after the initial incident.”
Jefferies actions have been widely commended on Tuesday, including by Albanese, Burke and the mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant.
“It’s got to be said here that at this dark and terrible time, an element of light is the fact that a good Samaritan, someone rushed to Helen’s defence in Wangaratta … and that person is a hero today,” Albanese told the Today Show.
“And I just think that he deserves enormous praise and thanks for his intervention, which could have prevented even further infliction of damage, which was aimed at Helen.”
Grant said she had spoken to the barber on Tuesday morning, saying he was taking it in his stride.
“He was extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took yesterday … he did an amazing job.”
Jefferies brushed the accolades aside, saying he doesn’t want to be seen as a hero and that – like all of the community – he is praying Haines recovers quickly.
“No one’s job should put them at risk. I can tell you from my own personal dealings that she is a genuine, kind person,” he said.
“I don’t think I’m the hero, I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way.”

theguardian.com.title: Milan luxury shops close as Italy prepares to deploy troops in the city after days of protests
theguardian.com.text:
Italy’s government will dispatch 500 army troops to “defend Milan” after two days of unrest that saw demonstrators clash with police, loot shops and vandalise property, deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday.
The deployment is expected to be included in a package of security measures to be approved at a cabinet meeting expected on Tuesday, and comes as shops in central Milan closed early and boarded up their windows, fearing a fresh outbreak of violence in Italy’s financial capital.
“From words to action: 500 more troops to defend Milan,” Salvini, head of the co-ruling right-wing League party, wrote on social media.
Most stores in Milan’s Via Montenapoleone luxury shopping district, home to brands including Chanel, Tiffany and Dior, had removed merchandise from their windows as a precaution, while police patrolled the street and a handful of tourists looked on.
Several hundred hooded protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze and looted shops in the city centre over the weekend after an initially peaceful demonstration on Saturday over poor public services and rising costs.
Among the stores ransacked were sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed. Clothing brands Levi’s and Under Armour, as well as Decathlon, covered their shop windows with cardboard and wooden panels.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs on Monday to discuss the situation.
“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X.
As part of the planned crackdown, the Corriere della Sera newspaper said Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, while bringing forward some provisions contained in an existing security bill currently being examined by parliament.
Italian police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of those taken to police stations, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.
The unrest followed clashes on Saturday in other northern cities including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday.
The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.

theguardian.com.title: Colorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report finds
theguardian.com.text:
Colorado officials have tracked herds of elk, bears, pronghorn and even northern leopard frogs ambling across its new wildlife overpass. According to a newly released report, the overpass, which acts as a bridge over a busy stretch of interstate, has helped cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago.
The overpass is the centerpiece of a larger system built by the state to assist wildlife crossing the highway, which also includes miles of 8-ft tall fencing and five large wildlife underpasses.
“One of the most heartwarming moments for me was when [Colorado department of transportation] sent me a picture of an elk mama taking her calf under [Interstate-25],” Brandon Marette, a wildlife biologist for Colorado parks and wildlife, told CBS News. “All came to fruition in that one moment. That elk with her calf was just standing there in safety.”
The Colorado department of transportation said before the overpass system was built, there was an average of one wildlife-vehicle crash a day in this corridor.
Such wildlife crossings are popping up across the country as a way to protect wildlife habitat and reduce collisions, which can result in injuries and deaths in humans and animals. Research has shown that overpass systems are successful in “nearly eliminating” these accidents and that such infrastructure buildouts often “pay for themselves” by preventing costly crashes.
